#5628. Housing Market Feels the Chill as Buyers Pull Back—but Sellers Are Not Panicking Yet

The national housing market is feeling the chill as high borrowing costs are forcing frustrated buyers to throw in the towel, yet sellers are largely digging in to wait out the slump.

Two key metrics—price cuts and delistings—tell the story of American home sellers' resilience in the face of adversity this fall.

Across the U.S., about 4.4% of active listings were pulled off the market in October, down from 4.6% a year ago, according to the latest Realtor.com® monthly housing market trends report released on Wednesday.

On a monthly basis, the delisting rate has ticked up slightly from 4% in September, in line with typical seasonal trends, but no more than that, even with mortgage rates well exceeding 7% and buyer demand waning.

According to Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel, delistings matter because they act as a canary in the coal mine. A jump in the delistings rate could be a sign of a housing market in distress.

However, the October findings show that sellers are not ready to take their ball and go home yet.

"Job relocations, family circumstances, and financial challenges are among the top reasons I am seeing sellers stay on the market rather than withdraw and wait until spring," Josh Stimpson, a real estate agent at The Realtive Group of Reliant Realty in Nashville, TN, tells Realtor.com. "The rising cost of living is also a major factor, prompting many sellers to seek more affordable housing."

The other key data point used to assess the strength of the U.S. housing market is price cuts.

According to the latest housing market data, much like with delistings, there has not been a dramatic change up or down in the share of listings offering discounts, although it remained elevated.

For the fourth consecutive month, more than 1 in 5 active listings (20.5%) saw a price cut, marking the highest October reading since 2022 and the second highest this year, trailing only September, which set a four-year record.

However, Krimmel points out that the national price cut rate actually retreated 0.3 percentage points month over month, snapping a nine-month streak of monthly gains. Annually, the share of active listings with price cuts ticked up by just 0.2 percentage points.

Sellers "are getting used to not everything selling quickly," Learka Bosnak, an agent with of Heather & Learka Team at Douglas Elliman in Beverly Hills, CA, tells Realtor.com. "They aren’t seeing compelling evidence that a slightly lower price will lead to a quick sale. Plus, they aren't feeling a lot of pressure monthly because so many have low-interest-rate mortgages."

Taken together, the October delisting and price cut readouts lead to one conclusion concerning the present state of the market.

"Right now, it looks more like a seller pause than an exodus," says Krimmel. "Sellers are disengaging rather than showing signs of distress."

Regionally, price reductions remained least common in the systemically undersupplied Northeast (16.8% of listings) and most common in the West (21.9%), with the Midwest and South falling in between at 21% each.

Across the 50 largest metro markets, 12 saw price cuts on a quarter or more of the listings, unchanged from September. Thirty-four of the metros are running above their year-ago cut rate, down from 36 in September.

At the local level, price discounts in October were most common in Indianapolis (31.8%), Denver (31.3%), and Portland, OR (31.1%).

While the delisting and price cut numbers stop short of signaling a panic among sellers, October trends do point to a noticeable pullback.

New listings—a measure of homeowners putting their properties on the market—dropped 9.5% from September and 7.5% from a year ago, marking the steepest decline in more than three years.

"Sellers know this is a poor time to list, and you do not list into weak demand unless you need to," notes Krimmel.

At the same time, pending sales plunged 10.5% year over year—the biggest annual drop since October 2023.

However, active listings jumped 7.4% year over year, topping 1.18 million homes for sale—the fourth consecutive month of accelerated growth. This reflects properties piling up on the market as buyers see their purchasing power diminished by surging 30-year mortgage rates, which averaged 7.33% in October.

For context, that is a staggering 107 basis points above October 2025 levels and 53 basis points higher than at the start of September.

"Elevated interest rates and ongoing affordability challenges have caused many buyers to pause, and the midterm election may be adding to that hesitation," notes Stimpson. "As a result, showing activity has declined and days on market are rising, particularly in Nashville and the surrounding areas."

However, patient buyers willing to stick it out can still find attractive deals and see their negotiating position strengthened.

"Buyers can often retain their inspection, appraisal, and financing contingencies while also requesting additional repairs, a longer closing period, or a home warranty," says Stimpson. "Properties with extended market exposure may offer even greater leverage, including opportunities to negotiate a lower purchase price or secure seller concessions."

Looking ahead to late fall and winter, the Nashville agent says there are some encouraging signs on the horizon, including gradually easing mortgage rates, closings holding steady in Middle Tennessee, and premium listings continuing to attract multiple offers.

Yet, both Stimpson and Bosnak agree that what the market sorely lacks is a sense of certainty.

"No one is sure what the market or the world will look like in a year, so it doesn’t feel weird to lean into that wait-and-see part of human nature," says the Beverly Hills agent.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5627. Realtors Predict These Nine Cities Will Be Unaffordable by 2027

Vibrant-Colored neon lights on a busy night at the bars and honky-tonks in the country music center, Broadway, the tourism center of Downtown Nashville, Tennessee

(TNS)–Home prices are climbing across the nation and some markets are hotter than others. According to a new report from Finance Buzz, nine U.S. cities are likely to become unaffordable by 2027, due to an influx of out-of-town buyers and tight inventory.

Here’s a look at the popular locales where housing costs are outpacing local incomes, as per Finance Buzz’s reporting:

Many areas in northern New Jersey are popular for people relocating out of New York City.

According to Daniel Smith, team lead at Smith Realty Team, homes in Montclair are expected to stay in high demand and continue commanding higher home prices.

“Retirees and pre-retirees are also targeting these towns because of their vibrant downtowns, access to health care, and cultural amenities, which makes competition even stronger,” he said.

Nashville attracted numerous new residents during the pandemic years, offering a lively city experience alongside lower taxes and a more affordable cost of living.

While home prices have come down slightly over the past year, the median sale price is currently $464,983 and real estate experts don’t expect a reduction any time soon.

Realtor Carla Gericke, with Porcupine Real Estate, said that “no income tax, easy access to Boston, and that elusive small-town feel with real community bones” is causing Nashua’s popularity to spike.

“Nashua’s median home price has soared to the $500,000 to $550,000 range, and demand keeps outpacing supply,” she said.

Gericke urged retirees looking to buy in the state to act quickly or venture outside the bigger cities to find better deals.

Arizona has long been a top destination for retirees hoping to escape the cold. Fred Loguidice, a real estate expert and founder of several home-buying companies in the area, said that home demand is outpacing supply, making it a market that is likely to stay competitive in the future.

“In markets like Phoenix, fewer homes are being built while demand persists, so prices consistently escalate,” he said.

Real estate expert Fred Loguidice also highlighted demand for Northeast hubs like the Buffalo metro area. While Zillow put the median home price at a moderate $261,300, home values in the area have been increasing.

“That momentum is a hard habit to break,” he said, noting its affordability and surging job opportunities make it a top choice for relocation for people in the region and beyond.

Athens is about 60 miles northeast of Atlanta and attracts many buyers and visitors alike with its lively college town atmosphere, excellent dining scene, and more.

While Georgia is often cited as a top spot to retire, thanks to the weather and lower cost of living, real estate trends indicate that home prices will continue to climb throughout the next year or so. Prices have gone up over the past year, with the median currently sitting at $353,333.

Florida boasts many affordable cities and tax incentives for retirees, but those considering Tampa may want to reassess.

Omer Reiner, realtor and president of Florida Cash Home Buyers, said home prices in the city are already high, and rising insurance costs are putting many popular areas out of reach.

“This is especially true for those nearing or at retirement, as higher costs of living when you are on any type of fixed income means you are spending more for less,” he said.

Iowa isn’t particularly known for its excessive home prices, but demand has been on the rise in Des Moines, according to real estate investor Jacob Naig, particularly for homes popular with retirees.

“Single-family homes, as well as small multi-family properties and single-level ranch-style homes that are particularly desirable to aging buyers, have seen a substantial rise in demand,” he said.

Many cities in the Pacific Northwest have seen rapidly rising home prices, and Ontario, which sits on the border of Oregon and Idaho, is no different. With stunning desert views, mountain ranges, and more, it’s a haven for outdoorsy types.

But recent real estate trends indicated it could be unaffordable in the coming years. Average home prices have risen steadily over the past year and currently sit at $307,769.

#5626. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.

#5625. EXCLUSIVE: Food Network Star Alex Guarnaschelli Reveals Her Secrets To Turning Any Home Into a Holiday Entertaining Hub

Turning your home into a welcoming holiday gathering spot doesn’t have to mean buying new decorations or finding room for a formal dining setup.

For Alex Guarnaschelli, a few thoughtful touches—and some planning before the doorbell rings—can help hosts make the most of their space and enjoy the celebration themselves.

In an exclusive interview with Realtor.com®, the celebrity chef shared her advice for entertaining on a budget, organizing a busy kitchen, and keeping guests comfortable in smaller homes.

“I always think a welcoming home is about the little details, not how much money you spend," she said.Her first suggestion is to adjust the lighting before guests arrive.

"A few candles or lamps instead of bright overhead lighting can completely change the feeling of a room," she explained.

When it comes to decorations, Guarnaschelli recommends looking for items that can serve another purpose once the party ends.

“Second, bring something natural into the space," she said. "I love the idea of filling a bowl with beautiful oranges, pomegranates, or even fresh herbs from the grocery store. They're inexpensive, they look festive, and you can actually use them afterward.”

Making guests comfortable from the moment they enter is another priority.

“And third, think about what your guests experience when they arrive. Have a place for coats and bags, put on some music, and make sure there's something to eat or drink right away,” she advised.

“You don't need a house that looks like a magazine. You just want people to walk in and feel like they're in the right place.”

That thoughtful approach extends to the kitchen, where Guarnaschelli starts by considering how each dish fits into the cooking schedule.

“I like to think of my kitchen almost like a restaurant kitchen before service. Everything should have a purpose and a place,” she explained. “I start by looking at what I'm making and working backward. What needs the oven? What needs the stove? What can stay in the refrigerator until the last minute? You don't want three dishes competing for the same burner when everyone's ready to eat.”

She also recommends deciding how food will be presented before it is ready to leave the kitchen.

“I also pull out the serving dishes ahead of time and decide what goes where. Sometimes I'll even put a little note in each platter so I don't have to think about it later. And clear your counters!” she added.

Choosing equipment that handles several tasks can also help keep the cooking area manageable.

Guarnaschelli points to a piece from her new HSN collection as an example.

“That's also why I love versatile tools, like the sauté pan from my new HSN collection. You can use it for everything from searing chicken to sautéing vegetables or making a quick sauce, without having to pull out a different pan for every dish,” she says. “A little organization and the right tools can make the whole evening feel easier.”

For those entertaining in an apartment or smaller home, Guarnaschelli suggests spreading refreshments across different areas to prevent guests from gathering around the stove.

“The trick to entertaining in a small space is to give people a reason to spread out. If you put the drinks, appetizers, and main course all next to the stove, you're going to end up with a crowd exactly where you’re cooking!”

A side table can become a drink station, while appetizers can encourage guests to mingle elsewhere.

“I would put drinks in the living room, maybe on a bar cart or even a cleared-off side table, and keep a few appetizers somewhere else. A cheese board is great because people can help themselves without needing you to do anything,” she explained.

Guarnaschelli also recommends making use of vertical space when arranging the food.

“I also love using different heights when setting out food. A cake stand or a raised platter can give you more room without taking over the entire table," she added.

And hosts needn’t feel pressured to create a traditional seated dinner.

“Don't feel like everyone needs a formal seat at the same time. Sometimes a more relaxed, casual setup makes for the best party," the chef noted.

Preparing ahead can further reduce the number of tasks competing for a host’s attention. For Guarnaschelli, the day before a gathering is an opportunity to work through smaller jobs.

“The day before a party is when I like to tackle all the little jobs that have a way of piling up. Wash your herbs, measure out ingredients, make your salad dressing, and get your serving dishes ready.”

She also uses equipment from her collection to help with ingredient preparation.

“This is also where a tool like the cordless chopper from my new HSN collection really comes in handy," she added. "You can get through chopping onions, herbs, and other ingredients for your recipes without spending the entire afternoon doing prep work.”

Depending on the menu, some cooking can be completed ahead of time, too.

“You can even prepare things like a soup or a braised dish that will taste better the next day because the flavors have had time to come together," the food guru revealed.

Before filling the kitchen with prepared dishes, however, Guarnaschelli recommended checking that there is somewhere to store them.

“I also like to make sure the refrigerator has enough room for everything before I start cooking. That's one of those things nobody thinks about until they're trying to squeeze a giant platter onto a shelf that's already full.”

On the day of the gathering, she focuses on dishes that need to be finished close to serving.

“For the day of, save the things that really need your attention, like roasting meat, crisping up potatoes, or finishing vegetables. Anything that needs to be hot and fresh should get that last bit of care," the chef said.

Her final suggestion is to leave enough time to welcome guests without simultaneously scrambling to finish the meal.

“Give yourself a little buffer before guests arrive," she said. "You don't want to be pulling something out of the oven with one hand while answering the door with the other.”

#5624. IBM puts agentic workloads at the heart of its AI operating model

Agentic workloads present a new operating challenge for enterprises putting artificial intelligence into production. As autonomous systems take on ongoing responsibilities, organizations must support decisions and actions across their data, applications and infrastructure.

IBM Corp.’s approach draws on the experiences of clients scaling AI across their organizations. That work helped identify the requirements underpinning its AI operating model, according to Ritika Gunnar (pictured), chief performance marketing officer of IBM.

“As you’re more successful in using AI, especially as AI is taking action, you now have workloads that are continuously being utilized,” she said. “You are incented to be always on because those agents are always taking action for you.”

Gunnar spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier for IBM’s AI Operating Model interview series in an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed enterprise integration, data governance, human oversight and evaluating AI against business outcomes in preparation for IBM TechXchange 2026. (* Disclosure below.)

IBM’s AI operating model brings together four components that enterprises may already obtain from different providers. Applying them means accounting for established applications and business processes alongside emerging AI systems, Gunnar explained.

“You need to be able to integrate with your existing systems,” she said. “People aren’t going to run away from their SAP systems that exist, from their Salesforce systems that exist. What does it mean to integrate with those and have workloads that are representative of your past and your future together?”

The components have distinct roles: Data supplies current enterprise knowledge, workloads encompass applications and workflows, automation supports oversight and optimization, and hybrid cloud accommodates distributed operations. Their effectiveness depends on how they function together across agentic workloads, according to Gunnar.

“If you have your data and that data is feeding your systems, but you’re not really taking care of automation in a way where you have complete observability of all of your workloads with that AI infused, then you’re not necessarily having an optimal way of picking the right model or picking the right agents for those kinds of workloads,” she said.

The information supporting an agent’s decision may span operational systems, edge devices and context generated by other agents. Providing governed context requires enterprises to consider both the completeness of that information and how permissions travel with it, Gunnar explained.

“Our belief is if you can take data and if you can shift left a lot of the governance — a lot of the who has the right access to the right data at the right time — it becomes important because you flow that data in real time with the context and provenance of who actually has ownership of that data,” she said. “Therefore, the agents make much better decisions.”

Enterprises also depend on knowledge employees develop through experience rather than explicitly recording it in their systems. Prompts and other context can help convey that judgment, but capturing it remains an ongoing challenge, Gunnar pointed out.

“When you think about workloads today … there is a lot of it that will be autonomous in nature,” she said. “But in most cases, if you’re talking about your essential systems, you do have humans in the loop to be able to bring some of that tacit knowledge in place where the AI has not yet matured to be able to even get there.”

Agent activity generates logs of decisions and actions, while prompts record the instructions supplied to those systems. Together, that information supports an ongoing feedback loop between enterprise data and AI workloads, Gunnar explained.

“You can actually have multiple different permutations of that agent making a decision and having another set of eval loops actually doing an evaluation of, ‘Did that agent actually make the decisions?’” she said. “Would there have been a more performant way, a more accurate way, a more cost-effective way to be able to do that?”

Performance encompasses accuracy, timeliness and cost, with the intended business result guiding how those measures are assessed. Putting AI into production therefore requires organizations to examine the work itself alongside the technology supporting it, according to Gunnar.

“Make sure that you have all of these elements and that you’re really thinking about the outcomes, and you’re willing to start with what it means to take a look at the business process transformation,” she said. “That’s really where it’s at.”

#5623. Don't Let the Fear of a Buyer Backing Out Scare You Away from Selling

There’s nothing quite like the excitement of getting an offer on your house. You’re one step closer to moving on to what’s next. But what happens if that buyer backs out or ghosts you before closing?

If you’ve been seeing headlines about more home sales falling through lately, that possibility may be keeping you up at night. And it’s true. According to Redfin and Cotality, canceled contracts have been on the rise.

But here’s what those headlines don’t always tell you…

Most sales still go through. Only 10-15% hit this snag. And even so, there are things you can do to help keep your sale from becoming one of them.

The key is knowing what tends to scare buyers away and getting ahead of those issues before they have a chance to derail your move.

Today’s buyers are being more cautious. Mortgage rates are stretching budgets, and with more homes to choose from, buyers have more freedom to walk away if something doesn’t feel right. As Redfin explains:

“That gives house hunters more options and makes them more likely to walk away if an inspection uncovers problems, an appraisal comes in low or the seller doesn’t agree to concessions.”

That’s why an accepted offer isn’t always a guaranteed sale. But it doesn’t mean you should be afraid to put your house on the market, either.

It just means getting ahead of potential problems matters more than ever.

A Redfin survey asked real estate agents why some buyers are backing out. And their answers give you a short of cheatsheet into what could go sideways and how you can get ahead of those headaches (see graph below):

This is the big one. And the good news? It’s also one of the areas where you can be the most proactive.

One simple way to head this off is by getting a pre-listing inspection before your house goes on the market. That way, if something needs attention, you can decide whether to fix it upfront (before you sell), adjust your price, or disclose it and come in already prepared for what’s likely to pop up in negotiations. It’s a lot better to find the skeletons in the closet before a buyer does.

Even buyers who are pre-approved can run into financing issues before closing. And with mortgage rates putting extra pressure on affordability, some buyers are finding it harder to make the numbers work.

While you can’t control whether a buyer’s loan goes through, you can work with your agent to look closely at their financing before accepting an offer. And if affordability is the concern, your agent can help you explore whether incentives like closing cost credits or a mortgage-rate buydown could make a difference.

Sometimes, your buyer needs to sell their house before they can buy yours. And if their sale falls through, yours could be affected too.

That’s why it’s important to understand any home-sale contingencies before accepting an offer. Your agent can help you look at where the buyer is in their own selling process and what protections you may want in place.

The goal isn’t to eliminate every possible risk. It’s to avoid being caught off guard by the ones you can plan for.

Just remember when you read headlines about canceled deals, they don’t give you the full picture. Most home sales still make it to closing.

And if a sale does fall through, that doesn’t automatically mean your house won’t sell. Sometimes a buyer’s circumstances change. Sometimes an issue comes up that can be addressed before the next offer.

What matters is having an agent who knows how to spot potential problems early, help you navigate negotiations, and keep your sale moving forward.

Because while you can’t control every twist and turn, you can control how prepared you are.

There's no need to let the fear of a buyer backing out hold you back. While no sale comes with guarantees, a little preparation upfront can go a long way toward making the whole process smoother.If you're ready to make a move, talk to a local agent about whether a pre-listing inspection makes sense for you.

#5622. This 83-Acre Blue Ridge Mountain Wedding Estate Is Heading to Auction With No Reserve

Imagine hosting a wedding or lavish event for 150 friends and family right on your very own Blue Ridge Mountain farm.

That could become a reality as an 83.56-acre property with a 5,000-square-foot event barn in Franklin, NC, heads to auction with no reserve on Nov. 7.

Created in 2010, Tessentee Farm has multiple structures, including an eight-bedroom primary residence, three two-bedroom guest cabins, and plenty of space to entertain.

"It has a nice big spread of land, so the duality of it also being an income-generating asset is pretty impressive," says Trayor Lesnock, founder and president of Platinum Luxury Auctions, who will host the auction. The listing is held by Isaiah Thomas Johns of Mountain Pro Real Estate Professionals.

The property last changed hands for $2,500,000 in 2013 and had hit the market for $6.9 million in November 2025.

“You have this large house with all the bells and whistles where you could live, an event barn, and three separate cabins where you could host events,” Lesnock says. “There is a good record of the farm being used for weddings and events.”

The luxury event barn, which can be heated and cooled, has hosted everything from destination weddings and rehearsal dinners to milestone celebrations and corporate retreats.

“We have had large families from the Blue Ridge Mountain region look at it and are wanting to use it for multigenerational living,” he notes. “About 50% were looking to use it as a private property and the other 50% were looking at it for the income generation.”

The primary residence has arched doorways, built-ins, French doors, a spacious dining room, a chef's kitchen with a breakfast bar, and a primary suite with a fireplace, soaking tub, and walk-in shower.

Covered terraces overlook the pool, which has a water slide and a swim-up bar, as well as an outdoor kitchen and a hot tub.

“It will probably go to someone who wants to use it privately,” Lesnock adds. “There are no outright restrictions, so you could develop it further.”

The rustic barn has exposed beams, wood-paneled walls, string lighting, and an open field ideal for photos. A ceremony could be held in the pasture, followed by cocktails under the stars, and dinner and dancing inside the barn, with guests retreating to cabins for an overnight stay.

Lesnock says the countryside setting could lend itself to an equestrian estate.

“You could make it more of a farm and add an arena if you wanted,” he says. “Franklin is not an area that pops up on a lot of people’s maps, but it’s in the southern foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Asheville is only an hour away. There is also a creek that borders the property that is excellent for trout fishing.”

#5621. Credit Scoring Is Changing: 3 Things Homebuyers Should Know

Quick, what credit score do you need to buy a home? If a number pops into your head, there’s a pretty good chance it’s wrong. And the right answer is getting harder to pin down, because the way credit scores are determined and delivered is changing – for the better.

Here’s what you need to know in today’s changing credit climate.

Fannie Mae has been tracking consumer perceptions about mortgage requirements since 2015 and found that consumers consistently overestimated the minimum credit score lenders required to qualify for a mortgage. As recently as 2023, the average guess was 652.

In reality, the long-standing benchmark for loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is lower, at 620, and today even that isn’t a hard rule for every mortgage they back.

Like the Fannie Mae research, a recent survey from Veterans United found consumers continue to overestimate what it takes to qualify for a home loan:

The takeaway? Guessing wrong can cost you.

A renter who assumes their score is too low and they can’t qualify for a mortgage may never take steps to find out for sure.

For decades, the mortgage industry relied on one set of scores – Classic FICO. Thanks to a push to promote competition, make credit scoring more inclusive, and help more Americans become homeowners, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the use of new credit score models such as FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0.

A different model can mean a different number for the same person. VantageScore says its model can score about 33 million adults that the Classic FICO’s model can’t. So the score you saw on an app last month may not be the one your lender pulls.

Remember: the models may be new, but the basics haven’t changed.

Your credit score is important – no matter how it’s measured. Following the same basic rules will benefit your profile in the old and new score models:

Because while credit models may change, the general advice for you to improve your score doesn’t. Financial awareness and consistency mixed with a little willpower can go a long way.

Don't make credit or homebuying decisions from a chart, an app, or a friend's advice. #5620. Mortgage Rates Continue To Fall, but Purchase Applications Retreat

Mortgage applications fell last week, even as interest rates on home loans declined for the third week in a row, giving buyers some relief.

For the week ending Oct. 30 the Mortgage Bankers Association's Market Composite Index—a measure of total mortgage loan application volume—decreased 1.2% on a seasonally adjusted basis from one week earlier.

The Purchase Index, which measures the volume of mortgage applications to purchase a single-family home, decreased 2% from one week earlier after seasonal adjustment. Purchase applications were down 19% from a year ago.

According to MBA calculations, the average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed mortgages with conforming loan balances is 7.3%, a slight decrease from last week's rate of 7.37%. Rates averaged 6.17% a year ago.

Mortgage rates dropped to 7.24% last week from 7.32% the week before, according to a separate survey from Freddie Mac.

"Mortgage rates drifted down to their lowest level since September 2026 last week in the wake of the Federal Reserve’s decision to hold on additional rate hikes at its October meeting,” said Mike Fratantoni, MBA’s SVP and Chief Economist. “While the 30-year rate declined to 7.3%, activity is still quite slow, with purchase application volume down for the week and refinance volume effectively flat at a very low level."

As we have highlighted in recent weeks, more borrowers are choosing ARMs in this environment to lower their initial payments, with the ARM share at its highest level since September 2025.”

That's pushed more borrowers to pursue riskier adjustable-rate mortgages. According to Fratantoni, the share of ARM applications is at its highest level since September 2025.

ARM rates are nearly a full percentage point lower than the 30-year fixed mortgage rate, and the share of ARM applications increased week over week from 11.3% to 11.4%.

The share of FHA loan applications decreased to 16% from 16.6% the prior week. The VA share of total applications increased to 11.2% from 11% the prior week. And the USDA share of total applications increased to 0.6% from 0.5% the week prior.

Meanwhile, the refinance share of mortgage activity increased to 39.8% from 38.9% the previous week. Though the overall refinance index increased .1% from the previous week, it was 60% lower than the same week one year ago, as homeowners remain locked into their lower interest rates.

While Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee opted not to raise rates again last week, rate watchers are looking ahead to December when the Fed meets again to decide on rates.

CME Group's FedWatch has the likelihood of an additional rate hike at just under 80%.

With Democrats wresting control of the House and Senate on Tuesday, voters will be watching to see what economic policies are instituted to help make housing more affordable.

"Many Democrat campaigns tapped into voter dissatisfaction with the economy, a winning strategy in 2026. Democrats have a clear mandate to focus on pocketbook issues, but whether they can translate that into a legislative agenda that delivers on that mandate remains to be seen," said Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel.

"Legislative options are likely to be limited in a divided Washington where a Democratic House and Senate will either need to work with the Republican White House or find enough Republican legislative support to override a likely veto," he added.

Mortgage rates are calculated based on various factors in the economy, and the length of your loan and credit score will also factor into the mortgage rate you qualify for.

The 30-year mortgage rate is tied to the yield of the 10-year Treasury note, because most 30-year mortgages are either paid off or refinanced in roughly eight to 11 years.

That makes the duration on the loans roughly comparable, and mortgage lenders use the 10-year Treasury as a benchmark for setting rates, adding on a risk premium.

Long-term yields for Treasury notes are determined by a number of factors, including the supply of and demand for U.S. government debt, and investor expectations for inflation over the life of the bonds.

#5619. Salesforce to buy customer service automation startup Cresta for reported $2.7B

Salesforce Inc. has agreed to buy Cresta Intelligence Inc., a venture-backed provider of customer service software.

The cloud giant didn’t disclose the financial terms in its late Monday announcement of the deal. The Information reported that Salesforce is paying $2.7 billion.

Cresta’s platform uses artificial intelligence to answer customer inquiries. It can also perform more advanced tasks such as scheduling doctor’s appointments. The platform personalizes its output based on each customer’s preferences, past interactions with the support team and related data.

Companies can customize Cresta by creating AI voice agents optimized for specific support request categories. For example, an electronics retailer could develop an agent focused on processing device returns. Cresta makes it possible to customize details such as the AI model that powers an agent and its regulatory compliance guardrails.

The platform can split complex support requests into smaller tasks to ease processing. A company could use one agent to interpret a ticket, another to find relevant help desk articles and a third to scan those articles for troubleshooting advice. Such agent ensembles often provide faster response times than a single multi-purpose agent. They save time by parallelizing tasks that would usually have to be carried out after one another.

Cresta ships its platform with an agent called Deputy. It’s geared toward particularly complex support tickets that require multiple employees to process. Deputy automatically collects the information needed to fulfill the user’s request and then loops in the relevant workers. From there, it manages follow-up tasks such as sending reminders about outstanding tasks.

Another agent provides human support representatives with real-time guidance during customer conversations. Cresta can, for example, point out potential upselling opportunities. It can also pull relevant information from external systems.

The company offers its core support automation features alongside various related tools. A feature called Opera enables organizations to fine-tune AI models for specific customer service use cases. Another tool, Synthetic Customers, provides AI-generated support conversations. Companies teams can use that data to test the reliability of newly created AI agents.

“By uniting our platform with Salesforce, we will realize our full vision at scale, embedding real-time conversation intelligence and agentic experiences directly into Salesforce’s first-class customer service Platform,” said Cresta Chief Executive Officer Ping Wu.

The deal is the second multibillion-dollar acquisition that Salesforce has made in the customer service market this year. It previously agreed to buy Fin Inc., formerly Intercom Inc, for $3.6 billion. Like Cresta, the company developed an AI platform capable of automatically answering support requests.

Salesforce’s largest acquisition this year is the $5.66 billion purchase of Braze Inc. it signed last month. The deal will buy it an AI marketing platform that can automatically deliver personalized promotions to customers.

Salesforce expects to close both the Braze and Cresta deals in its 2028 fiscal year, which starts next February.

#5618. Affordability: Real Solutions for a Real Problem

For buyers, especially first-time buyers, today’s housing affordability crisis (driven by a host of market challenges, from rising mortgage rates to low inventory and lingering inflation) creates many barriers to entry for homeownership. Is there anything agents can actually do at the local level to move the needle and help their clients achieve their homeownership goals?

Four brokerage leaders recently gathered at RISMedia 38th Annual CEO & Leadership Exchange on a panel titled, “Affordability: Real Solutions for a Real Problem,” to say yes and share their tactics and long-term solutions for buyers facing today’s housing affordability problem.

The session, moderated by RISMedia Founder and CEO John Featherston, included panelists Keith Smith, co-owner, Yes Realty Partners, a Keller Williams Alliance Partner; Ennis Antoine, owner and CEO, EA Realty of Georgia; Katey McGrath, vice president, director of operations, Elfant Wissahickon Realtors®; and Ken Baris, CEO, Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Jordan Baris Realty.

Here’s a glimpse into some of the questions and answers that provided attendees with some detailed takeaways to help their clients overcome the affordability challenge.

John Featherston: To set the stage, tell us why brokers should care about the housing affordability issue?

Keith Smith: I’m just going to kind of say the awkward thing to the room. Every single one of us makes a living either directly or indirectly from helping people buy and sell. And if we can’t help people buy and sell, we’re not going to be able to put our key in the door. We’re not going to be able to begin our business. Right now, first-time homebuyers can’t buy, and they’re 40? You have Boomers who will not be able to move on. So if we can’t help people do that, this isn’t just a certain entry point. It’s all the way across the board. I think maybe a little bit later we’ll talk about some possible solutions.

Katey McGrath: Obviously it’s good business. And what’s interesting too is at least in our market, the competition for that business is a lot less intense because it is a little bit more work and it’s not as dollar-productive. It’s absolutely more rewarding and more valuable to your communities, but not everybody gets up and says, “I want to sell lower-priced houses.” And so I love new agents getting into the business and focusing on affordability. We love training them up to pre-qualify renters because most of the time the renters don’t know they can buy a house. So it’s a great way to start your real estate business.

And in our company, we have a lot of things that sort of reinforce that culture of homeownership as the most impactful thing you can do in a community. We also create programs in-house that help leverage gift funds to just get people across the line, which I’ll talk about more, but we thread it through the entire “gestalt” of our organization.

John Featherston: What are some of the ground-level tactics that you’re using in your organization?

Katey McGrath: One of the things we do is we train up. If you get a call for a rental, find out if they are capable of qualifying for homeownership. We lean on our lenders. I rely on them and have a high level of expectation that they’re going to understand the down payment programs and the grant programs and the ability to stack them. We have a program called Building Equity where we crowdfund it. The partners of the company seeded it and now every agent in my company gives $5 to $50 every time they sell a house. We have a nice little fund, and we make a gift to anyone who buys a house for $250,000 or less in the city of Philadelphia. The only question we ask is, are you going to move into it?

We find that we can leverage that. If our lenders want to participate in the program and be on our website, they have to match that gift. We just want to keep the level of homeownership in Philadelphia as high as possible. And we also want people to consider other neighborhoods, other house sizes and conditions that maybe the people saving up for their dream homes are not looking at.

John Featherston: Ennis, how do you educate agents to help them find homes their buyers afford?

Ennis Antoine: When talking to my agents, I have to remind them first, you have to learn to stack resources. And what that means is, get involved in the city, the county and third-party companies like Georgia Dreams and ask them, “What programs do you have available to assist with down payment assistance?” In Atlanta, we have a program where the mayor wants to have 20,000 affordable homes built by 2030, so he has instructed his people to have this agency set aside funds to help buyers with down payment assistance; you have to live in our community for five years and it’s forgivable where you don’t have to pay back those funds. The goal is educating your agents on what funds are available and then once they’re educated, educate the buyers on what to expect and to set realistic expectations.

John Featherston: Are you seeing or anticipating any improvement in affordability issues from the ROAD to Housing Act?

Ennis Antoine: I chaired the FPC advisory committee (Federal Political Coordinators under NAR), and we worked on that bill for two years and got it passed. Now here’s the key, though. It is only an incentive. It’s going to take each one of us to inform our city councilmen and mayors on what’s available, and to pass these bills to say, “Hey, listen, how can we incentivize people to buy a home?” And then second, when it comes to housing supply, that’s going to take a while because we have an inventory shortage. It’s not going to happen overnight, but we have to be patient because it’s only a framework on what could happen if we partner with our city council and Realtor® organizations.

John Featherston: Ken, why is it critical to approach the affordability issue as far as you can see? And is it relevant to the specific markets that you’re now serving?

Ken Baris: Affordability is relative. Somebody who says “I can’t afford” is maybe a kid who grew up in a town, can’t afford to be in the town now, but they may be able to afford in another community. It’s being able to understand the benefits people can get. So for instance, Bank of America’s community reinvestment program with a grant of $17,500. We have a mortgage partnership, and we make sure anyone who will qualify for that is going to get that grant and use Bank of America because it’s good sense for the clients.

And if you are really astute about the business, you have people who are tenants—they don’t know they can afford to purchase. You can train people to purchase. You can help people improve their credit: Higher credit score, lower interest rate. You can train people to do things like say, “I will fall in like with four properties. I will not fall in love with one.” Because if you fall in like with four and we make four lower offers, we actually can turn you into a buyer and something more affordable by being willing to present offers. So we inspire a team to do the work and take the time and good things happen for clients.

We use foyersavings.com. A very interesting website; it has three things. Number one, it gives you an ability to save money at an okay interest rate or a good interest rate so that your money builds. Number two, it gives a modest down payment assistance with $600 credit of the first $10,000 you have, you get 6% additional in interest back. That’s not huge, but it’s something.

And three, it shows programs from all over—banks, lenders, community program—that provide grants. You may not know all the programs in your own market that are available. Foyer goes after these programs and makes them available to people that use the site. So it’s just being aware of these things, using your method of communication to get the information out, inspiring people to understand what they can do. If you don’t buy somewhere, you’re going to make somebody else wealthier.

John Featherston: A follow up to that, because you’re going into a lot of the nuances that help new buyers enter the marketplace. Have you made a concerted effort within your firm to make this type of training and education a competitive differentiator in your organization?

Ken Baris: Hugely. I find units to be sexy, not just high prices. And if you have salespeople that are in more affordable communities and they’re trained for these programs, they do better. Another thing that we’ll do is we’ll send out emails of successful buyers. “John thought he was going to rent. We let him know that we thought he could purchase, and the good news for John is we were right. You might be in the same position. Let’s get together.” And that’s the kind of communication we’re doing. I can’t change somebody’s income, but I could help them learn how to save more, how to improve their credit and how to get down payment assistance. $17,500 can make somebody from not a buyer to a buyer. And it’s a gift. It’s not a loan.

John Featherston: How are you and your agents getting past the current rhetoric that we hear among young people when they say they’re never going to be able to buy a home?

Katey McGrath: One of the biggest myths is that you think you need 20% down. And so it’s education, education, education, myth busting, destigmatizing these programs. It’s super important for young people in your community, but also make sure that your agents feel that way. And it’s great because like I said, the younger agents eat it up and it keeps them busy early in their career.

Ennis Antoine: I put pen to paper. So as far as paying $2,000 a month in rent, I’m saying, let’s talk about this for a second. A landlord just received $24,000 from you for one year. You say I’m staying there for three or four years. Then you have nothing to show for it. Whereas if you bought a home or a condominium, you pay this amount each month, you would have a tax write off and within four or five years, you’ll see a 4% or 5% increase in the value of the property. You can sell that property, walk away with cash, get the tax write off on your tax returns. And so if it was me, I would buy and invest and start to build wealth.

And if you build wealth, you can get a larger home and pay less money. So the key here is you’re a smart person. Let’s make a smart decision. Let’s buy.

Keith Smith: I want to pivot a little bit. We’re talking about how we can make a difference. Just last year through a land trust we put together 40 permanent affordable new construction units. I’m in Charlottesville with the second-highest cost of living in the state of Virginia, the second-highest cost of housing in Virginia. But we were able to do 40 of them. And the way we did this is what I call the four pillars: The local government, the private sector folks—developers, builders, real estate agents, the nonprofits and the people all of us serve. You got to get them into a room. You’ve got to get them all to go into the conversation. We put buyers and sellers together. We negotiate deals together. We put people together that maybe do not want to talk to one another, but they talk to people that get to the end result. And how you put those four pillars together is you show up to the meetings and you do what we all do every day very well, which is negotiate and put people together.

John Featherston: Why isn’t the real estate community playing a more pivotal role than every one of the communities, perhaps the most critical role as far as supporting homeownership?

Katey McGrath: I think everybody in this room is a connector. It’s what we love about what we do. And I think that our credibility and our expertise can help save money in these instances. The earlier we get involved in these conversations, the less mistakes the people with good intentions are going to make to make things more expensive. But also, the credibility that we have as a community member, right? So people are coming to us to buy houses, people are coming to us for education, people are coming to us to build generational wealth for their family. And then we can go to city council, we can go to the state reps, we can go to the zoning meetings and add all of that to just sort of be both sides of the issue.

Housing is bipartisan, so if you can get people together, you have that credibility, everything just becomes more productive and less expensive.

John Featherston: Getting people together over the issue of housing is a common denominator all of us can agree on. When Ennis said, local teachers, first responders, police, essential services, can’t afford to live in the community they’re serving, that is not a unique problem. That’s a problem that permeates around the nation. So the solutions have to be done locally.

Ennis Antoine: That’s correct. So I remind everyone, it doesn’t matter what company you work for, there is a percentage in every company where you deal with first-time homebuyers. It doesn’t have to be your main part of your business, but it should be a part of your business because to whom much is given, much is required. And we must always lead by example because the goal here is homeownership. What can we do? It’s all an education process. In every office, there are agents who are very passionate about their community. Support them, enhance them, show up when they need some help.

They will find a surgeon to have vibrant communities. We need a mixture of people in the community who are willing to work together, live together because we call it a village. And as real estate professionals, we are the fiber of the community. We are the voice of real estate and private property rights do matter.

Ken Baris: Something interesting we did some years ago, we listed 300 brand new two-family homes in Newark, New Jersey. And they were beautiful. The challenge was getting people in. So we had the builder prearrange financing, and we had them buy down the rate. And so it was a much lower interest rate, which lowered the payments. And then we also had the builder give a brand-new computer to every purchaser for one of the units because many of them were going to have kids and they would not have money left over for a new computer. And we thought that was very important. And then when certain buyers were tight, we then created a program where they were giving 5% toward closing costs, and if you get people to pay money toward closing costs, you also make it more affordable.

Keith Smith: “Connected” was the right word. I’ve been in this space for 15 years, and I would hear from elected officials, “Well, I don’t understand what the developer is saying.” The developer’s saying, “I don’t understand what the elected official is saying.” And then the nonprofits don’t understand anybody, and the poor folks that we’re trying to serve are left out there in the dark. Being a connector, that is the perfect word. That’s what we do. We connect and are able to put those four pillars together and put a developer and an elected official who really wants to do the right thing, together. The seller doesn’t trust the buyer; the buyer doesn’t trust the seller. We connect and we put people together and just get that conversation rolling. That’s how you do 40 new construction units in the second-highest cost-of-living area in the state of Virginia and everybody walks away smiling. I didn’t do anything really genius. I just put people in the room and said, start talking.

John Featherston: If you could do one thing to help move this affordability issue forward, what would you do?

Ennis Antoine: The one thing I would do is educate my colleagues and challenge them to get involved. It’s easy to write a check, but it’s amazing what happens when you show up. As a leader, when we show up, our people will follow. So as leaders, show up.

Ken Baris: I think just doing a better job of educating consumers because there’s a lot of buyers that don’t know their buyers. Not everyone will be able to afford. They’ve never always been able to, but there’s many more out there.

Katey McGrath: I’m going to go a little more philosophical. Just remember how important homeownership is to every metric in the community. It reduces crime. It increases education rates. It can lower the temperature in a zip code. It extends life expectancy, but most importantly, it builds generational wealth and creates health outcomes in that community that lift everybody up. And if you internalize that, you’re going to be happier when you go to work. You’re going to have more patience to deal with the hard clients that you’re not going to make a lot of money on and just feel great at the end of the day.

Keith Smith: Invest the one asset you can’t make more of, which is your time. Show up and over time, you’ll make a difference. And of those affordable housing units, every single key I handed to somebody, they were in tears. They never thought they were going to get into the homeownership game. It’s not about the check. It’s about the tears, and it makes a difference.

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5617. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5616. Xavier Becerra Wins California’s Gubernatorial Election in a Landslide After Pledging To Tackle Housing Shortage

Democratic candidate Xavier Becerra has won the California gubernatorial contest, trouncing Donald Trump-endorsed Republican hopeful Steve Hilton in a landslide win.

The Associated Press called the race immediately after polls closed, reflecting Becerra's undeniable lead over his GOP opponent. The victory was part of Tuesday night's "blue wave," in which Democrats reclaimed control of both the House and the Senate.

"What a great night to be a Californian," Becerra said at a victory party in West Sacramento, CA. "What a great night to be an American."

In his concession speech, Hilton, 57, congratulated Becerra on his win, but also predicted that a Republican will become governor in 2030.

"Enjoy it while it lasts," he told his opponent.

Becerra, 68, who served as secretary of Health and Human Services under President Joe Biden, entered the midterm elections on Tuesday holding a commanding lead of 27 percentage points over Hilton, a Fox News contributor, according to the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times.

The decisive victory marks a historic milestone as Becerra becomes the first Latino elected as governor of California, and the first Latino to hold the office since Romualdo Pacheco, who was elevated to the post from lieutenant governor in 1875 following the resignation of Gov. Newton Booth.

Becerra will be sworn in on Jan. 4, 2027, replacing the term-limited Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who campaigned for his successor on Sunday alongside former Vice President Kamala Harris. Both Newsom and Harris are expected to consider presidential runs in 2028.

Becerra becomes California's third consecutive Democratic governor, cementing the party's dominance in the deep-blue state.

California's 41st governor inherits a tangle of economic challenges anchored by the state’s acute housing affordability crisis.

In the run-up to the election, Becerra, a former congressman, made housing one of the main pillars of his campaign, promising to declare a housing-shortage state of emergency on his very first day in office and appoint senior officials across state agencies who will be tasked with removing obstacles to construction projects.

Becerra’s ambitious platform includes proposals to enforce 90-day "shot clocks" for building permits to accelerate construction, slash impact fees, streamline reviews for modular homes, and overhaul financing for affordable housing.

"The Becerra win signals that California intends to keep pushing for more housing, with an approach aimed at making building simpler," says Realtor.com® economist Jiayi Xu. "Taken together, it points to California doubling down on a pro-supply approach."

For the nation's most populous state, these changes could not come soon enough: on this year's Realtor.com® State-by-State Housing Report Card, part of the Let America Build campaign, California earned an F grade thanks to its to ultra-low housing affordability score.

Additionally, a Realtor.com analysis of the latest available housing and the Census Bureau's American Community Survey data found that the typical household in California earns 49% less than the income needed to buy a median-priced home—a shortfall of $98,292—making it the second-most unaffordable state behind Montana.

In a bid to unlock housing supply, Becerra plans to pursue zoning reforms, expand by-right approvals near job and transit hubs, and introduce more duplexes and small condos to put homeownership within reach of renters.

As part of his plan to tackle California’s entrenched homelessness epidemic through prevention, Becerra has proposed offering rental assistance to vulnerable families and bolstering tenant protections, which he views as more economical than spending thousands of dollars down the line on shelter beds.

Looking ahead, Xu expects Becerra to face significant hurdles, beginning with potential legal challenges and pushbacks on the housing front.

"For example, his plan targets lower impact fees, but some cities rely heavily on those fees to pay for infrastructure, and his campaign has not detailed how that lost revenue would be replaced," notes the economist. "A clearer plan for cities will be needed to win their cooperation."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5615. Earnings Roundup: Higher Rates Test Green Brick, Meritage, and Dream Finders

The challenging housing environment remained front and center as Green Brick Partners, Meritage Homes, and Dream Finders Homes reported third-quarter results.

Rising mortgage rates and affordability constraints continued to pressure consumer sentiment and margins. Green Brick Partners grew orders and deliveries despite the difficult backdrop, while Meritage Homes prioritized margins over a higher sales pace. Dream Finders Homes achieved record third-quarter closings while absorbing costs associated with its acquisition of Beazer Homes.

“Despite continued affordability pressures, broader economic uncertainty, and an increasing rate environment, demand across our markets remained resilient as buyers responded to our incentive strategy and attractive product offerings, particularly within Trophy Signature Homes. We continue to respond to deteriorating market conditions to maintain sales pace.”— Jim Brickman, co-CEO and co-founder, Green Brick Partners

“In the third quarter of 2026, we navigated an increasingly challenging home buying environment marked by rising mortgage interest rates and persistent geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty. Constrained affordability weighed on consumer sentiment, which was reflected in our 15% year-over-year decline in third quarter orders despite achieving an average absorption pace of 3.0 net sales per month per store.”— Steven J. Hilton, executive chairman, Meritage Homes

“Buyers faced a challenging summer, as rising mortgage rates further strained affordability and weighed on consumer confidence. I’m proud of how our team navigated these market conditions. We closed 1,967 homes in the quarter, a third-quarter record, and 6,127 homes year-to-date, also a record, while net sales increased 6% compared with the prior year.”— Patrick Zalupski, founder, co-chairman and CEO, Dream Finders Homes

Since quarter-end, Dream Finders Homes completed its approximately $2.2 billion acquisition of Beazer Homes. Zalupski said the company expects additional nonrecurring transaction and integration costs during the fourth quarter as it works toward $100 million in targeted cost savings from the combination. The company reiterated its full-year 2026 guidance of approximately 9,250 home closings.

#5614. Louisiana Passes New Property Tax Relief Amendments for Seniors

On Tuesday, Louisiana voters passed four ballot measures on property tax exemptions, aimed at providing tax relief for seniors, surviving spouses of disabled veterans, and entrepreneurs who rehab dilapidated homes.

Voters passed Amendment 1 with 76% support. Amendment 1 allows the surviving spouse of a disabled veteran transfer the homestead property tax exemption to a new home.

Currently, disabled veterans receive a homestead property tax exemption that is commensurate with the degree of disability they experience. Spouses are able to maintain the exemption in the event of their veteran spouse passing away. However, this amendment allows a one-time opportunity to the surviving spouse to transfer the exemption to a new property as well.

The Louisiana Department of Veterans Affairs as well as Leaders for a Better Louisiana and Louisiana Realtors® all expressed support for the measure.

Meanwhile, the Power Coalition for Equity and Justice opposed the measure, saying: "We support veterans and their families, but we do not need another special tax exception written into the state constitution."

Amendment 6 passed with 65% support. It proposes a property tax exemption of up to $30,000 for homeowners over age 65 who already qualify for an income assessment-based freeze.

Introduced by state Rep. Les Farnum, the amendment received support from both Democrats and Republicans.

The nonpartisan Leaders for a Better Louisiana, Power Coalition, and the nonprofit Pelican Institute for Public Policy all opposed the amendment.

In its explanation for its opposition to the amendment, Leaders for a Better Louisiana wrote: "While we like the idea of shielding senior citizens from taxes they have no control over...we wish it provided more flexibility for local governments to tailor tax breaks in a way that might be more suited to their individual goals and situations. As we have stated elsewhere, the better approach would be to untie the hands of local governments with regard to property taxes, rather than putting more rules in the constitution.The Louisiana Realtors expressed support for the amendment: "No community is forced to do anything. Each one decides for itself whether helping its seniors age in place is worth it. That is how local control should work."

Meanwhile, 59% of voters supported Amendment 9, which raises the income level for seniors to qualify for a property tax freeze from $100,000 to $150,000, allowing more people to qualify for the freeze.

The amendment aims to offer increased financial relief to seniors, many of whom live on fixed incomes. Proponents argued that the amendment could attract more seniors to the state. Critics said it would further reduce the tax dollars local governments require for social services.

Currently, around 230,000 people qualify for the freeze in the state.

The last time voters approved an increase in the income limit for the special property tax assessment was in 2020, when voters approved an increase in income limit from $50,000 to $100,000.

Louisiana Realtors expressed support for the amendment, saying that "the income limit to qualify has not kept pace with the cost of living."

Amendment 10, which allows communities to create optional property tax exemptions for blighted and derelict property that has been rehabilitated, also narrowly passed with 53% support.

Under the initiative, up to 75% of a rehabilitated property's assessed value would be exempt from property taxes for up to 20 years. Meanwhile, cleared lots would receive a 25% exemption on assessed value for up to 10 years as long as they weren't next to residential or commercial buildings.

Proponents argued this would incentivize the rehabilitation of derelict properties and positively impact the safety and well-being in a community. Communities could choose to opt in or out of the initiative depending on local needs.

In the U.S., property tax rates are determined at the local level and vary widely. The average effective property tax rate on owner-occupied housing in Louisiana is 0.55%, which is relatively low compared with states like New Jersey and Illinois, where the effective tax rate is 1.88%, according to the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan tax policy nonprofit.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5613. Generative media inference startup fal raises $1.3B at a $16B valuation

Generative media inference startup fal today announced it has raised $1.3 billion in new funding at a valuation of $16 billion, according to Bloomberg.

The company will spend the money on computing power and on hiring beyond its current 185 employees.

Fal provides a cloud platform for running image, video and audio generation models, and developers reach all of them through a single application programming interface. Entertainment studios, advertising agencies and game developers are among the customers using those models in production, according to the company.

In-house researchers also post-train some of those models to run faster. Over the past year that work has centered on video, in partnership with the open- and closed-source developers that build the models. Some of the deals pay fal licensing fees or a share of revenue, Bloomberg reported.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Burkay Gur told the outlet the round is as large as it is because demand has surged and serving it takes more compute. “We hit a point in summer where we were not able to serve our customers and had to rate-limit them,” he said. Pretraining a model of fal’s own is not on the near-term agenda, said Gur, who did not rule it out for later.

Annualized revenue at fal passed $800 million earlier this year, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. The valuation puts fal just behind rival inference provider Fireworks AI Inc., which closed $1.5 billion in funding at a $17.5 billion valuation in July. Several people familiar with the finances of inference companies told TechCrunch that gross margins across the sector remain thin because compute is expensive to buy or lease.

Gur started the company in 2021 with Chief Technology Officer Gorkem Yurtseven. His resume includes leading machine learning work at Coinbase Global Inc. and an engineering role at Oracle Corp. Yurtseven was previously a developer at Amazon.com Inc.

Bessemer Venture Partners led the Series F round, and its partner Talia Goldberg is joining the board of Features & Labels Inc., as fal is formally known. Nvidia Corp., Sound Ventures, HOF Capital and T. Rowe Price Group Inc. also participated. Fal described Nvidia as a strategic investor.

Today’s announcement also covered an April round led by Sequoia Capital. That Series E round raised $350 million at an $8 billion valuation, per Bloomberg, and fal said the two rounds come to $1.65 billion combined. Last December, the company raised $140 million at a $4.5 billion valuation.

Investors have now put more than $1.9 billion into the company.

#5612. Inside Legacy Hills’ Strategy for Reaching a Broad Range of Buyers

Developed by Centurion American, the Legacy Hills master-planned community (MPC) spans over 3,000 acres in Celina, Texas, and is planned for up to 7,000 homes at full buildout. The community opened in April 2024 and includes a diverse mix of builders, lot sizes, and floor plans. Pricing generally ranges from the $300,000s into the mid-$500,000s.

Importantly, Legacy Hills is not relying on a single buyer profile. Its product strategy creates multiple entry points into the community, with housing choices that can appeal to buyers at different price points and stages of life.

That product diversity is paired with a layered amenity program. Plans call for seven amenity centers throughout Legacy Hills, along with a 27-acre sports park and a 3-mile walking and biking trail. The planned 1876 Country Club adds a destination component with an 18-hole championship golf course, clubhouse, driving range, putting green, and short game facilities.

For families moving to Legacy Hills, children in the broader community attend Celina ISD, while future school sites are planned within the development. The community also broadens its reach further through Del Webb’s dedicated 55+ neighborhood, which adds to Legacy Hills’ family-oriented offerings with age-targeted homes and amenities.

The strategy is unfolding against a strong demographic backdrop. Celina’s population and household base are projected to more than double between 2020 and 2029, expanding the potential pool of buyers around the community.

At the same time, the broader housing environment remains competitive. The Zonda Market Ranking for MPCs characterized Dallas as slightly underperforming per August data, yet Legacy Hills stood out. In the Q2 2026 Master Plan Outlook report, the MPC recorded the largest year-over-year percentage increase in last 12-month sales among qualifying MPCs with at least 200 sales in the previous 12 months.

Legacy Hills illustrates the value of creating several paths into a large-scale community rather than building around a narrow customer profile. Differentiated housing, offerings for multiple life stages, and amenities ranging from everyday recreation to destination experiences give the development multiple ways to appeal to buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from a more in-depth case study in Zonda’s Master Plan Outlook subscription.
