#5539. Nationwide Equities debuts ReverseReach tool for mortgage broker lead generation help

Nationwide Equities has launched ReverseReach, a tool and help desk program that lets mortgage brokers and loan officers screen their existing customer databases for reverse mortgage opportunities without deep product expertise. The platform pairs a simple scenario runner with access to full-time underwriters, aiming to lower barriers to reverse lending and give originators a way to generate new business from past clients amid a challenging forward mortgage market.  AI Summary

Nationwide Equities Corp. has launched ReverseReach, a new tool and support program aimed at helping mortgage brokers and loan officers uncover reverse mortgage opportunities in their existing customer databases and referral networks, the company announced Tuesday.

The New Jersey-based wholesale reverse mortgage lender said ReverseReach is designed for originators who may not specialize in reverse products but have years of past customers who are now older, equity rich and potential candidates for reverse mortgages.

“Mortgage brokers may be sitting on substantial untapped business opportunities without even realizing it,” Paul Lamparillo, CEO of Nationwide Equities, said in a statement. “Over the years, brokers have built relationships with thousands of homeowners, many of whom may now qualify for reverse mortgage products.

“We created ReverseReach to make uncovering those highly lucrative opportunities simple, efficient and accessible — even for brokers who have never closed a reverse mortgage before — so they can confidently and comfortably begin originating them.”

The company has largely pivoted to proprietary reverse mortgage production, mirroring recent changes in the broader industry. Modex data shows that Nationwide Equities has originated 111 reverse mortgages for $216 million in volume over the past 12 months, while data compiled by Reverse Market Insight shows that it has endorsed 26 Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) through the first nine months of this year.

In 2020, Nationwide Equities launched its private-label reverse mortgage, EquityPower, which was built to offer higher loan proceeds than HECM products.

ReverseReach allows mortgage professionals to enter a borrower’s financial and property scenario and quickly gauge whether a reverse mortgage is worth pursuing. The program is positioned as a preliminary opportunity identification tool rather than a full underwriting engine.

Regardless of the initial result, brokers can connect with a live underwriter to discuss the file and potential structures, according to the company.

Nationwide Equities is pairing the technology with a help desk staffed by full-time Direct Endorsement (DE) underwriters who answer eligibility questions, help structure loans and walk brokers through complex borrower situations.

“One of the biggest obstacles to broader reverse mortgage adoption is simply recognizing when a borrower may be a good candidate,” Philip Parziale, president of Nationwide Equities said in a statement. “ReverseReach bridges that gap. Brokers don’t need to become reverse mortgage experts to identify a potential transaction. They need a simple way to recognize the opportunity and a knowledgeable lending partner to help them execute it.”

Parziale added that direct access to underwriters is a central part of the offering. “Regardless of how good your technology is, there is something special about being able to speak to a live person on the phone and walk you through a scenario and respond to follow ups,” he said.

The launch comes as volume in the broader forward mortgage market remains under pressure from higher rates, tighter affordability and intense competition for a smaller pool of qualified borrowers. Many retail and broker shops are looking to diversify into reverse mortgages, home equity products or nonqualified mortgages (non-QM) to stabilize production.

For brokers, the reverse space has historically been constrained by product complexity, reputation concerns and training requirements. ReverseReach aims to lower that barrier by giving originators a simple screening workflow across their existing loan origination system and past client lists, backed by lender-side expertise.

Lenders are investing in education and simple tools to capture aging-in-place demand from older homeowners with significant home equity. Brokers who have closed thousands of loans over the past decade may find that a meaningful share of these clients now meet age and equity thresholds for reverse products.

Nationwide Equities positions ReverseReach as a business development strategy focused on reengaging existing borrowers rather than purchasing new leads or ramping up paid marketing. Potential applications include:

#5537. Laza Medical Raises Up to $160 Million in Series B Financing Led by GE HealthCare to Advance Intelligent Imaging for Transforming the Cath Lab

Company's first-of-a-kind intelligent imaging system aims to expand patient access, streamline high-quality cardiac care, and establish the foundation for future robotic interventions

LOS GATOS, Calif., Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Laza Medical, Inc., a Shifamed portfolio company pioneering AI-powered robotic imaging solutions for cardiac interventions, today announced it has raised up to $160 million in Series B structured financing. GE HealthCare led the round, with participation from returning investors Unorthodox Ventures, PA MedTech, and AMED. The financing will support the company's mission to transform the cardiac catheterization laboratory through intelligent imaging technology designed to simplify procedures, increase autonomy, alleviate resource constraints, and unlock the possibilities for future robotic-enabled interventions.

"The future of cardiac intervention must be one where access, consistency, and quality of care are no longer barriers to better outcomes," stated Jyoti Gera, CEO of Cardiovascular and Interventional Solutions, Advanced Imaging Solutions at GE HealthCare. "Integrating imaging modalities so they work seamlessly together has the potential to redefine the cath lab, enabling more efficient workflows today and paving the way for smarter, robotic procedures tomorrow. We're excited to expand our collaboration with Laza and work together toward this shared vision."

As cardiovascular procedures become increasingly complex, care teams need more intuitive and consistent image guidance amid growing demands for specialized imaging expertise. By combining AI and robotics, Laza has the potential to simplify procedural imaging, extend the reach of specialized imaging expertise, and help care teams navigate and guide complex cardiac interventions with greater confidence.

"High-quality imaging is foundational to all successful cases," said Dr. Firas Zahr, Head of Interventional Cardiology at Oregon Health Sciences University Hospital, who had experience with the software during the first-in-human clinical study last year. "Consistent anatomic and spatial context simplifies procedures and helps clinicians navigate the anatomy with confidence and precision."

"The cath lab is poised for a fundamental evolution, and intelligent imaging powered by AI will play a defining role in what comes next," said Amr Salahieh, Founder and Board Chairman at Laza Medical. "As we reimagine the role of imaging in interventional care, we are grateful for the strong support from our investors, which validates our approach and reinforces our conviction that this solution will streamline processes, reduce variability, and ultimately improve the quality and reach of cardiac procedures."

The Laza Medical System is under development and is not approved for commercial sale in any geography.

Laza Medical is a privately held portfolio company of Shifamed, LLC. The company focuses on developing a high-quality, AI-powered robotic imaging solution for cardiovascular interventions. For more information, visit www.lazamedical.com.

Founded by serial entrepreneur Amr Salahieh, Shifamed is a highly specialized medical innovation hub focused on developing solutions that accelerate time to market, reduce risk, increase impact, and forge a path toward a world where patients are able to lead longer, healthier lives.

Shifamed's goal is to lead the way in next generation of cardiac cath lab innovation, bringing together breakthroughs in advanced imaging, artificial intelligence (AI), and robotics to transform how interventional cardiovascular procedures are performed.

#5536. LGI Homes Q3 2026 earnings reveal leadership test in downturn

LGI Homes posted higher Q3 2026 revenue and improved gross margin while cutting SG&A dollars. Demand weakened materially, with orders down 61.2% and cancellations up, putting focus on leadership, culture, and capital discipline.  AI Summary

A peculiar phenomenon in homebuilding has fascinated me for much of the past two-plus decades.

In virtually every market, across almost every customer segment and price point, a handful of homebuilders consistently outperform competitors facing essentially the same business conditions.

They face the same mortgage rates, land and development costs, labor constraints, household purchasing-power challenges and regulatory obstacles. They work with essentially the same raw materials, including people, capital, building products, subcontractors and operating processes. Yet their results can differ dramatically, especially when business conditions turn difficult.

A decade or so ago, a highly regarded homebuilding business strategist mused aloud to me about this phenomenon. He was struck by how companies dealt with essentially the same competitive hand, yet a few outlier leaders figured out how to produce better results than the rest.

I’ve thought about that observation often, particularly during periods when the industry’s cyclical pressures expose the difference between companies that can withstand adversity and those that can turn adversity into an opportunity to strengthen their businesses.

The distinction is especially relevant now. U.S. homebuilders are facing an unforgiving mix of weak selling conditions, elevated capital costs, stubbornly high land and development expenses, and households whose purchasing power has failed to keep pace with the cost of homeownership. These pressures have persisted long enough to strain business plans based on more favorable assumptions, and little is certain about when conditions will improve.

Which brings us to LGI Homes, its Q3 2026 earnings report, and a question that extends well beyond a single company’s quarterly performance:

What distinguishes homebuilding enterprises whose leaders and organizations can emerge from a prolonged downturn stronger than they entered it?

LGI Homes’ November 3 earnings report is a useful case study because its operating results show both encouraging evidence of management’s execution and unmistakable signs that the business faces tough sledding ahead.

The Woodlands, Texas-based builder reported 1,222 home closings in the third quarter, including 33 currently or previously leased homes, a 10.4% increase from the year-earlier quarter. Homebuilding revenues rose 10.3% to $437.5 million, and net income increased to $24.6 million, or $1.05 per diluted share, compared with $19.7 million, or $0.85 per share, in the year-earlier quarter.

Profitability and expense management emerged as clear strengths. Homebuilding gross margin reached 20.2%, and adjusted homebuilding gross margin was 23.7%, both up 40 basis points sequentially. Selling, general and administrative expenses declined 2.5% in absolute dollars, while SG&A as a percentage of total revenue improved 180 basis points year over year, reflecting operational rigor and executional excellence.

The company also reduced its net debt-to-capital ratio to 40.6%, up 420 basis points from a year earlier, and ended September with $447.7 million in liquidity. Its active community count increased by 7.1% year over year to 151.

Yet a forward-looking lens tells a far less rosy story. Net orders plunged 61.2% to 609 homes, down from 1,570 a year earlier, while the cancellation rate rose to 53.8% from 33.6%. Backlog declined 47.5% to 685 homes. Management narrowed its full-year closing guidance to 4,600 to 4,800 homes, reflecting weaker sales activity and ongoing affordability pressures.

These results speak of the vulnerability of LGI’s business model at a time when the company’s core customer is among the most financially constrained in the housing market.

LGI has built much of its business around helping renters become homeowners through a direct-to-consumer sales model, speculative construction, and a value proposition that emphasizes attainable monthly payments. These capabilities have helped distinguish the company for years. They also leave its sales performance especially vulnerable to turbulent headwinds, such as mortgage-rate movements and changes in buyer qualification.

The third-quarter numbers make it clear that LGI’s operational strengths have not shielded it from those pressures. Will the capabilities that helped the company develop its distinctive business model now enable it to adapt more effectively than competitors under the same conditions?

Wolfe Research’s November 3 assessment of LGI serves as an important counterweight to any temptation to interpret the company’s earnings performance as evidence that it has already mastered the current downturn.

Analyst Trevor Allinson and his team credited LGI’s Q3 operating performance, namely its gross-margin strength and SG&A expense reductions, while maintaining a Peer Perform rating. Wolfe noted that LGI’s predominantly self-developed land position supports margins at a time when several competitors have sustained hits to sequential margins.

Wolf Research’s analysis also explicitly recognizes LGI’s process-driven organization as a competitive strength, citing the company’s ability to pare back operating errors in land acquisition, construction efficiency and warranty management.

This is not to say that Wall Street exactly overlooks the value of management execution or organizational capability. Wolfe’s analysis shows that analysts recognize those strengths and attempt to account for their financial impact. What’s hard to quantify is how much those muscle-memory operational capabilities can influence future results when demand remains both tepid and unpredictable.

Wolfe’s assessment highlights that LGI’s order decline creates a difficult trade-off between sales pace and profitability. With third-quarter net order absorption averaging about 1.3 homes per community per month, the company faces pressure to accelerate sales, potentially through additional incentives that would erode margins.

The firm reduced its 2027 earnings-per-share estimate by 30.1%, from $3.42 to $2.39, reflecting its expectation that weaker demand and the need to balance price against sales volume will constrain profitability. Its concerns also extend to LGI’s leverage, its comparatively high SG&A expense ratio, and its substantial owned-land position, all of which can weigh on returns when inventory turnover slows.

Those financial risks aren’t merely temporary obstacles that a strong corporate culture can surmount through resolve.

LGI’s net debt-to-capital ratio of 40.6% remains elevated relative to many competitors, despite recent improvements. Its 50,270 owned lots represent a substantial capital commitment, especially given current sales rates.

The company therefore enters the next phase of this downturn with meaningful strengths, but also with structural exposures that could constrain its flexibility if weak demand persists.

In a conversation earlier this week, Tony Avila, founder of Builder Advisor Group and Avila Real Estate Capital, offered a useful framework for identifying homebuilders best positioned to weather and grow stronger in the current environment.

Avila cited stronger margins, lower leverage, attractive finished-lot positions, higher returns on capital, and the ability to serve a broader range of buyers as key indicators of financial strength. Geographic diversification can provide additional protection, although builders operating in individual markets with favorable supply-and-demand dynamics may also be well positioned.

His observations reflect a reality that homebuilding’s financial fundamentals become especially important when market conditions deteriorate and access to capital becomes more expensive or more restrictive. Builders with stronger balance sheets and favorable land positions can preserve liquidity, maintain operational flexibility, and pursue opportunities that weaker competitors may be forced to abandon.

Avila also cautioned that the industry’s current difficulties could persist into 2028, suggesting that the ability to withstand a prolonged period of weak demand may become an increasingly important competitive distinction.

These characteristics provide an essential foundation for evaluating resilience. They identify which companies have the financial capacity to withstand adversity and retain strategic options while competitors face mounting constraints.

I would argue that they represent the table stakes of resilience rather than its full measure.

Financial strength can give an enterprise room to maneuver, but it does not necessarily indicate whether management will recognize changing opportunities, make the right adjustments, or mobilize its organization to perform better.

By the same token, a company that falls short of some of these financial criteria may possess organizational capabilities that enable it to improve its position over time, provided its financial constraints do not undermine those efforts.

For LGI, its land holdings and leverage are sources of financial risk, yet its operating history and recent management decisions suggest an organization actively attempting to adapt rather than simply waiting for market conditions to improve.

At the recent HousingWire Homebuilder Summit in Dallas, I introduced a framework for evaluating the organizational qualities that distinguish homebuilding enterprises capable of sustained improvement.

I described five interdependent characteristics: Character. Capability. Collaboration. Competitive fire. And customer-first culture.

Together, they form what I think of as a leadership stack, analogous to the technology stack, the capital stack, or a coordinated network of subcontractors that supports other essential elements of a homebuilding business.

Character builds the trust that enables leaders and teams to confront difficult realities and make decisions that serve the enterprise’s long-term interests. Capability reflects the organization’s accumulated knowledge, skills, and ability to execute, while collaboration enables people across functions and markets to learn from one another and solve problems more effectively.

Competitive fire fuels the determination to improve performance rather than accept prevailing conditions as an excuse for disappointing results. A customer-first culture keeps the entire organization focused on delivering homes and experiences that people genuinely need, value, and can afford.

These qualities are not substitutes for sound financial management. Their value lies in how they influence the decisions, processes and behaviors that ultimately drive financial results.

Nor can they be established simply through executive declarations about corporate culture. More convincing evidence comes from what leaders and their organizations actually do when prior assumptions break apart.

LGI’s predominantly owned and self-developed land position has long been central to its operating model. By keeping much of the land development process in-house, the company has sought to manage lot costs, maintain product consistency, and preserve margins that might otherwise be surrendered to third-party developers.

During the earnings call, Chairman and CEO Eric Lipar emphasized the importance of the strategy.

“Our on-balance sheet predominantly owned land strategy, together with our in-house development capabilities reflects the long-term decisions we’ve made to set LGI apart from much of the industry. It remains a competitive advantage, generating strong margins while giving us flexibility to adapt to changing market conditions.”

LGI’s Q3 margin performance reflects these advantages. However, the risks of tying up capital in land become more pronounced when demand slows and projected absorption rates prove overly optimistic.

Management has reduced its owned-lot position for six consecutive quarters, from a peak of 61,893 lots in the second quarter of 2022 to 50,270 as of September 30, 2026. Meanwhile, controlled lots increased 18.1% sequentially to 8,130, reflecting opportunities to pursue finished-lot takedowns and smaller projects that meet the company’s current underwriting requirements.

These adjustments do not transform LGI into an asset-light builder, nor do they eliminate the financial consequences of its current land investments. They do, however, demonstrate a willingness to adjust capital commitments while preserving the capabilities that have historically differentiated its business.

CFO Charles Merdian offered another example during the earnings call, explaining that the company has adjusted the size and timing of future development sections to reflect slower absorption assumptions.

Those tactics involve altering project execution, even after initial land acquisitions and infrastructure investments. Management cannot recover all previously committed capital, but it can adjust the timing and amount of additional investment required to bring future lots to market.

This is organizational adaptability expressed through capital allocation and operational execution. It reflects the capacity to revisit assumptions, coordinate decisions across land development and construction functions, and change course without necessarily abandoning the underlying strategy.

LGI’s speculative construction and direct-to-consumer sales model offers another example of the distinction between adapting an operating strategy and abandoning its core customer proposition.

The company has historically focused on renters and first-time buyers whose purchasing decisions depend heavily on affordable monthly payments and the ability to move into a completed home on a relatively predictable schedule.

That positioning has become more challenging as mortgage rates and household expenses have tightened qualification standards. LGI’s elevated cancellation rate and sharp decline in orders indicate that its core customers are struggling to convert interest in homeownership into completed transactions.

Yet Lipar’s comments suggest management views the company’s customer knowledge and operating specialization as reasons to maintain its basic approach while modifying the supporting processes.

“We continue to see interest in homeownership, and our job is to remain disciplined while adapting our sales and financing strategies, production plans and product offering to current conditions.”

The company has expanded its sales process to accommodate buyers who need more time to qualify, while using closing-cost assistance, mortgage-rate buydowns and forward rate commitments to improve payment affordability. Management has also emphasized the need to adjust production plans and product offerings without sacrificing the features and customer experience that support the company’s value proposition.

These measures cannot eliminate the underlying affordability problem. Their effectiveness will depend on whether enough prospective customers can ultimately qualify and close at prices that maintain acceptable returns.

But they illustrate the strategic value of an organization that understands its customers well enough to adapt how it serves them while remaining committed to the needs that originally shaped its business model.

In this context, a customer-first culture becomes more than a statement of corporate values. It becomes a source of operating intelligence that informs decisions on financing, product, inventory, and the allocation of sales resources.

Of the five characteristics in the leadership stack, competitive fire may be the hardest to measure and the easiest to misunderstand or even overlook.

It is not merely optimism about an eventual market recovery, an appetite for expansion, or an unwillingness to acknowledge deteriorating conditions. Competitive fire becomes a meaningful organizational advantage when it fosters a persistent determination to improve performance while maintaining the discipline needed to protect the enterprise.

Founded in 2003, the company gained much of its early operating experience during the period surrounding the Great Financial Crisis, when collapsing housing demand, restricted credit and widespread industry failures forced homebuilders to reconsider fundamental assumptions about their businesses.

LGI emerged from that period and later expanded into a national homebuilder operating in 36 markets across 21 states. The company reports that it has earned a profit every year since its founding, a record that spans both the financial crisis and the industry’s more recent cycles of disruption.

That history does not establish that LGI will outperform during the current downturn. The industry’s competitive environment, capital structures, and affordability challenges have changed substantially since the GFC.

It does, however, suggest the company has developed institutional familiarity with adversity and a management culture shaped by operating without favorable market conditions. Its current community expansion strategy will be a significant test of that culture.

LGI expects to end 2027 with more than 180 active communities, approximately 20% above its third-quarter 2026 count. Management says much of the capital needed to support those openings has already been invested, allowing the company to expand its selling capacity without taking on incremental debt specifically to fund the openings.

At the same time, management expects the new communities to achieve absorption rates and margins similar to those currently seen, rather than assuming an imminent recovery in buyer demand. LGI is positioning itself for greater market reach while attempting to underwrite growth against the difficult conditions it observes, not the more favorable conditions it might prefer.

The strategy carries substantial execution risk. Expanding into more communities does not automatically translate into stronger earnings or higher returns when the pool of qualified buyers is constrained, and additional operating capacity can become a financial burden if sales productivity remains weak.

Still, the decision reflects an effort to preserve future growth opportunities while aligning investment and production plans with current market realities. Whether competitive fire becomes a genuine advantage will depend on how effectively LGI’s leadership and team execute those plans, learn from setbacks, and improve results in the coming quarters.

Nassim Nicholas Taleb’s concept of antifragility offers a useful way to frame the distinction between companies that merely survive adversity and those that become stronger because of it.

Resilience is the ability to absorb shocks, withstand disruption, and recover. Antifragility goes further, describing systems that benefit from volatility, stress, and uncertainty rather than merely enduring them.

Now, homebuilding is inherently cyclical, capital-intensive, and exposed to forces beyond the control of even its most capable executives. A resilient homebuilder may retain enough financial strength to weather a prolonged downturn and resume growth when demand improves. An antifragile homebuilder would use that same period to improve its processes, strengthen its people, sharpen its understanding of customers, and develop competitive advantages that leave it better positioned than before.

A single quarter of improved margins or successful cost reductions cannot establish the difference. It requires evidence that the organization has turned difficult experience into durable improvements in performance and competitive capability.

LGI has not yet demonstrated that outcome in the current cycle, but it has shown a willingness to adapt key elements of its operating model while preserving the strategic capabilities that management believes distinguish the company. Its land development adjustments, inventory management, sales-process changes and disciplined approach to balancing margins against volume provide observable evidence of that effort.

The next several quarters will show whether those decisions can improve absorption rates, cash generation, returns on capital, and competitive position, particularly if the industry’s difficult demand conditions persist through 2027 and beyond.

The industry’s current challenges are likely to produce meaningful differences in performance among homebuilders that appear superficially similar in their geographic exposure, customer segments and product offerings.

Homebuilding’s outliers are not necessarily the companies that begin a downturn with the strongest balance sheets, the most favorable markets, or the fewest obstacles. Those advantages matter enormously, but they do not fully explain why certain competitors consistently outperform.

The more elusive advantage lies in how organizations use their resources, learn from changing conditions, and translate leadership into sustained operational improvement.

That is where competitive fire – the determination that drives an organization to keep finding ways to improve when headwinds make improvement hardest – plays a role in homebuilding business outcomes that’s all too unappreciated.

#5534. VIAVI Announces First Quarter Fiscal 2027 Results

CHANDLER, Ariz., Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- VIAVI (NASDAQ: VIAV) today reported results for its fiscal first quarter ended October 3, 2026 with the following highlights.

"Fiscal 2027 is off to a strong start with first quarter performance coming in above the high end of our guidance. We expect our growth momentum to continue driven by the inherent market demand and expanding opportunities in data center and aerospace and defense end markets," said Oleg Khaykin, VIAVI's President and Chief Executive Officer.

The tables below (in millions, except percentage and per share data) provide comparisons of quarterly results to prior periods, including sequential quarterly and year-over-year changes. A full reconciliation between the GAAP and non-GAAP measures included in the tables is contained in this release under the section titled "Use of Non-GAAP (Adjusted) Financial Measures."

Fiscal First Quarter Ended October 3, 2026

Optical Security and Performance Products

On November 1, 2026, the Board of Directors authorized a new common stock repurchase program that will allow the Company to repurchase up to $500 million of the Company's common stock. This authorization is in addition to the $300 million previously authorized by the Board of Directors under the 2022 Repurchase Plan, which has approximately $18.4 million remaining. Under the new repurchase program, the Company may purchase shares of common stock from time to time through a variety of methods, which may include but are not limited to open market purchases, the implementation of a 10b5-1 plan, accelerated stock repurchases, privately negotiated transactions and/or any other available methods in accordance with Securities and Exchange Commission and other applicable legal requirements. The Company is not obligated to repurchase any particular amount of common stock, and the repurchase program will remain in effect until the amount authorized has been fully repurchased or until the Company suspends or terminates the program.

Business Outlook for the Second Quarter of Fiscal 2027

For the second quarter of fiscal 2027 ending January 2, 2027, the Company expects net revenue to be between $505 million to $515 million and non-GAAP EPS to be between $0.50 to $0.52.

With respect to our expectations above, the Company has not reconciled GAAP net income (loss) per share to non-GAAP EPS in this press release because it is unable to provide a meaningful or accurate estimate of certain reconciling items described in the "Use of Non-GAAP (Adjusted) Financial Measures" section below and the information is not available without unreasonable effort as a result of the inherent difficulty of forecasting the timing and/or amounts of certain items, including certain charges related to restructuring, acquisition, integration and related charges. For the same reasons, the Company is unable to address the probable significance of the unavailable information, which could have a potentially unpredictable and potentially significant impact on our future GAAP financial results. In addition, the Company believes such reconciliations would imply a degree of precision that may be confusing or misleading to investors.

The Company will discuss these results and other related matters at 1:30 p.m. Pacific Time on November 4, 2026 in a live webcast, which will also be archived for replay on the Company's website at https://investor.viavisolutions.com. The Company will post supplementary slides outlining the Company's latest financial results on https://investor.viavisolutions.com under the "Quarterly Results" section concurrently with this earnings press release. This press release is being furnished as a Current Report on Form 8-K with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and will be available at www.sec.gov.

VIAVI (NASDAQ: VIAV) is a global leader in test and measurement and optical technologies. Our test and measurement, and resilient position, navigation and timing solutions enable and secure critical infrastructure ranging from data center ecosystems and communication networks to military, aerospace, railway and first responder communications. In addition, we develop and advance technologies used in high-volume optical applications across anti-counterfeiting, consumer electronics, aerospace, industrial and automotive end markets.

Learn more about VIAVI at www.viavisolutions.com. Follow us on VIAVI Perspectives, LinkedIn and YouTube.

(d) competitive pressures; (e) unforeseen changes or deceleration in the demand for current and new products, technologies, services, delays or unforeseen events in the roll-out of new industry platforms or evolving technology such as 3D sensing and customer purchasing delays due to macroeconomic conditions, tightening of expenditures or as they assess or transition to such new technologies and/or architectures, all of which limit near-term demand visibility, and could negatively impact potential revenue; (f) continued decline of average selling prices across our businesses; (g) notable seasonality and a significant level of in-quarter book-and-ship business; (h) various product and manufacturing transfers, site consolidations, product discontinuances and restructuring and workforce reduction plans, including the number of employees impacted by a restructuring plan, the estimated expenses the Company will recognize, the timing of these payments and expenses, and anticipated cost savings associated with such plans; (i) challenges in execution of business strategy; (j) financial projections and growth strategies, including those tied to sustained customer demand and capital expenditure related to the data center ecosystem, continued growth in aerospace and defense, multi-year service provider refresh cycles and longer-term recovery of our Wireless business; (k) expectations regarding profitability of certain business units, synergies, benefits and other matters related to the acquisition of the high-speed ethernet, network security and channel emulation testing business of Spirent Communications plc; (l) challenges integrating the businesses the Company has acquired and realizing all of the expected benefits and savings; (m) supply chain and materials constraints, including component constraints and the ability of our suppliers and contract manufacturers to meet production and delivery requirements to our forecasted demand; (n) potential disruptions or delays to our manufacturing and operations due to climate conditions and natural disasters in the regions where we operate, such as wildfires, drought conditions and related water shortages in Arizona, as well as wildfires in Northern California and related blackouts and power outages in that region; (o) the uncertain and ongoing impact to our supply chain of geopolitical tensions, such as the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine and the instability in the Middle East, evolving global trade and tariff negotiations and the uncertain tariff landscape, sanctions and other trade measures imposed by domestic and foreign governments, adverse actions and escalating tensions with foreign governments, including China, and the possibility of escalation of "trade wars," cyber-attacks, and retaliatory measures; (p) the impact of infectious disease outbreaks, epidemics, and pandemics on our financial results, revenues, customer demand, business operations and manufacturing and on the business operations of our customers, contract manufacturers and suppliers; and (q) inherent uncertainty related to global markets, including inflationary pressures, recessions, stock price and equity market volatility, tightening monetary policy and liquidity, and the effect of such markets on demand for our products. Use of Non-GAAP (Adjusted) Financial Measures

The Company provides non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP operating margin, non-GAAP net income and non-GAAP EPS financial measures as supplemental information regarding the Company's operational performance and believes providing this additional information allows investors to see Company results through the eyes of management, to evaluate more clearly and consistently the Company's core operational performance and expenses and evaluate the efficacy of the methodology used by management to measure such performance. The Company uses the measures disclosed in this release to evaluate the Company's historical and prospective financial performance, as well as its performance relative to its competitors. Specifically, management uses these items to further its own understanding of the Company's core operating performance, which the Company believes represents its performance in the ordinary, ongoing and customary course of its operations. Accordingly, management excludes from core operating performance items such as those relating to certain purchase price accounting adjustments, amortization of acquisition related intangibles, amortization expense related to acquisition related inventory step-up, stock-based compensation, legal settlements, restructuring, changes in fair value of contingent consideration liabilities, certain investing and acquisition related expenses and other activities and income tax expenses or benefits that management believes are not reflective of such ordinary, ongoing and core operating activities. The non-GAAP adjustments are outlined below.

Cost of revenues, costs of research and development and costs of selling, general and administrative: The Company's GAAP presentation of gross margin and operating expenses may include (i) additional depreciation and amortization from changes in estimated useful life and the write-down of certain property, plant and equipment and intangibles, (ii) charges such as severance, benefits and outplacement costs related to restructuring plans with a specific and defined term, (iii) costs for facilities not required for ongoing operations, and costs related to the relocation of certain equipment from these facilities and/or contract manufacturer facilities, (iv) stock-based compensation, including related employer payroll taxes, (v) amortization expense related to acquired intangibles, (vi) amortization expense related to acquisition related inventory step-up, (vii) changes in fair value of contingent consideration liabilities, (viii) acquisition related transaction and integration costs related to acquired entities, (ix) significant legal settlements and other contingencies and (x) other charges unrelated to our core operating performance comprised mainly of other costs and contingencies unrelated to current and future operations, including transformational initiatives such as the implementation of simplified automated processes, site consolidations, and reorganizations. The Company excludes these items in calculating non-GAAP operating margin, non-GAAP net income and non-GAAP EPS.

Non-cash interest expense and other expense: The Company excludes certain non-cash interest and other expenses, including loss on debt extinguishment, accretion of debt discount, and other non-cash activities that management believes are not reflective of such ordinary, ongoing and core operating activities, when calculating non-GAAP net income and non-GAAP EPS.

Income tax expense or benefit: The Company excludes certain non-cash tax expense or benefit items, such as (i) the utilization of net operating losses (NOLs) where valuation allowances were released, (ii) intra-period tax allocation benefit and (iii) the tax effect for amortization of non-tax deductible intangible assets, in calculating non-GAAP net income and non-GAAP EPS.

Non-GAAP financial measures are not in accordance with, preferable to, or an alternative for, generally accepted accounting principles in the United States. The GAAP measure most directly comparable to non-GAAP operating income is operating income. The GAAP measure most directly comparable to non-GAAP operating margin is operating margin. The GAAP measure most directly comparable to non-GAAP net income is net income. The GAAP measure most directly comparable to non-GAAP EPS is earnings per share.

#5533. VMware gets simpler AI deployment and low-cost version for basic private clouds

Broadcom Inc. is expanding its VMware portfolio with new capabilities that simplify artificial intelligence workload deployment, strengthen infrastructure security and simplify disaster recovery.

The company is also introducing a lower-cost virtualization platform aimed at smaller customers that don’t need a full private cloud platform.

Today’s updates span VMware Cloud Foundation, the company’s flagship private cloud platform, and a collection of optional advanced services. Several capabilities are already available in VCF 9.1.1, which was released in September, while others are scheduled for the first quarter of Broadcom’s 2027 fiscal year, which began on Monday.

The changes are part of a broader Broadcom effort to position VCF as a common infrastructure platform for traditional virtual machines, containers and increasingly demanding AI workloads.

More than 2,600 customers had deployed VCF 9 as of September, representing more than 24 million allocated cores, according to Prashanth Shenoy (pictured), Broadcom’s chief marketing officer and vice president of marketing for cloud platform, infrastructure and solutions.

Broadcom is introducing AI Infrastructure Quickstart, an automated deployment capability designed to simplify the initial configuration of private AI environments.

It combines vCenter cluster deployment, vSphere Supervisor activation and VMware Kubernetes Service cluster provisioning into a single workflow, replacing multiple manual configuration processes. “We have consolidated all of that, made a quick start workflow and streamlined the workflow completely so they can get it up and running day zero in a matter of minutes,” Shenoy said.

Broadcom is also adding native S3-compatible object storage through VMware vSAN. The feature, expected to become generally available in the upcoming VCF release, supports AI applications that depend heavily on unstructured data and lets developers provision storage through self-service interfaces.

On the security front, Broadcom is incorporating additional capabilities directly into VCF rather than requiring customers to purchase them separately. These include confidential computing support for Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. processors, which was already available in VCF 9.1.1, as well as planned policy-based virtual private cloud connectivity and automated infrastructure configuration compliance.

Broadcom said the compliance features will continuously monitor infrastructure settings against industry benchmarks, identify configuration drift and provide remediation guidance.

The virtualization maker is also moving disaster recovery functionality into the core VCF and VMware vSphere Foundation platforms. The capability will provide orchestrated recovery across thousands of workloads, including recovery from outages, equipment failures and natural disasters.

Additional protection will be available through VMware HyperArmor, a previously announced service that provides hypervisor-level defenses including virtual patching, continuous monitoring and multifactor authentication.

Two other advanced services, VMware Live Recovery and VMware Compliance and Configuration Management, address cyber recovery and continuous compliance enforcement for virtual machines and containers.

The company is also broadening its portfolio at the lower end with VMware vSphere Express, a new offering for environments containing up to 128 processor cores. Based on vSphere 9, Express includes live virtual machine migration, high availability, distributed networking, security and simplified patching.

Shenoy said the product is intended for customers that need basic virtualization without purchasing the more comprehensive and costly VMware vSphere Foundation or VCF platforms. “They don’t need a whole cloud in their two-server environment,” he said.

Customers can upgrade to the larger platforms as their requirements grow. Broadcom didn’t disclose pricing, although Shenoy indicated Express would be substantially less expensive than its higher-end offerings.

#5532. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#5531. Ballot roulette: Florida voters pick property tax break over local services

Florida voters approved a homestead exemption expansion with 62% support, with increases to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Opponents warned of public safety and service impacts, and state analysts projected nearly $5 billion in lost local revenue in 2027-28.  AI Summary

With the cost of living on the ballot, Florida voters approved a major tax break for homeowners.

The amendment to increase the Sunshine State’s homestead exemption won the 60% it needed on election night. Voters weren’t swayed by warnings that the higher exemption would devastate municipal coffers and services.

The ballot measure was given little chance of winning. But current economic conditions proved an insurmountable obstacle for the argument against the measure.

Unofficial returns showed it finishing with 62% of the vote. The changes take effect in phases starting in 2027.

“An incredible victory for Florida homeowners!” the Florida Republican Party wrote on social media. “More money stays in your pocket.”

Neil Schiller, managing partner at Government Law Group, told HousingWire TBD the result will change how cities weigh development.

“Projects that generate jobs, economic activity, and alternative tax revenues may become more attractive, while developments that require significant public services and infrastructure will face greater financial scrutiny,” Schiller said. “Amendment 3 may be remembered as the moment Florida cities had to fundamentally reinvent how they do business.”

The vote shows how important affordability has become, Andrew Hellinger, co-principal at Urban-X Group, developer of River Landing Shops & Residences in Miami, said in an e-mail to HousingWire TBD.

Hellinger added, “However, people still need roads, public transportation and essential community services, and those have to be paid for.”

The amendment replaces the $50,000 homestead exemption with a phased increase. It rises to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Only primary residences qualify, so second-home and investment-property owners get nothing.

Homeowners must establish Florida residency by Dec. 31, 2026, to get the full benefit. Later arrivals get the $50,000 exemption for four years before qualifying. The school board levy is excluded.

The measure also cuts the annual assessment cap on non-homestead commercial property from 10% to 5%. That change starts Jan. 1, 2027. Renters, who occupy about a third of Florida’s housing units, get no relief.

Gov. Ron DeSantis called a special session to put the amendment on the ballot. Lawmakers approved it with changes protecting school funding. DeSantis had sought a broader exemption.

DeSantis cast the measure as a fix for tax bills inflated by pandemic-era migration. Newcomers, led by New Yorkers, overwhelmed the housing supply and lifted values and tax burdens for longtime residents. Florida home prices rose more than 50% between 2020 and 2022.

Prices have since stalled, and the average home value fell 3.7% over the past year. Assessments haven’t followed: under the Save Our Homes recapture rule, they keep rising until they meet market value. The annual increase is capped at 3% or inflation, whichever is less.

Most counties held millage rates steady or cut them, yet bills still climbed. City tax bills statewide rose about 50% on average over several years.

The Florida Sheriffs Association said in August it was “significantly concerned.” By mid-September, it was running ads featuring sheriffs from four counties. One said, “We want a tax cut too, but Amendment 3 is the wrong way to do it.”

Association President Billy Woods warned of fewer deputies, slower 911 response and more crime. Opponents also included the Florida State Fraternal Order of Police, Florida Professional Firefighters and Florida Fire Chiefs Association. The Florida League of Cities and Florida Association of Counties opposed it, citing too much uncertainty.

According to the legislature’s economic research office, estimated local governments would lose nearly $5 billion in 2027-28.

The Florida Policy Institute, a progressive think tank, created Floridians for Shared Prosperity, which sponsored a campaign urging a no vote.

“Amendment 3 will leave working families and seniors with a lose-lose choice: pay more through new fees and higher taxes or face major cuts to the services you depend on,” the campaign’s website stated.

Voters approved the amendment anyway, with encouragement from the Florida Realtors and others in real estate.

“This is your one shot at real property tax relief,” apartment owner and investor Grant Washington wrote on social media Monday. “Vote Yes on Amendment 3 and put your money back where it belongs. In your pocket!”

#5530. Dave Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results

Q3 Revenue Growth Accelerates to 31% Y/Y to $198 Million, Driven by Record New Member Acquisition as well as Continued MTM Growth and ARPU Expansion

28-DPD Rate Improves Y/Y and Q/Q to 2.09%, Falling Below 2.00% in September; Net Monetization Rate Expands to 5.2%, Its Highest Level in Five Years

Net Income of $64 Million; Adj. EBITDA Increases 39% Y/Y to $82 Million, Representing a 41% Margin

Raises 2026 Revenue, Adj. EBITDA and Adj. Diluted EPS Guidance

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Dave Inc. ("Dave" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: DAVE), one of the nation's leading neobanks, today reported its financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026.

"Q3 was another strong quarter, with revenue growth accelerating to 31% year-over-year, driven by faster MTM growth and continued ARPU expansion," said Jason Wilk, Founder and CEO of Dave. "Our 28-day past due rate improved year-over-year and sequentially to 2.09%, even as originations grew 23% from a year ago. In September, with CashAI v6.0 fully deployed, average ExtraCash size reached $225, our 28-day past due rate fell below 2.00%, and our gross monetization rate was approximately 7.0% as we relaxed legacy fee caps. Together, these changes let us responsibly extend more credit while delivering greater value to members and strengthening unit economics. Based on this momentum, we are raising our full-year 2026 guidance for Revenue, Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Diluted EPS."

Wilk added, "We are also seeing solid early traction with Dave Flex, our new Pay in Four credit card that gives members greater flexibility in managing everyday purchases. During Q3, we grew Dave Flex adoption from single- to double-digit thousand actives, through both cross-selling to existing members and direct customer acquisition at better-than-expected acquisition costs. We are additionally encouraged by strong cross product adoption with ExtraCash that suggests significant upside to baseline member lifetime value. We are excited to continue expanding access to more members ahead of a broader rollout planned for 2027."

1 Beginning in the third quarter of 2026, the Company updated its calculation of MTMs to exclude Members whose only monthly activity was low-engagement, non-monetized activity related to Goals accounts. Prior periods have been recast to ensure comparability.

Liquidity SummaryAs of September 30, 2026, the Company had $315 million in cash and cash equivalents, investments, and restricted cash, compared to $254 million as of June 30, 2026. The Company's funding structure with Coastal Community Bank had approximately $159 million outstanding at quarter end, up from $93 million as of June 30, 2026. During the third quarter, the Company deployed approximately $20 million to reduce its share count through restricted stock unit net settlements and open market share repurchases, leaving $88 million available under its share repurchase authorization. Subsequent to quarter end, in early October 2026, the Company repaid the $75 million outstanding under its debt facility with Victory Park Management, LLC.

The variability of these items could have a significant impact on our future GAAP financial results.

Dave's CFO and COO, Kyle Beilman, commented: "Q3 demonstrated the operating leverage of our model. Adjusted EBITDA grew 39% year-over-year to $82 million, even as we increased marketing investment by over 50%. Attractive returns at higher spend levels supported investment above our prior plan.

"Non-GAAP gross margin was 70%, up from 69% a year ago and compared with 72% last quarter. Coastal funding costs accounted for about 100 basis points of the sequential change, as the transition moved faster than expected and freed up significant liquidity. Provision accounts for most of the remaining change. Provision reflects portfolio growth, mix, and credit performance so it can move differently from static pool delinquency and loss rates, which we believe more directly measure credit quality. Static pool loss rates are tracking flat to down year-over-year, though our prior provision forecast assumed a larger improvement based on the strong early repayment performance we had observed coming out of spring. We've recalibrated our forecast accordingly, and our raised outlook reflects that adjustment.

"Q4 credit is tracking in line with September, and we expect the quarter's 28-day past due rate to be below 2.00%. Based on our updated forecast, we expect better sequential loss rates and Q4 non-GAAP gross margin above Q2 levels. Strong credit, higher monetization, seasoning of record new-member cohorts and more capital-efficient funding position us to accelerate growth and capital return."

The Company defines and calculates adjusted EBITDA as GAAP net income before the impact of interest income and/or expense, and funding costs, provision for income taxes, depreciation and amortization, and adjusted to exclude legal settlement expenses, litigation expenses related to the FTC/DOJ matter, stock-based compensation expense, other strategic financing and transactional expenses, discretionary or non-recurring income, changes in fair value of earnout liabilities and changes in fair value of warrant liabilities. The Company defines and calculates adjusted EBITDA margin as adjusted EBITDA as a percentage of GAAP operating revenues, net. The Company defines and calculates variable operating expenses as provision for credit losses, processing and servicing costs and financial network and transaction costs. The Company defines and calculates non-GAAP gross profit as GAAP operating revenues, net excluding variable operating expenses. The Company defines and calculates non-GAAP gross profit margin as non-GAAP gross profit as a percentage of GAAP operating revenues, net. The Company defines and calculates adjusted net income as GAAP net income adjusted to exclude stock-based compensation, discretionary or non-recurring income, legal settlement expenses, litigation expenses related to the FTC/DOJ matter, other strategic financing and transactional expenses, changes in fair value of earnout liabilities and changes in fair value of warrant liabilities, the income tax impact related to the release of the valuation allowance and the income tax impact related to stock-based compensation. The Company defines and calculates non-GAAP adjusted net income per share - basic and non-GAAP adjusted net income per share - diluted as adjusted net income divided by weighted average shares of common stock-basic and adjusted weighted average shares of common stock-diluted, respectively. The Company defines and calculates adjusted weighted average shares of common stock-diluted as GAAP diluted weighted average shares, adjusted to include the benefit expected to be provided by existing capped call transactions entered into in connection with the 2031 convertible notes to offset the dilutive impact of the notes.

These non-GAAP financial measures may be helpful to the user in assessing our operating performance and facilitate an alternative comparison among fiscal periods. The Company's management team uses these non-GAAP financial measures in assessing performance, as well as in planning and forecasting future periods. The methods the Company uses to compute these non-GAAP financial measures may differ from the methods used by other companies. Non-GAAP financial measures are supplemental, should not be considered a substitute for financial information presented in accordance with GAAP and should be read only in conjunction with our condensed consolidated financial statements prepared in accordance with GAAP.

#5529. Smartsheet AI-powered platform bridges gap between planning and results

Smartsheet Inc. today introduced an artificial intelligence-powered planning and execution platform designed to help enterprises identify when projects are veering off course and take corrective action before delays and cost overruns become serious problems.

Announced at the company’s Engage 2026 conference, the new vsActual platform — pronounced “versus actual” — uses AI agents to continuously monitor work across multiple enterprise systems, compare progress against strategic objectives and recommend adjustments. The company also announced new agentic workflow capabilities, integrations and security controls for its existing work management platform.

The centerpiece of vsActual is what Smartsheet calls Execution Graph, a knowledge graph built from what the company said are two decades of workflow data encompassing millions of projects and nine petabytes of information. The graph maps relationships between tasks, projects, programs and strategic objectives to help AI agents understand how changes in one part of an organization affect others.

The company’s goal is to address a growing disconnect between individual productivity improvements enabled by AI and measurable organizational results, said Pratima Arora, Smartsheet’s chief product and technology officer.

“We were seeing a lot of intelligence and productivity gains getting stuck at an individual level and not translating to a team and organization level,” she said.

VsActual is designed to operate across existing enterprise applications rather than require organizations to consolidate work onto a single platform. It can connect to applications from Oracle Corp., SAP SE, Workday Inc., Atlassian Corp. PLC and ServiceNow Inc. to gather information about budgets, schedules, staffing and project dependencies.

Smartsheet said AI agents can turn strategy documents, spreadsheets and budget proposals into structured plans, model alternative scenarios and monitor execution against those plans. A drift-detection agent (pictured) continuously searches for emerging problems, while other agents generate executive reports and recommend changes as business priorities evolve.

The system can also trace the consequences of disruptions across organizational hierarchies. “If there is a delay in a Jira ticket that has impact five levels up, we can detect it and tell you what is happening,” Arora said.

Smartsheet said its historical workflow data provides an advantage over competing planning and work management products. Execution Graph builds on an existing Amazon Web Services Inc. Neptune knowledge graph containing approximately 100 million nodes and incorporates information about workflow patterns, dependencies and collaboration, Arora said.

The company uses multiple foundation models, selecting them based on workload requirements and cost. AWS and Databricks Inc. are its major underlying technology providers. Arora said Smartsheet isn’t training its own large language models.

The announcements also expand Smartsheet’s existing AI capabilities. New Agentic Workflows allow users to schedule recurring activities such as status reports and risk assessments. Specialized creation and data-quality agents can generate project structures, dashboards and reports or identify problems in underlying data.

New integrations include native connections to ServiceNow, Microsoft Corp. Dynamics 365, HubSpot Inc. customer relationship management, Workday Inc. human resources software and Intuit Inc.’s QuickBooks. Conversational integrations with GitHub, Zendesk Inc., Airtable and Monday.com Ltd. are entering early access, with additional AI-assisted integrations planned for early 2027.

Arora emphasized that agentic workflows combine conventional automation with AI rather than relying exclusively on large language models. “This industry overuses LLMs sometimes where it is just simple deterministic action,” she said.

Although some agents can execute scheduled tasks automatically, Arora said human approval remains the default approach for consequential actions. “Our default stance is human in the loop,” she said.

The compay also announced International Organization for Standardization/International Electrotechnical Commission 42001 certification, security event streaming and data classification capabilities intended to strengthen oversight of AI operations.

Smartsheet developed vsActual with about a dozen enterprise design partners. The company publishes pricing on its website.
