#5514. Mortgage policy faces tight runway in split Washington

Democrats now control both chambers of Congress while President Trump retains the White House and agency leadership. Trade groups including the MBA and ALTA are pushing for cost relief, FHA premium cuts and stronger consumer protections, while analysts warn that geopolitical tensions, looming debt ceiling fights and tougher confirmations at agencies like the CFPB will keep rates and regulatory timelines uncertain.  AI Summary

Housing and mortgage industry leaders say there is room for housing policy to move in Congress even as Washington, D.C., divides power between a Democratic-controlled House and Senate and a Republican-led White House.

Democrats captured both chambers on Tuesday night, but any housing bills under the new leadership will need support from President Donald Trump and enough Republican votes to clear the Senate. “Voters made it clear that affordability is a central concern, and housing is the biggest line item in most family budgets,” said Isaac Boltansky, head of public policy at Pennymac. “The ROAD to Housing Act laid a solid foundation, and we believe lawmakers on both sides of the aisle should work on a ROAD to Housing 2.0 package that builds on it and helps more families buy and keep a home.”

Asked what should be included in a 2.0 package, Boltansky cited the lock-in effect created by capital gains taxes, which can discourage homeowners from selling, and the Neighborhood Homes Investment Act as a “good starting point.”

The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) said in a statement that housing remains a bipartisan issue and it will “work with new and returning lawmakers as well as the Trump administration to advance common sense proposals to lower costs.”

The trade group in October released a policy road map to reduce closing costs, expand credit access and lower rental housing financing costs. Its proposals include easing tri-merge credit report use, aligning loan-level price adjustments (LLPAs) and lowering the annual mortgage insurance premium for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans.

Scott Norman, CEO of the Texas Mortgage Bankers Association, told HousingWire that the election shifts power but also creates opportunity for policy changes.

“It was a surprising night, but every election brings opportunity,” Norman said. “In Austin and in Washington, a gavel is something you borrow, and last night voters took a few back. That’s the system working as designed. No chairmanship belongs to the person holding it, and no majority is permanent. In much of the world, a change in power signals a crisis. Here, it simply means new leadership and a fresh look at policy.”

The American Land Title Association (ALTA) said that as policymakers continue addressing housing affordability challenges, consumer protection must remain part of the conversation.

“Fraud is unaffordable, and increasingly sophisticated schemes are putting American homeowners and their property rights at risk,” ALTA said.

Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said many Democratic campaigns emphasized economic issues, but the impact of the elections on the broader economy and mortgage rates is still unclear.

“Democrats have a clear mandate to focus on pocketbook issues, but whether they can translate that into a legislative agenda that delivers on that mandate remains to be seen,” Krimmel said.

Krimmel pointed to the conflict in the Middle East as a key variable. He said uncertainty remains around how the election outcome will affect the Iran war, which has been a source of inflation pressure. Democrats have been vocal critics of the conflict, and a resolution that improves oil supply would likely ease inflation and “potentially provide relief for mortgage rates.”

“Wanting the conflict to end, and finding terms that work for all involved are two different things,” Krimmel said.

On fiscal policy, Boltansky said another debt ceiling confrontation is likely in 2027: “Any focus on addressing the country’s harrowing fiscal trajectory would be welcome for the bond market, which obviously has a direct impact on rates,” he said.

While Congress can set agendas and control oversight, executive branch leadership will still drive most regulatory implementation for housing and mortgage markets.

Tim Rood, founder and CEO of Washington, D.C.-based advisory and technology firm Impact Capitol, said in his newsletter that Democratic majorities can control the agendas for the House financial services and Senate banking committees, investigate agencies, shape spending negotiations and withhold Senate confirmation of nominees when the new Congress convenes in January.

But he pointed out that Trump retains executive authority and leadership at agencies “does not change automatically with Congress.”

Rood said that for mortgage executives, the new alignment means more hearings, tougher confirmations and a more contested implementation calendar, “not an overnight rewrite of the rules.”

“The real fight will be over which existing policies can still be executed, funded and defended,” he said.

One closely watched appointment is Brian Johnson’s nomination to lead the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). An attorney told HousingWire the confirmation is now at risk as Democrats may demand additional representation across financial agencies as part of broader negotiations.

The same attorney said one of the industry’s top regulatory priorities — changes to the loan originator compensation rule — remains unresolved.

“There are things that both sides of the aisle could help, like increase the availability of credit to borrowers by allowing lenders to claw back compensation in certain situations or compete. Maybe something will happen that is coordinated, but I think it’s kind of open in the air at the moment,” the attorney said.

Editor’s note: Sarah Wheeler contributed reporting to this story.

#5513. First Trades of Tokenized U.S. Equity under SEC Innovation Exemption Executed on the Canton Network

Shares of CNTN, Canton Strategic Holdings' Common Stock, Traded Between Verified Counterparties including Five North, DRW Cumberland, and Flowdesk on Tradecraft's TSV

Trades Mark the First Transactions in Issuer-Sponsored Tokenized NMS Stock, with Fairmint's Onchain Transfer Agent, Under the SEC's Innovation Exemption for Onshore U.S. Equities

NEW YORK, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Canton Strategic Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: CNTN) ("Canton Strategic Holdings" or the "Company") today announced the first trades of its issuer-sponsored tokenized common stock on TSV LLC ("TSV"), the permissioned venue for tokenized NMS stocks on the Canton Network. Fairmint TA LLC ("Fairmint"), the Company's SEC-registered transfer agent, recorded the shares in token form. The trades were executed on November 4 through a permissioned pool on Tradecraft, the automated market maker protocol that powers TSV, and settled atomically on the Canton Network, with Five North, the existing shareholder and seller; DRW Cumberland, the buyer; and Flowdesk Liquidity Solutions LLC ("Flowdesk"), the liquidity provider. These trades are the first of their kind under the SEC's September 17 Innovation Exemption and follow the Company's October 29 announcement of its agreement to make its shares of common stock available to trade on TSV.

Five North, an existing shareholder of the Company, requested that its shares of CNTN common stock be registered in tokenized form. Fairmint, on behalf of the Company, recorded the issuer-sponsored tokenized shares directly with Five North's verified Loop Wallet, moving its position from a broker-dealer account onto the Company's onchain shareholder register. A pool operated by TSV was then established among liquidity providers, including Flowdesk and DRW Cumberland, where Flowdesk provided liquidity and DRW Cumberland executed the first purchases of tokenized CNTN common stock.

TSV offers shareholders of the Company's tokenized shares the ability to participate in its automated market maker on the Tradecraft protocol, allowing for 24/7 trading availability, atomic settlement, and limiting access to verified holders. Only holders whose identity and wallets have been verified and approved to get a holder account by the transfer agent Fairmint can hold and trade the tokenized shares, with requirements for identity verification and sanctions screening.

"We set out to make our first listing the standard for how tokenized U.S. equities should work under the SEC's Innovation Exemption," said Ryan Trinkle, Co-Founder of TSV. "The token is issuer-sponsored and carries the same rights as the CNTN stock that trades on Nasdaq. Fairmint, an SEC-registered transfer agent, keeps the official record, and every holder is verified before they can hold or trade. On Tradecraft, approved investors can now trade at any hour, and shares and payment settle atomically on the Canton Network."

The Company's tokenized shares are issued on behalf of the Company as issuer-sponsored shares by Fairmint, the Company's SEC-registered transfer agent and a subsidiary of Fairmint, Inc. Fairmint maintains the official onchain record of ownership on the Canton Network, operates the allow list of verified holders and wallets, and applies the Company's transfer controls. Holders of these issuer-sponsored tokenized shares receive the same rights and privileges as those holding the Company's stock via Nasdaq.

"This is a landmark for U.S. equity markets: a Nasdaq-listed company's actual stock trading onchain, with shareholder rights intact and Fairmint maintaining the official ownership record," said Joris Delanoue, CEO and co-founder of Fairmint. "A blockchain can settle a trade, but it takes an accountable transfer agent to say who legally owns the share. Since we founded Fairmint, we've been building toward a market where equity is programmable and ownership moves with it. Today, we've put our infrastructure to work on the Canton Network with Canton Strategic Holdings and TSV. This trade opens a path for public companies to bring their shares onchain while retaining control."

"The SEC has opened a path for U.S. listed securities to trade onchain. Our job is to make sure that path has reliable liquidity from the very first trade. Being among the first covered firms under the Innovation Exemption is exactly what we've been building toward," said Reed Werbitt, U.S. CEO and Global CRO of Flowdesk.

"Canton was built so institutions could move real assets on chain with confidence. Today a Nasdaq-listed company's shares were tokenized, held in Loop Wallet, and settled on the network within the SEC's new framework. We're proud Five North helped make the first trade happen," said Yiannis Varelas, Founder and CEO of Five North.

Canton Strategic Holdings is an investor and active participant in the Canton Network ecosystem, providing both capital and insights to further the integration of the network into modern financial systems. As a Super Validator on the Canton Network and a member of the Canton Foundation, the Company continues to support and help secure the network in line with its commitment to strengthening the ecosystem.

Canton Strategic Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: CNTN) is the first publicly traded company to leverage Canton Coin and support the Canton Network to advance institutional blockchain adoption and the digitization of financial markets. In addition to its operating business that drives value through activities on the Canton Network, the Company is a strategic investor in the Canton ecosystem. For more information, visit www.cantonstrategic.com.

TSV LLC, founded by Ali Abrar and Ryan Trinkle, is the first Tokenized Securities Venue to complete the SEC's Innovation Exemption process set out in Release No. 34-106402. The venue and platform enable approved participants to provide liquidity and trade tokenized NMS stocks through automated market maker pools on the Tradecraft protocol on the Canton Network. The Tradecraft protocol is the leading automated market maker protocol on the Canton Network, developed by Obsidian Software LLC. The venue is designed to be available 24/7 subject to regulatorily required trading stoppages, maintenance, risk controls, and trading volume limits. Settlement is atomic on Canton: both sides of a trade transfer together, or neither does, in an instantaneous Delivery versus Payment transaction. Participants and their wallets must be approved before trading, including identity verification and sanctions screening, and smart contracts enforce these rules on every token transfer. Learn more at tokenizedstockvenue.com.

Fairmint is building the onchain Equity Capital Markets platform to bring recordkeeping and liquidity onto the same rails. Its subsidiary Fairmint TA LLC (formerly Fair FP LLC) is an SEC-registered transfer agent (file no. 084-06901) offering issuers an onchain solution to preserve issuer control and maintain shareholder rights. Founded in 2019 by Joris Delanoue and Thibauld Favre, Fairmint developed the Open Cap Table Protocol, and is a governing member of the Open Cap Table Coalition, which stewards the industry's open-source standard. For more information, visit fairmint.com.

Since its founding in 2014, DRW Cumberland has provided liquidity across global digital asset markets and helped build the systems and relationships institutions rely on to trade them. Across DRW, our teams bring Cumberland's digital asset expertise together with more than three decades of the firm's experience in traditional markets, trading, risk management, market structure and technology. Together, we bring the right capabilities to each opportunity and provide institutions with deep liquidity and sophisticated execution as traditional finance and digital assets converge. Learn more at drw.com.

Five North operates and builds for the network it invests in. As a Super Validator on the Canton Network, Five North takes part in securing and governing the network, backs the teams building on it through Canton Ventures, and develops Loop, the wallet, data and developer tools that connect institutions to Canton. Learn more at fivenorth.io and looptech.io.

Flowdesk Group is a full-service digital asset trading and technology firm specializing in liquidity solutions and OTC trading. With offices globally, Flowdesk Group combines deep financial and crypto expertise with algorithmic and proprietary trading systems to connect digital assets to global liquidity. Flowdesk Group's technology is engineered to bring clarity and precision to digital asset and tokenized asset markets. Learn more at flowdesk.co.

#5512. Vitalik Devcon Cosplay Steals the Show as Bitmine Loads Up on More Ethereum

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Devcon attendees got an unexpected laugh when Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin appeared on stage wearing a green cloak and a smiling mask. The unusual cosplay stole the spotlight as Bitmine ETH accumulation continued, with the company adding another 8,573 Ethereum to its massive treasury.

Buterin’s costume looked more suited to a fantasy game than one of crypto’s biggest developer gatherings. The playful Vitalik appearance offered a lighter moment at Devcon 8 in Mumbai, where developers and researchers are discussing Ethereum’s future.

Meanwhile, Bitmine Immersion Technologies is pursuing a much more serious mission: accumulating enough ETH to control 5% of its total supply. The company’s latest disclosure showed holdings of 6,060,506 ETH as of November 1, worth $13.7 billion at its current price of $2,261. Bitmine now controls around 4.9% of Ethereum’s supply, putting it close to its ambitious accumulation target.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Devcon 8 runs from November 3 to November 6 in Mumbai, bringing Ethereum developers, researchers, and ecosystem participants together for four days of talks and workshops. But Buterin’s unusual outfit delivered an unexpected highlight during the event.

The Vitalik Devcon appearance showed the lighter side of Ethereum’s culture, even as the network faces serious questions about adoption, scaling, and ETH’s market performance.

@VitalikButerin just opened Devcon and set the tone for the week.A formally verified OS, open silicon, self-sovereign healthtech, free discourse, private communication, trustworthy AI — these are all part of Ethereum's mission. https://t.co/51UfMsxk5o pic.twitter.com/TynzSuzmhX

Bitmine, however, appears unfazed by the market uncertainty. The company purchased 8,573 ETH during the latest reported week, worth roughly $19.4 million at its disclosed valuation. Its total crypto, cash, and other investments reached $14.5 billion, including 216 BTC and $498 million in cash and marketable securities.

🧵1/BitMine provided its latest holdings update for November 2, 2026$14.5 billion in total crypto + "moonshots":– 6,060,506 ETH at $2,261per ETH (per @coinbase)– 216 Bitcoin (BTC)– $180 million stake in Beast Industries @MrBeast– $82 million stake in Eightco Holdings…

Bitmine has also staked 5.23 million ETH, representing 86% of its holdings. The company estimates that its current staking position could generate around $358 million in annualized rewards, potentially rising to $415 million if its entire ETH treasury were staked.

That creates a second part of its Ethereum thesis. Accumulating the asset while generating yield from the network.

Ethereum’s bullish outlook rests on more than Bitmine’s buying activity. Staking removes ETH from immediate trading circulation, while institutional treasury accumulation can add another source of demand. Bitmine’s holdings alone now represent nearly one in every 20 ETH in existence.

The company’s growing staking position also shows Ethereum’s proof-of-stake model, where holders can earn rewards by helping secure the network. Bitmine’s projected staking income gives it an incentive to maintain its ETH exposure rather than simply trade around short-term price moves.

Price forecasts remain ambitious. Bitmine Chairman Tom Lee has suggested Ethereum could revisit its previous all-time high near $4,954 before the end of 2026, with $6,000 also emerging as a potential year-end target.

At $2,261, ETH would need to climb 119% to reach $4,954 and around 165% to hit $6,000. The technical picture still needs improvement. Ethereum faces resistance around the $2,315 area, identified as a key moving-average level in recent market analysis.

A sustained move above that zone could strengthen the recovery case, while a failure to reclaim it would leave ETH vulnerable to further downside.

There are risks to the bullish thesis. U.S. spot Ethereum ETFs recorded substantial outflows during October, while ETH’s price performance remained under pressure. Institutional accumulation has not yet translated into a decisive market reversal.

Still, Bitmine’s continued buying, its massive staked position, and Ethereum’s potential price recovery are keeping long-term bulls engaged.

Vitalik and his Devcon cosplay may have provided the conference’s funniest moment, but Bitmine’s growing treasury is the more serious signal. If institutional demand returns and ETH breaks through key resistance, $6,000 could move back into the conversation.

#5511. Oracle rethinks the lakehouse as AI agents become data consumers

A shared semantic layer is fast becoming the dividing line between lakehouses built for reporting and those built for artificial intelligence.

As AI agents join human analysts in querying corporate data, enterprises need platforms that make sense of information scattered across clouds, formats and rival systems. Oracle Corp. has spent the past year rebuilding its data stack around that shift, part of a broader database modernization push. The company now pitches its Autonomous AI Lakehouse as an open layer that sits across an enterprise’s existing data estate rather than replacing it, according to Nipun Agarwal (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering, Oracle Database, at Oracle.

“Lakehouses were the platform which customers use for running analytics,” Agarwal said. “Now, lakehouses have become the decision backbone for AI.”

Agarwal spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Oracle’s Autonomous AI Lakehouse combines a shared semantic layer with fast, real-time access to data across platforms to support AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

Oracle’s approach rests on a catalog that can mount other catalogs, such as Databricks Inc.’s Unity Catalog, along with Postgres and MySQL databases, so data is queried in place rather than copied. The company announced a business semantic layer and broader Apache Iceberg support at the October event, with table and column descriptions the system generates applying to non-Oracle sources as well, according to Agarwal. Crucially, Oracle does not see the offering as competing with other lakehouses, he added.

“We really believe that for any enterprise, they’re gonna have a choice,” he said. “They’re gonna be using multiple data sources. They’ll have multiple lakehouses.”

Oracle’s Lake Cache speeds up queries by moving the most-used Iceberg tables into Exadata’s flash cache. Real-time access is also becoming essential as software agents become the main consumers of the data: Scheduled refreshes of copied data can fall short when agents request it on demand, according to Agarwal.

“With AI that’s no longer the case, because for AI, the consumer is not a human necessarily,” Agarwal said. “The need for real-time access is a lot more with AI.”

Grows Bitcoin Reserve Through Mining Operations, Increases Satoshis Per Share by Approximately 5%

MIAMI, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- American Bitcoin Corp. (Nasdaq: ABTC) ("American Bitcoin" or the "Company"), a Bitcoin accumulation platform focused on building America's Bitcoin infrastructure backbone, today reported its financial results for the third quarter of 2026.

Mike Ho, Chief Executive Officer of American Bitcoin, said: "Our third-quarter results demonstrate our commitment to building a disciplined, Bitcoin-denominated operating business. Despite seasonal power cost pressures, we continued mining Bitcoin at a structural discount to spot, grew our strategic reserve, and increased Satoshis Per Share by approximately 5%, all without issuing shares through our ATM program or purchasing Bitcoin during the quarter. That is an important distinction in today's market. Our focus remains on efficiently accumulating Bitcoin, maintaining flexibility in our operations, and allocating capital in ways that support long-term Bitcoin-per-share growth. We believe that discipline positions American Bitcoin to create lasting value for shareholders across market cycles.

Eric Trump, Co-Founder and Chief Strategy Officer of American Bitcoin, said: "We're building American Bitcoin with the conviction that Bitcoin and American energy will play an increasingly important role in the future of our economy. This quarter, we delivered approximately $126 million in net income and $221 million in Adjusted EBITDA, while growing our Bitcoin reserve and increasing Bitcoin per share. These are significant results, particularly in a challenging digital asset market, and they reflect the discipline and long-term conviction behind this business. But our opportunity extends beyond any single quarter. As demand for energy and critical infrastructure accelerates across America, I believe we're particularly well-positioned at the intersection of two industries that will help define the future of our economy. We're building American Bitcoin for the long term, and I'm excited about what lies ahead."

#5508. 8 winter workouts and how many calories they burn

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These winter workouts that burn calories range from skiing and ice skating to shoveling snow, with AccuWeather's calorie estimates for each of the eight activities

Cold weather changes where people exercise more than whether they can. Snow, ice and short days close off some routines, but they open up others. Many of the activities that define winter in northern climates ask a lot of the body, from gliding across a frozen pond to clearing a driveway after a storm.

This guide covers eight winter workouts that burn calories, drawn from a longer list of cold-weather activities published by AccuWeather. The eight include sports such as skiing, snowboarding and hockey. They also include snowshoeing and ice skating, along with running, hiking and walking. The final entry covers outdoor chores that AccuWeather also counts as exercise: shoveling snow, chopping wood and raking leaves.

For each activity, this article gives AccuWeather's calorie estimate. Most of those figures are expressed per hour. Raking is the exception. The source gives that range without a time unit. The estimates cover a wide spread. Walking starts at 200 calories an hour, the low end of AccuWeather's range for it. Running reaches as high as 1,200 calories an hour at the top of its range. For cross-country skiing, the source notes that dedicated skiers sometimes pass 1,000 calories an hour.

These numbers are estimates, not fixed values. AccuWeather does not state the body weight, intensity or method behind any of them. The calories a person burns will vary with factors the source does not spell out. The figures offer a rough basis for comparing activities, not a precise count for any single workout.

The slides follow the order in which AccuWeather presents the activities. That order is not a ranking. Each slide stands on its own. Readers can go straight to the activity that fits their location, budget or schedule. Some entries, such as hockey, revolve around a rink. Others fit into daily life, such as walking the dog or running errands on foot.

AccuWeather also offers one general caution. It warns that anyone exercising outdoors in winter should dress for the weather to avoid hypothermia and frostbite.

Skiing of any kind, whether downhill or cross-country, can burn 500 or more calories in an hour, according to AccuWeather. That one estimate covers both forms of the sport.

The figure climbs for the most committed athletes. AccuWeather reports that dedicated cross-country skiers sometimes go past 1,000 calories per hour. The outlet presents that as a high-end figure for serious devotees of cross-country skiing.

Neither number is fixed. AccuWeather does not give the body weight, pace or effort level behind its skiing estimates, so an individual skier's burn will differ.

Cross-country skiing has two main methods. CBC describes the classic method as the traditional style of the sport. A classic skier glides along parallel tracks with a rhythmic motion that resembles running or walking.

The second method is skate skiing. Skate skiers push off their skis at an angle instead of gliding straight ahead. CBC compares that motion to the stride a hockey player uses on the ice.

Snowboarding burns an estimated 300 to 450 calories per hour, according to AccuWeather. That range falls below the outlet's estimate for skiing, which it puts at 500 or more calories an hour for both downhill and cross-country skiing.

Even the top of the snowboarding range, 450 calories an hour, sits under the 500-calorie floor AccuWeather gives for skiing.

AccuWeather describes snowboarding as less intense than skiing. It also presents the sport as more oriented toward fun than skiing is.

Ice hockey burns an estimated 400 to 600 calories an hour, according to AccuWeather. The source sets hockey apart from the other winter workouts it lists as the one built around a team.

The estimate spans 200 calories from its low end to its high end. AccuWeather gives the same 400 to 600 range for snowshoeing.

AccuWeather points to two ways to get into a game. The first is to join a team that plays at a rink. That route connects a player with an existing group and a place to play.

The second route is less formal. A player rounds up friends who have their own gear and organizes a game with them.

Both routes depend on other people to make a game happen. AccuWeather does not say how many players a game needs, how often rink teams play or what joining one costs.

Snowshoeing burns an estimated 400 to 600 calories an hour, according to AccuWeather. The forecaster presents it as a beginner-friendly alternative to skiing that costs less.

The equipment is simple to put on. Snowshoes go on over a regular pair of winter boots.

AccuWeather's estimate for snowshoeing is the same 400-to-600 range it gives for ice hockey.

Snow depth changes the workload. The National Park Service notes that snowshoeing a trail can take far more effort than walking the same trail on foot without snow. How much more depends on how deep the snow lies.

Particularly deep snow calls for a different technique. The park service recommends the kick-step for those conditions. The snowshoer kicks the foot while lifting it. That motion shakes extra snow off the front of the snowshoe.

The basic walking motion also changes on snowshoes. They force a wider stride than a normal walk. The park service warns that this wider gait can lead to achy hips.

Snow builds up on the gear itself, too. The agency advises stopping now and then to clear clumps stuck in the snowshoe's spikes. A trekking pole can help with that task, according to the park service.

Running burns an estimated 600 to 1,200 calories per hour, according to AccuWeather. The weather company treats running as a year-round workout. A routine built in spring or summer does not have to stop when temperatures fall.

The top of that range is double the bottom. The low end, 600 calories, matches the upper limit of the 400 to 600 calories an hour AccuWeather estimates for both hockey and snowshoeing.

Running's range overlaps with AccuWeather's hiking estimate of 430 to 650 calories an hour only between 600 and 650. Its low end also sits above the 470-calorie ceiling AccuWeather gives for walking. Ice skating, which AccuWeather puts at up to 700 calories an hour with real effort, tops out near the bottom of running's range.

Winter changes the ground underfoot. AccuWeather advises runners to plan their routes with icy patches in mind before heading out.

Timing is its second point. Temperature and visibility both shift over the course of a day. AccuWeather suggests weighing both when choosing a time to run.

Clothing is the third consideration. AccuWeather recommends breathable layers for cold-weather runs. AccuWeather's three tips for winter runners cover the route, the hour and the clothing.

Footwear matters on slick surfaces too. The National Institute on Aging recommends nonskid, rubber-soled shoes with low heels for people exercising outdoors in snow and ice. That kind of shoe makes a slip less likely.

The institute also lists precautions for anyone exercising outside in the cold. It recommends learning the signs of hypothermia. It also advises telling others where you will be and carrying a fully charged mobile phone.

The National Institute on Aging suggests considering an indoor workout when it is very windy, cold, icy or wet outside. An online workout video or a person's own routine can fill in on those days.

Ice skating can burn up to 700 calories an hour, according to AccuWeather. That estimate applies when the skater puts real effort into the session.

That condition shapes how to read the number. AccuWeather presents 700 calories as a ceiling for hard skating, not as the typical result of a trip to the rink. The source gives no figure for a slow, casual loop around the ice. That kind of outing falls outside what the estimate describes.

The way AccuWeather states the figure also sets skating apart from most of the activities in this article. Snowboarding, snowshoeing, running, hiking and walking each come with both a low and a high estimate. Skating has only an upper limit. The one other activity here described the same way is vigorous snow shoveling, covered with the other winter chores.

Without a stated floor, the skating figure is most useful for comparing upper limits. On that basis, the ceiling for hard skating sits above the top of AccuWeather's ranges for snowboarding and snowshoeing. A skater who wants to approach that ceiling has to keep the effort high for the full hour.

Winter hiking burns an estimated 430 to 650 calories an hour, and walking burns an estimated 200 to 470 calories an hour, according to AccuWeather. Of the two, hiking has the higher range.

The two ranges do not sit apart. They share a band from 430 to 470 calories an hour. Near the top of its range, walking matches the low end of the hiking range. The activity's name alone does not settle which outing burns more on a given day.

Walking also needs no special trip. AccuWeather counts walking the dog and running errands on foot toward this activity. A walk to the store or a loop around the block with a pet fits that description. Those examples fold the exercise into routine outings rather than setting it apart as a separate workout.

AccuWeather gives less detail on hiking. It does not describe the terrain, pace or distance behind its hiking range. It also gives no separate figure for hiking through snow. That leaves the hiking estimate as a general guide, not a figure for any particular trail or condition.

Shoveling snow, chopping wood and raking leaves can each burn hundreds of calories, according to estimates from AccuWeather. It puts vigorous snow shoveling at up to 500 calories per hour and chopping wood at 400 to 500 calories per hour.

The shoveling number is an upper limit. AccuWeather attaches it to vigorous shoveling, not to shoveling in general. The source gives no figure for shoveling at an easier pace.

Chopping wood comes with a range rather than a single ceiling. The bottom of that range is 400 calories per hour. The top, 500 calories per hour, matches the most AccuWeather gives for hard shoveling.

Those chore figures sit near several of the sports on AccuWeather's list. The wood-chopping range falls inside the 400 to 600 calories an hour the source gives for ice hockey and for snowshoeing. The shoveling ceiling equals the floor of its estimate for skiing, which starts at 500 calories an hour.

Raking leaves carries an estimate of 250 to 400 calories. AccuWeather does not attach a time frame to that range. Without one, the raking figure cannot be lined up against the hourly numbers for shoveling and wood chopping.

AccuWeather groups these three tasks as winter chores alongside sports such as skiing, hockey and ice skating. Unlike hockey or skating, none of the chores requires a rink or a team. The source does not say how much snow, wood or leaf cover its estimates assume.

#5507. As AI takes over coding, Oracle rethinks how applications are built

As vibe coding moves from novelty to everyday practice, enterprises face a new problem: Machine-generated software still has to be maintained, governed and understood by people.

Low-code platforms were built to speed up application development, and AI is now rewriting that mission. Oracle Corp. previewed its answer ahead of its annual conference, and the tipping point for software development has already arrived, according to Mike Hichwa (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering at Oracle.

“In 2025, the majority of code was human-authored, and in 2026 and forever afterwards, the majority of code is going to be machine-generated,” Hichwa said. “We’re probably not going back. What we’ve done to address this change is we invented our own language. We call it APEXlang.”

Hichwa spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed vibe coding and the need to maintain and govern AI-generated code. (* Disclosure below.)

APEXlang is a highly abstracted application definition language that captures intent rather than implementation. Oracle introduced it with the APEX AI Application Generator and is publishing its grammar, skills and documentation in the public domain so coding agents such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex can generate it. Oracle is also working with OpenAI to train models to generate the language more efficiently, Hichwa explained.

“What you’re generating actually matters, because once you generate it, and you generate it 100 times or 1,000 times within your enterprise, then you’re going to need to maintain it. You’re going to need to look after it,” Hichwa said. “What people want with their portfolio of applications, they want consistency, they want governance, they want ease of understanding.”

Governance comes from the runtime, too. Generated APEXlang is interpreted by the APEX engine, which Oracle patches and updates monthly, so customers don’t have to revisit what they built. The same design is meant to curb AI slop, since a compact definition is easier to read than sprawling generated code, according to Hichwa.

“What we’re generating is much, much smaller, much more human understandable, so it is less sloppy because it is more abstracted,” Hichwa said. “It’s like a CliffsNotes. It’s not the full book.”

#5506. Year-end giving campaign launches for the AAN Research Program

Support the urgent need for brain research funding

MINNEAPOLIS, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The need for brain research funding has never been more urgent. That is why the American Academy of Neurology (AAN) today announced its year-end giving campaign for the AAN Research Program, inviting people to support the researchers working to find new treatments and cures for brain diseases and disorders.

One hundred percent of every tax-deductible donation will go directly to brain research.

"Scientific breakthroughs begin with researchers who have the ideas and expertise to pursue important questions," said American Academy of Neurology President Natalia S. Rost, MD, MPH, FAAN, FAHA. "The AAN Research Program gives all of us the opportunity to help advance high-quality brain research, bringing hope to people affected by brain disease."

Brain research is what makes it possible to prevent, diagnose, treat, and eventually even cure conditions of the brain and nervous system. It also advances our understanding of memory, learning, sleep, mental health, and healthy aging, helping people live healthier lives.

The AAN Research Program has funded brain research for more than 30 years, owing to its success the exceptional pool of talented researchers in the AAN community, the world's largest association of neurologists and neuroscience professionals.

Demand for funding, however, continues to outpace available resources. Hundreds of researchers apply for AAN grants. The AAN invested nearly $1.8 million in 2026, but millions in viable neuroscience research went unfunded.

"We know that excellent research proposals go unfunded," said American Academy of Neurology Chief Executive Officer Mary E. Post, MBA, CAE. "We want to make sure that we have the funding to support the research that may eventually lead to a cure for MS or a way to prevent Alzheimer's. Every contribution can help researchers pursue discoveries as they work toward improving brain health for all."

With neurologists leading the AAN Board of Directors, Science Committee, and Research Program Subcommittee, the AAN is guided by trusted experts who understand both the science and the real-world application of research.

Help advance research by making a tax-deductible gift on the BrainHealth.com "Donate to Research" page. Organizations interested in supporting the AAN Research Program may contact donations@aan.com.

The AAN Research Program is administered through the American Academy of Neurology Institute, the Academy's 501(c)(3) charitable organization.

Discover more about brain health at BrainHealth.com, a free public resource from the American Academy of Neurology. It offers a website, podcast, and books, connecting you with trusted information from the world's leading experts in brain health. Follow BrainHealth.com on Facebook, X, and Instagram.

The American Academy of Neurology is the leading voice in brain health. As the world's largest association of neurologists and neuroscience professionals with more than 44,000 members, the AAN provides access to the latest news, science and research affecting neurology for patients, caregivers, physicians and professionals alike. The AAN's mission is to enhance member career fulfillment and promote brain health for all. A neurologist is a doctor who specializes in the diagnosis, care and treatment of brain, spinal cord and nervous system diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, stroke, concussion, epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, headache and migraine.

Explore the latest in neurological disease and brain health, from the minds at the AAN at AAN.com or find us on Facebook, X, Instagram, LinkedIn, and YouTube.

#5505. From carbon monoxide to norovirus: 9 winter health risks that aren't the flu

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These winter health risks, from carbon monoxide poisoning to snow-shoveling heart strain, have nothing to do with the flu and are worth understanding before temperatures drop

Flu shots dominate most conversations about staying healthy in winter. Yet the season's cold, darkness, dry air and ice create a separate set of hazards. Many of them have no connection to any virus. They come from the way people heat their homes, move through icy streets, spend their days indoors and adjust to shorter hours of daylight.

Some of these hazards are environmental. Furnaces, space heaters, fireplaces and portable generators all burn fuel. A poorly vented one can fill a closed-up house with carbon monoxide. Outdoors, prolonged exposure to cold can lower the body's core temperature or freeze exposed skin. The risk rises when clothing gets wet or the wind picks up.

Others are physical. Icy sidewalks, driveways and parking lots turn an ordinary walk into a fall risk. Those falls can end in broken wrists, hips and ankles or in head injuries. Clearing heavy snow places heavy demands on the heart. Cold air narrows blood vessels, and heavy lifting raises heart rate and blood pressure.

A third group is tied to the season's biology. Shorter days are linked to seasonal affective disorder, a form of depression that returns on a seasonal pattern. Winter sunlight at higher latitudes is weaker, and people spend more time indoors. Both conditions mean the skin makes less vitamin D. Low humidity outside and forced-air heating inside pull moisture from the skin and can trigger eczema flare-ups.

Then there is norovirus, a stomach virus often called the winter vomiting bug. It is frequently labeled "stomach flu," but that name is a misnomer. Norovirus has no relation to influenza, and a flu shot offers no protection against it.

The nine winter health risks below are a selection, not a ranking. Each slide explains what the risk is, why the season raises it, which warning signs to look for and what steps reduce it. Many of the precautions are simple. They include a working carbon monoxide detector, dry layered clothing, footwear with good traction, a slower pace with a snow shovel and thorough handwashing with soap and water. Anyone with a heart condition, persistent low mood or questions about vitamin levels should talk with a doctor. A clinician can assess individual risk and recommend testing or treatment.

Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas released when fuel burns, and it can build up indoors without any warning a person can see or smell. A working carbon monoxide detector is the standard safeguard against poisoning.

The gas comes from any appliance or engine that burns fuel. Furnaces, gas space heaters, wood stoves, fireplaces, water heaters and gas ranges can all produce it. Portable generators and cars left running in garages are other common sources. Winter raises the risk. Homes are sealed tight against the cold, and heating equipment runs for long stretches.

Carbon monoxide harms the body by taking the place of oxygen in the blood. Red blood cells pick it up more readily than they pick up oxygen. Organs such as the brain and heart are then starved of the oxygen they need. Exposure can cause lasting damage or death.

Early symptoms include headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness and confusion. Those signs are easy to mistake for a cold or another viral illness. A few clues point toward carbon monoxide instead. Several people or pets in the same home may feel sick at once. Symptoms may also ease after time spent outside and return once everyone is back indoors.

People who are asleep or intoxicated may never notice symptoms at all. That is why detectors matter most near bedrooms. Place one on every level of the home and outside sleeping areas. Test them regularly, and replace batteries or units according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Generators need particular care during winter storms and power outages. Never run one inside a home, basement or attached garage, even with doors or windows open. Set it up outdoors and well away from windows, doors and vents. Charcoal grills and camp stoves are built for outdoor use and follow the same rule.

Routine maintenance lowers the risk at the source. Have furnaces, chimneys and other fuel-burning appliances inspected by a qualified technician before the heating season begins. Keep vents and flues clear of snow and debris. Never warm up a car inside a garage, even with the garage door open.

If a detector sounds or poisoning is suspected, leave the building immediately and get to fresh air. Then call 911 or local emergency services from outside.

Hypothermia is a medical emergency that sets in when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, pushing core temperature below 95°F (35°C). Shivering, confusion and slurred speech are among its warning signs, and anyone showing them needs warmth and medical attention.

The body normally holds its core temperature within a narrow range. Cold air pulls heat away from the skin. The body responds by shivering and by narrowing blood vessels near the surface to protect vital organs. Hypothermia begins when those defenses can no longer keep up.

Moisture and moving air speed the process. Wet clothing loses much of its insulating value. Water also draws heat from the body far faster than air does. Wind strips away the thin layer of warm air that sits next to the skin. A person soaked by rain, sweat or a fall into water can become dangerously chilled even when the air temperature is above freezing.

The early signs are easy to dismiss. Uncontrollable shivering usually comes first, followed by fumbling hands, clumsiness and exhaustion. As core temperature keeps falling, a person may become confused, drowsy or slow to respond. Their speech may slur. In severe cases, shivering can stop altogether. That change signals worsening, not recovery.

Confusion makes hypothermia hard to recognize from the inside. People affected by it often do not realize what is happening and may make poor decisions about seeking shelter. Companions, neighbors and family members play a key role in spotting it.

Some groups face higher risk. Older adults can lose body heat in a poorly heated home without noticing. Infants lose heat quickly and may show bright red, cold skin and very low energy. People who spend long periods outdoors, including hikers, outdoor workers and people experiencing homelessness, face prolonged exposure. Alcohol can mask the sensation of cold while increasing heat loss through the skin.

Response starts with getting the person out of the cold and into a warm, dry place. Remove wet clothing and replace it with dry layers or blankets. Warm the center of the body — chest, neck, head and groin — before the arms and legs. Skin-to-skin contact under loose, dry coverings can help. Warm, nonalcoholic drinks are appropriate only if the person is fully alert.

Rewarming should be gradual, and the person should be handled gently. Call emergency services for anyone showing confusion, drowsiness or loss of consciousness. Severe hypothermia requires professional medical care, even after the person seems to have warmed up.

Frostbite is the freezing of skin and the tissue beneath it. It most often affects the fingers, toes, nose and ears. Mild early cases usually heal with careful rewarming, but deep frostbite can permanently destroy tissue.

Those body parts are vulnerable for a basic physiological reason. In cold conditions, the body narrows blood vessels near the skin to protect its vital organs. Hands, feet and the face sit farthest from that warm core, so they lose blood flow first. Cheeks and the chin are also common sites.

The mildest stage is frostnip. Skin turns cold, numb and pale or red, and it may tingle or sting. Frostnip does not cause lasting damage. It is a signal to get out of the cold.

Superficial frostbite goes further. The skin can change color and may start to feel oddly warm. Fluid-filled blisters can form within a day or two after rewarming.

In deep frostbite, the freezing reaches the lower layers of tissue. The skin becomes hard and waxy, and the area may lose all sensation. Nearby joints and muscles can stop working normally. Severe cases can lead to tissue death and sometimes amputation.

Color changes vary with skin tone. Frostbitten skin can look white, bluish-white, grayish-yellow, purplish or ashen. Numbness is often the more reliable clue. Because the area goes numb, a person may not notice the injury until someone else points it out.

Damp gloves and exposed faces freeze sooner because moisture and wind pull heat from the skin faster. Tight boots or gloves that restrict circulation add to the risk. Smoking, alcohol, diabetes and other conditions that affect blood flow also make frostbite more likely.

Rewarming should use warm water, not hot water. Numb skin cannot sense heat, so heating pads, fires and stoves can burn it unnoticed. Rubbing the area, or rubbing it with snow, can damage frozen tissue further. Rewarming is best delayed if the area could freeze again before reaching shelter. Thawing followed by refreezing causes more harm than staying frozen a little longer. Anything beyond frostnip calls for medical care.

Prevention centers on staying dry and covered. Mittens keep hands warmer than gloves because the fingers share heat. A hat that covers the ears, a scarf or face mask, and moisture-wicking socks inside waterproof boots protect the other common sites. Changing out of wet socks or gloves promptly removes a major source of heat loss.

Seasonal affective disorder, often shortened to SAD, is a form of depression that follows a seasonal pattern. For most people who have it, symptoms begin in fall or winter and lift in spring. Reduced daylight is the factor most commonly linked to it.

The DSM-5, the American Psychiatric Association's diagnostic manual, classifies the condition as major depressive disorder with seasonal pattern. That label means depressive episodes recur at roughly the same time each year and then ease.

Winter-pattern SAD has a recognizable set of symptoms. People often sleep more than usual yet still feel tired. Many report carbohydrate cravings, weight gain and a pull toward social withdrawal that some describe as hibernating. Persistent low mood, loss of interest in usual activities and trouble concentrating are also common.

The link to daylight helps explain the timing. Shorter days and later sunrises can shift the body's internal clock, which regulates sleep, alertness and hormone release. That disruption is one leading explanation for why symptoms cluster in the darkest months. Living farther from the equator, where winter days are shortest, is associated with higher risk.

The winter blues and SAD are not the same thing. Many people feel sluggish during a dark January without meeting the criteria for depression. The difference lies in severity, duration and whether symptoms interfere with work, relationships or daily routines.

Light therapy is one recognized treatment. It involves sitting near a bright light box for a set period each day, usually in the morning. Boxes intended for SAD are designed to filter out ultraviolet light. Side effects can include eyestrain and headache. People with bipolar disorder should use light therapy only under medical supervision. Bright light can trigger mania in some cases.

Light therapy does not work for everyone. Talk therapy, particularly cognitive behavioral therapy, and antidepressant medication are other options a clinician may recommend. Anyone whose low mood lasts for weeks, disrupts daily life or includes thoughts of self-harm should contact a doctor or mental health professional.

Vitamin D levels can fall in winter because the skin makes most of its supply from sunlight. At higher latitudes, the winter sun delivers too little of the right kind of light. The body needs vitamin D to absorb calcium, which keeps bones strong.

The process depends on ultraviolet B radiation, known as UVB. When UVB reaches bare skin, it triggers a reaction that produces vitamin D. The liver and kidneys then convert it into the form the body uses.

In winter, the sun sits lower in the sky. Its light travels a longer path through the atmosphere, and much of the UVB is absorbed before it reaches the ground. The effect grows stronger the farther a place is from the equator. In much of northern Europe, Canada and the northern U.S., winter sunlight produces little or no vitamin D in the skin.

Daily habits widen the gap. Cold weather keeps people inside for longer stretches. The skin they expose outdoors is usually limited to the face and hands. Window glass blocks UVB, so sitting in a sunny room does not help the body make vitamin D.

Some groups face a higher risk. Melanin, the pigment in darker skin, reduces how much vitamin D the skin produces from a given amount of sunlight. Older adults make less vitamin D in their skin than younger people do. People who are housebound, or who cover most of their skin outdoors, also get less exposure.

The main consequence involves the skeleton. Severe, prolonged deficiency can cause rickets in children, a condition that softens and deforms growing bones. In adults, it can cause osteomalacia, which brings bone pain and muscle weakness. Mild deficiency often produces no obvious symptoms.

Food can supply some vitamin D, though few foods contain much of it naturally. Fatty fish such as salmon, mackerel and sardines are among the richest natural sources. Egg yolks contain smaller amounts. Many countries fortify milk, breakfast cereals or plant-based drinks with it.

A blood test is the reliable way to know whether levels are low. A doctor can order the test and advise whether a supplement makes sense, and in what amount. Very high doses of vitamin D taken over time can raise calcium in the blood to harmful levels.

Cold outdoor air and indoor heating both draw moisture out of the skin, leaving it dry, tight and prone to cracking in winter. For people with eczema, also called atopic dermatitis, the same conditions often trigger flare-ups of itchy, inflamed patches.

The problem starts with the air. Cold air holds less water vapor than warm air. A furnace or radiator then warms that air indoors without adding any water. As the air heats up, its relative humidity drops further. The result is dry indoor air that pulls water out of the outer layer of the skin.

That outer layer, the stratum corneum, works as a barrier. It is made of flattened skin cells held together by fats such as ceramides. When the barrier loses moisture, gaps open between those cells. Water escapes more easily, and irritants get in more easily. Skin can look flaky, feel rough and develop small cracks, especially on the hands, shins and lips.

Eczema makes the problem worse. People with atopic dermatitis tend to have a weaker skin barrier to begin with. Dry winter air can push that barrier past its limit. The resulting itch leads to scratching, and scratching damages the skin further. Broken skin gives bacteria an easier way in, which can lead to infection.

Daily habits can deepen the dryness. Long, hot showers strip away the natural oils that help skin hold water. Harsh soaps and heavily fragranced products can irritate skin that is already compromised. Wool and other rough fabrics can also aggravate eczema-prone skin when worn directly against it.

Small changes reduce the damage. Shorter showers in lukewarm water remove less oil. Applying moisturizer within a few minutes after bathing, while the skin is still damp, helps seal in water. Thick creams and ointments, such as those made with petrolatum, generally hold moisture better than thin lotions. Fragrance-free products lower the chance of irritation.

A humidifier can put moisture back into heated indoor air. It needs regular cleaning, because standing water can grow mold and bacteria. Soft, breathable layers such as cotton next to the skin cut down on friction. Gloves outdoors shield the hands from cold, drying wind.

Some symptoms call for a doctor or dermatologist. Skin that cracks and bleeds, oozes, crusts or shows signs of infection needs medical attention. So does itching severe enough to disrupt sleep. Prescription treatments can calm an eczema flare when moisturizers alone are not enough.

Shoveling snow is a recognized trigger for heart attacks and other cardiac events in people at risk. The danger comes from hard physical work done in cold air, a combination that drives heart rate and blood pressure up at the same time.

Cold exposure causes blood vessels to constrict. That narrowing raises blood pressure and forces the heart to work harder to move blood through the body. It can also reduce blood flow to the heart muscle itself.

Shoveling then adds a demanding workload. Lifting and throwing snow relies heavily on the arms and upper body. Arm work tends to raise heart rate and blood pressure more sharply than walking or other leg-based activity at a similar effort.

Many people also hold their breath while heaving a full shovel. That straining, known as the Valsalva maneuver, causes sudden swings in blood pressure. Wet, heavy snow makes each load harder to lift and adds to the strain.

Timing matters too. People often clear driveways first thing in the morning, when blood pressure naturally runs higher. For someone who is mostly sedentary the rest of the year, a sudden burst of hard labor in the cold places a heavy load on the heart.

People with a history of heart attack, coronary artery disease, high blood pressure or high cholesterol face greater risk. So do smokers and older adults. Anyone in those groups should talk with a doctor before taking on heavy snow removal. Another person or a snow blower can take on the job instead.

Technique can reduce the load. Pushing snow to the side instead of lifting it cuts the effort. Smaller scoops, frequent rest breaks and clearing snow in stages during a storm keep any single session lighter. A few minutes of gentle movement beforehand helps the body warm up. Skipping a heavy meal right before shoveling also keeps extra demand off the heart.

The warning signs of a heart attack call for an immediate stop. They include chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, and discomfort spreading to the arm, jaw, neck or back. Lightheadedness, nausea and a cold sweat can also appear. Anyone with these symptoms should stop shoveling and call emergency services right away.

Falls on ice are a common cause of winter injuries, including broken wrists, hips and ankles and blows to the head. Shoes with good traction, a slower walking style and treated surfaces all lower the risk.

Someone who throws out a hand to break a fall can fracture the wrist. The break usually occurs at the end of the radius, the forearm bone on the thumb side.

A sideways fall onto the hip is more serious for older adults. Their bones may already be weakened by osteoporosis, and a hip fracture can require surgery and a long recovery. Ankles can twist and break when a foot slides out at an awkward angle.

A backward fall can drive the head into pavement, causing a concussion or bleeding inside the skull. A worsening headache, confusion, vomiting or unusual drowsiness after a fall calls for emergency care. People who take blood thinners should get checked after any blow to the head, even if they feel fine.

Black ice is a thin, clear glaze that takes on the color of the surface beneath it. A sidewalk coated in it can look merely wet. It tends to form first on bridges, overpasses and shaded patches, where surfaces cool faster.

Rubber soles with deep treads grip better than smooth leather or worn-down soles. Slip-on ice cleats stretch over regular shoes and add metal studs or coils for grip on packed snow and ice. They should come off indoors, where the metal can slide on tile and other hard floors.

Short, flat-footed steps with body weight centered over the feet help keep balance. This style is often called the penguin walk. Keeping hands out of pockets lets a person steady themselves or catch a fall.

Rock salt melts ice but works poorly in severe cold. Calcium chloride keeps working at lower temperatures. Sand and cat litter do not melt anything, but they add grit underfoot. Clearing steps and walkways before foot traffic packs the snow down helps keep ice from forming.

Norovirus is a highly contagious stomach virus that causes sudden vomiting and diarrhea, and it has no connection to influenza. Washing hands with soap and water is the most reliable everyday defense against it.

The illness is often called "stomach flu," but that name is a misnomer. Influenza is a respiratory virus that infects the nose, throat and lungs. Norovirus infects the gut instead. It inflames the stomach and intestines, a condition known as gastroenteritis.

In the U.K., norovirus is widely known as the winter vomiting bug. Cases tend to rise during the colder months in the Northern Hemisphere. Outbreaks are common where many people share space, such as schools, nursing homes, hospitals and cruise ships.

Symptoms tend to come on suddenly. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and stomach cramps are the most common. Some people also develop a low fever, headache or body aches. Most healthy adults recover within a few days.

The virus spreads through contaminated food and water. It also spreads when people touch a contaminated surface and then their mouth, or through close contact with someone who is sick. A very small amount of virus is enough to cause illness. People can remain contagious for days after they feel better.

Alcohol-based hand sanitizer works less well against norovirus than against many other germs. Scrubbing with soap under running water removes the virus more reliably. Hand washing matters most after using the toilet, after changing diapers and before eating or preparing food.

Norovirus can survive on countertops, doorknobs and other hard surfaces. Cleaning with a chlorine bleach solution, or a disinfectant labeled as effective against norovirus, helps limit spread at home. Soiled clothing and bedding should be handled carefully and washed promptly.

No specific medicine cures norovirus, and no vaccine is currently available. Treatment focuses on replacing lost fluids. Dehydration is the main danger, especially for young children, older adults and people with other health conditions.

Signs of dehydration include reduced urination, a dry mouth and dizziness when standing up. Anyone showing those signs, or unable to keep fluids down, should contact a doctor. People who are sick should stay home and avoid preparing food for others until well after their symptoms end.

#5504. CertiK Verified 40.68M TPS for Sui, Here Is What It Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The biggest throughput figure a blockchain security firm has ever signed off on is sitting on CertiK's homepage right now: 40.68 million transactions per second.

It isn't CertiK's own number, and it isn't an on-chain number either. If you read the 2,000-word report behind it, you'll come to become more interested in what CertiK chose not to verify than in what it did.

Scroll past the client logos and media mentions on CertiK and you'll find it in the "Latest Research And Market Insights" strip. One card says CertiK independently verified Sui's Mainnet Tunnel performance campaign, which recorded more than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions across 7,680 tunnels at a peak of 40.68 million TPS.

Most readers will see "CertiK" next to "40.68 million TPS" and stop there. Crypto social media mostly did the same. Sui's own post described the figure as set live on stage at Sui Basecamp 2026 and certified by CertiK, and added that the network now clears in under 20 seconds what Visa processes in a day.Walking through CertiK's verification method when the report first came out. Now that the number has been promoted to CertiK's front page, it's worth looking at exactly what it represents.

According to CertiK's announcement, Sui ran a live Mainnet performance campaign on October 7, 2026, during Sui Basecamp Day. It recorded 15,241,348,297 tunnel transactions across 7,680 tunnels, and every tunnel was opened and settled on chain.

A Sui Tunnel works roughly like a private room. A small group of participants carries out many application actions without sending each one to the blockchain. Sui records the starting terms when the tunnel opens and the final result when it closes. Everything in between happens off-chain as signed receipts. CertiK compares the design to Bitcoin's Lightning Network but notes that tunnels can handle more than payments.

The test was more varied than a single payment loop. The campaign ran 10 runs across five workload types: simple payments, flash, blackjack, tic-tac-toe and battleship. Payments still made up most of the activity. Its 6,144 tunnels committed more than 12 billion transactions, or 78.98% of the total.

This is the part of the report I respect most. The peak came from the busiest complete second, between 08:46:17 and 08:46:18 UTC, when 40,682,328 qualifying tunnel transactions were committed. The highest 60-second rolling average was 40,339,143.65 TPS.

Doing the math on the gap between those two figures. It's about 343,000 transactions, or roughly 0.84%. In other words, the network held near-peak throughput for a full minute rather than spiking for one second.

CertiK also avoided the easiest way to inflate a number like this. For concurrent tunnels sharing the same time window, it added up their transaction counts once and divided by a single shared duration. It did not add individual per-tunnel rates together or multiply one tunnel's rate by the number of tunnels.

The checking itself was thorough. All 7,680 executions and all 960 slots reached VERIFIED status, and the 15.24 billion committed transactions matched the full-history admitted receipts exactly. The work ran on dedicated AWS infrastructure with 128 vCPUs and 247 GiB of RAM.

There's also a small correction in the story. Sui's first announcement reported 40,614,180 TPS. CertiK's audited peak came in about 68,000 higher, a 0.17% difference. A verifier landing slightly above the project's own claim is unusual, and I think it reflects well on the method.

The homepage card doesn't mention any of this, but the full report is clear about its limits.

First, this isn't on-chain throughput. CertiK states that Tunnel TPS measures off-chain tunnel transactions and is not a measurement of Sui's on-chain capacity.

Second, the data came from the project being tested. The Sui team supplied the campaign data and executed all test scenarios, and CertiK examined the retained evidence and recalculated the totals.

Third, the cryptographic checks were not exhaustive. CertiK reconciled the arithmetic, receipt counts and timestamps, but it did not re-run individual signatures or do a fresh cryptographic replay of every receipt.

Fourth, the report can't speak to how the system would behave in normal use. The records don't establish clock accuracy, failure rates, latency percentiles or results across repeated runs. The sustained figure is the best 60-second window observed, not a guaranteed minimum.

Put simply, CertiK verified that the accounting is correct. It did not verify that Sui can handle 40 million real users' actions every second.

The number that's most telling isn't the TPS figure. More than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions were anchored to Sui through just 1,920 on-chain lifecycle transactions: 960 openings and 960 settlements.

By simple calculation, that's about 7.9 million off-chain actions for every on-chain transaction. That ratio is what the tunnel design is built to achieve. It's an impressive engineering result, but it measures how well Sui compresses activity, not how fast its base layer runs.

This isn't the first speed record CertiK has signed off on, and the earlier ones show why comparisons are tricky. In its earlier TON verification, CertiK worked from per-minute transaction count data and arrived at 104,715 TPS for TON's testnet. In April 2025, Qubic announced 15.52 million TPS verified by CertiK, measured over 10 peak ticks on its Layer 1 mainnet.

On paper, Sui's tunnel figure is about 2.6 times Qubic's and nearly 390 times TON's. But these were three different kinds of tests: a sharded testnet, a base-layer burst and an off-chain channel network. They don't belong on the same leaderboard.

My view is that the 40.68 million figure is real, well documented and carefully bounded. It's also a measure of what an off-chain system can process, not what Sui's blockchain itself handles. CertiK's report is honest about that, even if the one-line homepage card isn't.
