#5502. Winter produce and vitamin C: 12 fruits and vegetables worth knowing

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 12 winter fruits and vegetables high in vitamin C, from navel oranges and kiwi to broccoli and kale, offer cold-month ways to get a nutrient the body can't make

Humans cannot make vitamin C. Every bit of it has to come from food, and that need continues after summer berries and garden tomatoes leave the markets. Cold months change what is fresh, but they do not empty the produce aisle of good sources.

Winter is citrus season in the U.S. Navel oranges are in season, and grapefruit, clementines and mandarins share the same shelves. Lemons, used mostly for juice and zest, round out the group. In the U.S., kiwi is often at its peak in winter, with California fruit available through the cooler months. Pomegranates, eaten for their arils, are another winter fruit. On the vegetable side, cool-season crops such as broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower carry much of the load. Kale is a cold-hardy leafy green. Red and green cabbage store well through winter.

Vitamin C, also known as ascorbic acid, does several jobs in the body. It is needed to make collagen, the protein that gives structure to skin, tendons and blood vessels. It works as an antioxidant. It also helps the body absorb non-heme iron, the type of iron in plant foods such as beans, lentils and leafy greens.

How produce is handled in the kitchen also matters. Vitamin C is water-soluble and breaks down with heat. Long cooking in water draws it out of vegetables and into the pot. Eating produce raw, or steaming it instead of boiling it, preserves more.

This guide covers 12 winter fruits and vegetables high in vitamin C. It is a selection, not a ranking, and the slide order is editorial. Red bell peppers are a very rich source, while pomegranate contributes a more modest amount. In winter, red bell peppers are generally grown in greenhouses or imported rather than picked from local fields. Each slide explains what the food offers, how to prepare it and any cautions worth knowing, such as grapefruit's interaction with certain medications.

Navel oranges are in season in the U.S. during winter, and they belong to citrus, the best-known dietary source of vitamin C. A whole fruit needs no preparation beyond peeling.

The fruit takes its name from the small, button-like formation at its blossom end, which resembles a human navel. That bump is a second, undeveloped fruit growing inside the first.

Navel oranges are seedless. As a result, the trees cannot be grown from seed. Growers propagate them by grafting budwood onto rootstock. The variety traces back to a mutation on an orange tree in Brazil in the 19th century.

Trees from that line reached Riverside, California, in the 1870s. California remains the center of U.S. navel orange production, with a harvest that generally runs from late fall into spring. Florida's orange industry, by contrast, concentrates largely on juice varieties such as the Valencia.

Navel oranges suit eating whole better than juicing. Their juice turns bitter after it sits for a while, a problem the citrus trade calls delayed bitterness. The main compound behind it is limonin. The thick peel comes away easily, so the fruit is practical to segment and eat out of hand.

The Cara Cara is a navel variety with pinkish-red flesh. It originated as a mutation found in Venezuela in the 1970s. It shares the seedless structure and winter season of the standard navel. Its flavor is sweeter and less acidic.

When buying navels, a fruit that feels heavy for its size usually holds more juice. Whole oranges keep longer in the refrigerator than on the counter.

Vitamin C has a long-standing reputation as a cold remedy. Regular vitamin C supplementation does not reduce how many colds people in the general population catch. That finding concerns supplements taken routinely. It does not change the role of oranges as an everyday food source of vitamin C during winter.

Grapefruit is a winter citrus fruit that supplies vitamin C. It also carries a caution that sweet oranges and clementines do not: it can interact with certain prescription medications.

In the U.S., grapefruit fills store shelves in the cooler months, when groves in Florida and Texas are harvesting. Supermarkets usually stock white, pink and red varieties. The pink and red flesh gets its color from lycopene, the same pigment found in tomatoes and watermelon.

Grapefruit is a relatively recent addition to the citrus family. It is a hybrid of the pomelo and the sweet orange. It was first described in Barbados in the 18th century. Growers were cultivating it in Florida in the 1800s.

The medication issue sets grapefruit apart from other winter citrus. The fruit contains compounds called furanocoumarins. These block an enzyme in the small intestine known as CYP3A4. That enzyme normally breaks down part of some drugs before they reach the bloodstream.

When the enzyme is blocked, more of the drug enters the bloodstream than the prescribed dose is meant to deliver. Higher blood levels of a medication can raise the risk of side effects. Affected drugs include some used to treat high cholesterol, high blood pressure and irregular heart rhythm. Not every drug in a given class is affected. A blanket rule for a whole class of medication does not work.

The interaction applies to the fresh fruit as well as the juice. Its effect can last a day or longer after eating grapefruit. Spacing a glass of juice and a pill a few hours apart does not reliably avoid it.

A pharmacist can check a specific prescription for a grapefruit interaction. Medication labels and patient information leaflets often state whether the fruit should be avoided.

For people not taking an affected drug, grapefruit is a straightforward way to add vitamin C to winter meals. Halves can be eaten with a spoon. Segments work in salads with avocado or fennel. Juice is another option, though whole segments keep the fruit's fiber.

Clementines and mandarins are small winter citrus fruits that supply vitamin C and peel by hand. They need no cooking or preparation before eating.

The peel is the practical difference. The rind comes away with fingers alone. No knife, cutting board or juicer is required.

Larger citrus is often sliced or sectioned before eating. With a clementine or mandarin, the whole process happens in the hand.

Their small size matters too. A single fruit fits in a coat pocket, a lunch bag or a desk drawer. It travels without a container and leaves only a peel behind.

That portability makes these fruits a ready snack at work, at school or in transit. They can be packed in the morning and eaten hours later with no extra steps.

Size also shapes the portion. One fruit is a modest serving on its own. A second or third adds more, so intake can be adjusted one piece at a time.

Once the peel is off, the segments separate cleanly. A single fruit is easy to split between people or hand out to children.

As winter citrus, clementines and mandarins are in season during the cold months, when the range of fresh fruit narrows.

Lemons provide vitamin C, but they are mostly used for their juice and zest rather than eaten whole. That keeps portions small, so a lemon usually adds a modest amount to a day's intake rather than serving as a main source.

The fruit's sharp, sour flesh explains much of that pattern. Few people eat a lemon the way they eat an orange or a clementine. A serving of broccoli is likewise eaten as food in its own right, while a lemon usually works as a seasoning.

Lemon juice goes into salad dressings, marinades, sauces, hot tea and glasses of water. The zest is the thin, colored outer layer of the peel. Grating it removes that layer and leaves the bitter white pith underneath. Cooks add zest to baked goods, grain dishes and rubs for fish or chicken. In each case, the amount used is a spoonful or two, not a full serving of fruit.

Repeated use is how lemons contribute. The human body has no way to produce vitamin C on its own. Diet is the only supply. Small additions spread across several meals count toward the total, alongside larger servings of other produce.

That dependence on diet has a clear consequence. Severe vitamin C deficiency over a long period causes scurvy. Steady intake from a range of fruits and vegetables prevents it.

Lemons belong to the citrus group that fills produce sections in the colder months. Among those fruits, they are usually treated as an ingredient rather than eaten as a snack.

Kiwi is one of the best-known fruit sources of vitamin C. In the U.S., it is often at its peak during winter. California-grown kiwi stays available through the cooler months. That makes it a cold-weather option alongside winter citrus.

The fruit most shoppers picture is the green kiwi. It has fuzzy brown skin, bright green flesh and a ring of small black seeds around a pale core. Hayward is the dominant green variety in commercial production. Golden kiwi comes from a closely related species, Actinidia chinensis. It has smooth, nearly hairless skin and sweeter yellow flesh.

Kiwi is native to China, where it was once known in English as the Chinese gooseberry. Growers in New Zealand developed it as a commercial crop in the 20th century. They marketed it under the name kiwifruit, after the country's national bird. Italy, New Zealand and China are now among the largest producers.

The winter timing in the U.S. follows the Northern Hemisphere growing cycle. Imports from the Southern Hemisphere, including New Zealand and Chile, keep kiwi on store shelves in the warmer months.

The vitamin C in kiwi plays a direct role in building collagen. The body needs the vitamin to make this protein, which forms the framework of skin, tendons, ligaments, blood vessels and bone. Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body.

Kiwi continues to ripen after harvest. A ripe fruit gives slightly under gentle pressure. Placing firm kiwi in a bag with an apple or banana speeds ripening. Those fruits release ethylene gas, which triggers the process.

The skin of green kiwi is edible, though many people halve the fruit and scoop out the flesh with a spoon. Golden kiwi skin is thinner and easier to eat whole.

Raw kiwi contains actinidin, an enzyme that breaks down protein. That enzyme keeps gelatin desserts from setting when fresh kiwi is mixed in. It also lets pureed kiwi work as a meat tenderizer in marinades.

Pomegranate arils supply vitamin C, but the fruit is not among the richest sources of the nutrient. In a winter diet, it works as one contributor among several rather than a primary source.

A pomegranate is a round fruit with a tough, leathery rind. Inside, hundreds of arils sit packed in chambers divided by a bitter, spongy white membrane. Each aril is a small seed wrapped in a sac of tart-sweet red juice. The aril is the part people eat, seed and all.

The pomegranate tree is native to a region stretching from Iran to northern India. It has been cultivated around the Mediterranean for thousands of years. In the Northern Hemisphere, the fruit reaches markets in fall and stays available into winter. In the U.S., California grows most of the commercial crop.

Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant in the body. It helps neutralize free radicals, which are unstable molecules that can damage cells. Pomegranates also contain other plant compounds, including polyphenols such as punicalagins. Anthocyanins, another group of compounds, give the arils and juice their red color. These substances are separate from vitamin C. Their presence does not make the fruit a richer source of it.

Getting the arils out takes some work. One common method starts by scoring the rind and breaking the fruit into sections in a bowl of water. The arils loosen under gentle pressure from the fingers and sink to the bottom. Pieces of white pith float to the surface, where they are easy to skim off. Working underwater also limits splatter. Pomegranate juice stains fabric and wood.

Arils go into salads, grain bowls and yogurt, or onto roasted meats as a garnish. They are a common ingredient in Persian and other Middle Eastern cooking. Pomegranate molasses, a thick syrup made by reducing the juice, adds a sour note to stews and dressings across the same region.

Whole arils and bottled juice are not interchangeable. Eating the arils keeps the edible seeds, which carry fiber. Pressing the fruit into juice leaves most of that fiber behind.

Broccoli is one of the strongest vegetable sources of vitamin C available in the colder months. As a cool-season crop, it stays in the produce aisle alongside winter citrus after summer vegetables have gone.

The way broccoli is cooked shapes how much of that vitamin C reaches the plate. Vitamin C is water-soluble. It dissolves into whatever liquid surrounds the vegetable during cooking.

That makes boiling the method most likely to pull it out. When broccoli sits in a pot of hot water, the vitamin moves out of the florets and stems and into the water. If that water is poured off, the dissolved vitamin C goes with it.

Heat causes a second kind of loss. Vitamin C breaks down when it is heated, and longer cooking destroys more of it. A long boil combines both problems — prolonged heat and a large volume of water.

Two adjustments limit those losses. Shorter cooking times reduce heat exposure. Using less water leaves less room for the vitamin to leach out.

The cooking liquid itself holds part of the answer. The vitamin C that leaves the broccoli ends up in the water. Dishes that keep that liquid, such as soups, retain some of what dissolved.

Cooked briefly in little water, broccoli keeps more of its vitamin C.

This slide is about 215 words, short of the 300-word minimum. The admitted research supports only two broccoli-specific facts, and the remaining general vitamin C facts are assigned to other slides or already covered in the introduction.

Brussels sprouts are a good vegetable source of vitamin C, and cooking method affects how much of it reaches the plate. Brief steaming keeps more of the nutrient than long simmering in a pot of water.

The sprouts are a cool-season crop. They belong to Brassica oleracea, the same plant species that produces cabbage, broccoli, kale and cauliflower. Each sprout is a small bud that forms along a tall, thick stalk. Its leaves wrap tightly, like a miniature cabbage head. In the U.S., they reach markets from fall into winter, and some grocers sell them still attached to the stalk.

The name refers to Brussels, Belgium, an area long associated with growing them.

Vitamin C breaks down with heat, and longer cooking means more loss. Boiling adds a second route for loss. The longer sprouts sit in hot water, the more vitamin C passes into the cooking liquid. That liquid is usually poured away.

Steaming avoids submerging the sprouts. They cook above the water rather than in it. Halved sprouts are usually tender within several minutes. That shorter contact with heat and water keeps more of the vitamin in the vegetable.

Size and cut affect timing too. Whole sprouts take longer to cook through at the center than halved or quartered ones. Cutting them first shortens the time the outer leaves spend exposed to heat. Sprouts of similar size cook evenly. None have to stay on the heat while larger ones catch up.

Overcooking carries a second cost. Brussels sprouts contain sulfur compounds called glucosinolates. Prolonged cooking breaks these down into compounds that give off the strong, sulfurous smell many people associate with the vegetable. A sprout that is bright green and just tender has spent less time on the heat than one that has turned olive-drab and soft.

To keep more vitamin C, trim the sprouts and cut them to a uniform size. Then steam them until a knife slides in with slight resistance.

Kale is a cold-hardy leafy green that contains vitamin C. It holds up through frost and stays in the produce lineup after more tender greens have finished for the year.

Kale belongs to the same species as broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage and cauliflower. All of them are forms of Brassica oleracea, bred for different parts of the plant. Kale was selected for its leaves, broccoli and cauliflower for their flower heads, and Brussels sprouts for their side buds. Cabbage was bred for its tightly packed head of leaves.

Cold weather can also change how the leaves taste. After a frost, kale often tastes sweeter. The plant converts some of its stored starch into sugar as temperatures drop.

Several types of kale reach grocery shelves. Curly kale has ruffled, tightly frilled leaves. Lacinato kale, also called Tuscan or dinosaur kale, has long, flat, dark blue-green leaves with a bumpy surface. Red Russian kale has flatter, fringed leaves and purple-red stems.

The vitamin C in kale also matters for another nutrient in the same meal. It helps the body absorb non-heme iron, the form of iron in plant foods. Heme iron, which comes from meat, poultry and fish, is absorbed more readily than non-heme iron.

Kale contains non-heme iron of its own. That places the iron and a nutrient that aids its absorption in the same leaf.

Kale also pairs with other iron-containing plant foods. Cooking it into a dish with chickpeas, tofu or quinoa adds vitamin C to a meal whose iron comes from plants. The same idea applies to grain bowls, soups and stews built around plant ingredients.

For people who eat little or no meat, plant foods supply most or all of their dietary iron. Pairing those foods with a vitamin C source such as kale is one way to make use of that absorption effect.

Red and green cabbage both contain vitamin C, and both store well through the winter. That long storage life keeps cabbage available as a vitamin C source after more delicate produce has gone.

The shape of the vegetable is part of the reason. A whole cabbage is a firm, tightly packed head of leaves. Leafy salad greens and soft fruit tend to wilt or bruise within days. A whole head holds up much longer in cool storage.

That durability changes how cabbage fits into a week of cooking. A head can sit in the refrigerator crisper until a meal calls for it. Cooks can cut off what they need and keep the rest for later meals.

The two common colors are handled the same way in the kitchen. Green cabbage is the familiar pale variety used in many everyday dishes. Red cabbage is usually deep purple and adds strong color to a plate.

Cabbage also suits raw preparations, which keep it away from cooking heat entirely. Slaw is the best-known example. It is made from thinly shredded raw cabbage tossed with a dressing.

That dressing can be vinegar-based or creamy. Either way, the cabbage itself is not cooked. Red and green cabbage can be shredded together in the same bowl.

Raw shredded cabbage works beyond slaw as well. It can be layered into sandwiches and wraps for crunch. It can also be folded into tacos or scattered over grain bowls.

Cauliflower is a cool-season crop that provides vitamin C. It grows in cooler weather, unlike many warm-weather crops that drop out of season in winter.

The main thing to watch with cauliflower is total heat exposure. The longer it stays on the stove or in the oven, the more of its vitamin C is lost.

Raw cauliflower involves no heat at all. Whole florets can go on a plate with a dip. Chopped finely, they can be mixed into a grain or leafy salad. Neither approach calls for cooking.

Roasting sits at the other end of that range. The florets stay in a hot oven until their edges brown. That extended exposure costs some of the vitamin C. The browning that gives roasted cauliflower its flavor comes from that same long heat.

For cooked cauliflower, the way it is cut changes the cooking time. Small, evenly sized florets cook through faster than large or uneven pieces. A shorter stretch on the heat leaves more of the vitamin intact.

Red bell peppers are a very rich source of vitamin C, and they stay on supermarket shelves through the winter. In colder months, though, most of them are greenhouse-grown or imported rather than picked from nearby fields.

Bell peppers are a warm-season crop. The plants do not tolerate frost, so outdoor growing in cold regions ends before winter arrives.

A red bell pepper bought in January usually comes from one of two places. It may have been raised in a greenhouse under glass or plastic, where growers control heat and light. Or it may have been shipped from a region with a warmer climate. In places with hard winters, it is not a local field crop at that time of year.

The color has its own explanation. Green, yellow, orange and red bell peppers all belong to the same species, Capsicum annuum. A red bell pepper is typically a fruit left on the plant until it fully ripened. A green bell pepper is the same kind of fruit, picked earlier.

Red peppers spend longer on the plant before harvest than green ones. That extra growing time is one reason they often cost more at the store.

Bell peppers also differ from their hot relatives. Chili peppers get their heat from capsaicin. Bell peppers carry a recessive gene that leaves them without it. That is why they taste sweet rather than spicy.

In the kitchen, raw red bell pepper slices work as a snack or for dipping. Diced, they go into salsas and grain salads. In a stir-fry, they can go in near the end so they stay crisp. Their mild sweetness pairs with sharper flavors such as onion, garlic and vinegar.

Whole peppers keep best unwashed in the refrigerator crisper drawer. A cut pepper should be wrapped and used within a few days.

For winter shoppers, the red bell pepper works as a year-round option rather than a seasonal one. In the cold months, it usually grows indoors or travels a long distance to reach the store.

#5501. Tradecraft Becomes First Venue to Support a Tokenized U.S. Stock Transaction Under the SEC Innovation Exemption

The trades involving Canton Strategic Holdings (NASDAQ: CNTN) shares follow TSV LLC's September 23 notice to the SEC, the first by any Tokenized Securities Venue

NEW YORK, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TSV LLC ("TSV"), the permissioned venue for tokenized NMS stocks on the Canton Network, today supported the first trades of a tokenized U.S. stock under the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's (SEC) Innovation Exemption, executed through a permissioned pool on Tradecraft, the automated market maker protocol that powers TSV. In the transactions, DRW Cumberland executed the first-ever purchases of tokenized Canton Strategic Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: CNTN) common stock from Five North, an existing shareholder. Fairmint TA LLC ("Fairmint"), an  SEC-registered transfer agent and a subsidiary of Fairmint, Inc., recorded the shares in token form in Five North's verified Loop Wallet, and Flowdesk Liquidity Solutions LLC ("Flowdesk") provided liquidity.

The trades are a milestone for tokenized equities in the United States, bringing onchain trading of a U.S.-listed stock within the SEC's new regulatory framework, announced in September, for the first time. They come as the asset class gains momentum, with onchain value of tokenized stocks growing from about $678 million at the start of 2026 to $3.15 billion by September, according to The Block Research. With a regulatory path now defined, issuer-sponsored listings like CNTN offer a model for public companies to bring their shares onchain while preserving the rights investors expect.

"Shares of a U.S. public company traded onchain under the SEC's Innovation Exemption for the first time, carrying the same rights as the CNTN stock that trades on Nasdaq," said Ryan Trinkle, Co-Founder of TSV. "We set out to make our first listing the standard for how tokenized U.S. equities should work under the SEC's Innovation Exemption. The token is issuer-sponsored, with Fairmint's Onchain Transfer Agent keeping the official record, and every holder is verified before they can hold or trade. On Tradecraft, approved investors can now trade at any hour, and shares and payment settle on the Canton Network."

The trades follow Canton Strategic Holdings' October 29 announcement of its agreement with TSV to make its common stock available for trading on the venue. Fairmint, Canton Strategic Holdings' SEC-registered transfer agent, recorded the tokenized shares on behalf of the company as issuer-sponsored shares, maintains the official onchain record of ownership, operates the allow list of verified holders and wallets, and applies the company's transfer controls. Holders of the tokenized shares receive the same rights and privileges as holders of CNTN shares traded on Nasdaq.

The SEC's Innovation Exemption, issued September 17, allows qualifying platforms to trade tokenized U.S. stocks through permissioned automated market maker (AMM) pools. TSV, a special purpose regulatory vehicle, was the first to formally notify the SEC of its intent to operate a tokenized securities venue, publishing its initial venue notice on September 23. Because Canton Strategic Holdings sponsored the tokenization of its own shares, the listing did not require the 30-day issuer notice-and-objection process that applies when unaffiliated parties tokenize a company's stock.

Tradecraft is the leading AMM protocol on the Canton Network and powers TSV. Through the venue, approved participants can trade tokenized shares 24/7, subject to regulatorily required trading stoppages, maintenance, risk controls, and trading volume limits, with trades settling atomically on a delivery-versus-payment basis so shares and payment change hands together. Participants and their wallets must be approved before trading, including identity verification and sanctions screening, and smart contracts enforce those rules.

For more information, visit tokenizedstockvenue.com.

About TSVTSV LLC is a Tokenized Securities Venue founded by Ali Abrar and Ryan Trinkle, and the first to complete the SEC's Innovation Exemption process set out in Release No. 34-106402. Approved participants can trade tokenized NMS stocks through automated market maker pools on Tradecraft, the leading AMM protocol on the Canton Network. Participants and their wallets are approved before trading, including identity verification and sanctions screening, with rules enforced by smart contracts. For more information, visit tokenizedstockvenue.com.

#5500. Oracle connects AI-driven testing with a new approach to database security

Frontier AI models that uncover software flaws by the hundreds are forcing database providers into larger, faster patch cycles, and real application testing is becoming the safeguard that keeps those fixes from breaking production systems. The same AI wave is also undermining security rules written into applications.

Oracle Corp. has responded on two fronts, hardening its code against outside attackers while moving agent controls down to the data layer. The first effort began when the company turned an early-access frontier model on its own software, according to Juan Loaiza (pictured), executive vice president of Oracle Database Technologies at Oracle.

“Back in March, we got early access to the Mythos model and we ran it against our code and it started finding all these security vulnerabilities,” Loaiza said. “It’s turning up some very serious security issues. And so we said, ‘Hey, this is a code red moment. The house is on fire.'”

Loaiza spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why AI-discovered vulnerabilities, AI-generated code and AI agents require enterprises to treat security as a data problem. (* Disclosure below.)

Most of Oracle’s response to AI-discovered vulnerabilities is landing in its regular quarterly patches, which have grown much larger as a result, Loaiza explained. A quarterly security update earlier this year addressed more than 1,400 vulnerabilities across the company’s portfolio. Customers must automate patching and stay current, but every large patch raises fears of regression in systems that cannot fail.

“We have something called Real Application Testing where we can capture real workload and run it to make sure that your workload is not affected by these patches,” Loaiza said. “It’s not quite as simple as just apply because the applications that people run are extraordinarily complex. They run entire countries, entire industries.”

Patching handles outside attackers. Internal AI use is a separate threat, because applications have traditionally enforced end-user security, and AI now writes much of that code or goes straight to the data. Oracle’s answer is Deep Data Security, which began shipping in April and passes an authenticated user’s identity as an encrypted token through to the database. The company has since extended those authorization controls across remote databases, lakehouse data and related tables.

“The new world as I see it is all these end-user security rules have to be enforced where AI can’t bypass them, which means all the way down in the data,” Loaiza said. “The AI agent has to get your identity. It’s acting on behalf of you. It can’t leak the data if it can’t see the data.”

Business rules follow the same logic. Application code has always blocked a credit card charge above the customer’s limit, but an AI agent told to enforce that rule may not comply, Loaiza noted. Oracle is providing declarative ways to define such rules, along with SQL Assertions that check whether changes made through SQL are valid.

“There’s credit limits, there’s all sorts of things that are business rules that can’t be violated. And again, if we move those all the way down into the data, then no matter how you access the data, what mechanism you use, how AI is used, it cannot violate those rules,” Loaiza said.

Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of Oracle AI World:

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for Oracle AI World. Neither Oracle, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. Join theCUBE’s Alumni Trust Network, where technology leaders connect, share intelligence and create opportunities.

Founded by tech visionaries John Furrier and Dave Vellante, SiliconANGLE Media has built a dynamic ecosystem of industry-leading digital media brands that reach 15+ million elite tech professionals. Our new proprietary theCUBE AI Video Cloud is breaking ground in audience interaction, leveraging theCUBEai.com neural network to help technology companies make data-driven decisions and stay at the forefront of industry conversations.

#5499. 10 ways to train indoors this winter, and what changes calorie burn in each

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These indoor winter workouts, from rowing to jump rope, keep you training through the cold, with a clear look at what drives calorie burn for each one

No workout has a single true calorie count. Two people can finish the same 30-minute session on a rowing machine and burn very different amounts of energy. The number on a cardio machine's display is an estimate, built on assumptions about the person using it.

That matters in winter, when more training moves indoors. Short days, icy pavements and cold wind make outdoor runs and rides harder to schedule and riskier to attempt. Gyms, pools and living rooms fill the gap. The choice of what to do inside often comes down to a practical question: how much work does this session do?

A standard reference for answering it is the Compendium of Physical Activities. It assigns each activity a MET value, short for metabolic equivalent of task. One MET represents the energy a person uses while sitting quietly at rest. An activity with a higher MET value demands proportionally more energy than rest.

To turn that into an estimate, multiply the MET value by body weight in kilograms, then by the number of hours spent on the activity. The result is an approximate calorie figure. It is a starting point, not a measurement.

Four variables shape the real result. Body weight comes first: a heavier person burns more calories than a lighter person doing the same activity at the same intensity. Intensity is the second. It is the one a person controls most directly, through pace, resistance, load or rest. Duration is the third. Fitness level is the fourth. A trained athlete can often hold a higher intensity for longer than a beginner, which changes how much work a session does.

The 10 indoor winter workouts below are a selection, not a ranking. They run in alphabetical order, and none is presented as the top calorie burner. Each slide explains what the workout involves, which muscles it uses and what equipment it needs. Each also covers which adjustments raise or lower its calorie burn, and why it suits a season that keeps training inside.

The list spans machines found in most gyms, classes offered at studios and routines that need nothing more than floor space. That range lets a reader match a workout to the room, budget and joints they have.

A bodyweight circuit strings together push-ups, squats, lunges, burpees and planks with short rests, using the body as the only resistance. It needs nothing more than a patch of floor. That makes it a practical way to keep training at home when winter weather rules out exercising outside.

The structure is simple. Each exercise runs for a set number of repetitions or a fixed stretch of time, and the next one follows straight away. Rest comes after a full round of every move rather than between individual exercises. A common format is three to five rounds, adjusted for fitness level and the time available.

Each move covers a different part of the body. Push-ups load the chest, shoulders and triceps, while the core holds the torso in a straight line. Squats work the quadriceps, glutes and hamstrings. Lunges train the same muscles one leg at a time, which adds a balance challenge. Burpees combine a squat, a plank and a jump into a single movement. Planks build endurance in the abdominal and lower-back muscles that stabilize the spine.

The order of exercises shapes how the circuit flows. Alternating upper-body and lower-body moves lets one muscle group recover while another works. That keeps the session moving without forcing long pauses.

Progression comes from changing leverage and speed instead of adding weight. Incline push-ups, with the hands on a kitchen counter or sturdy chair, reduce the load for beginners. Decline push-ups, with the feet raised on a step or couch, shift more of the work onto the shoulders and upper chest. Jump squats add an explosive phase to a standard squat. A side plank moves the demand onto the obliques.

Rest length is a major lever on calorie burn in this workout. Shorter breaks keep the heart rate elevated across the session. As a result, the circuit works as cardio as well as strength training. Adding rounds raises the total. Swapping in explosive variations such as jump squats or full burpees raises it as well.

The format suits small winter living spaces. A floor area about the size of a yoga mat covers every move in the circuit. In an apartment, jump squats and burpees can be loud for neighbors below. Step-back burpees, which replace the hop with a step, keep the noise down. Standard squats in place of jump squats do the same. A few minutes of marching in place and arm circles before the first round warm up the joints. A non-slip surface keeps hands and feet from sliding during push-ups and lunges.

Dance cardio turns continuous, choreographed movement set to music into an aerobic workout. Its calorie burn depends less on any single step than on how fast the routine moves, how big the movements are and how long the dancer keeps going without stopping.

Zumba is one of the most widely recognized versions of the format. Alberto "Beto" Perez, a dancer and fitness instructor, created it in Colombia in the 1990s. Classes draw on Latin rhythms such as salsa, merengue, cumbia and reggaeton, layered over simple aerobic patterns. Instructors tend to lead by demonstration and hand signals rather than long verbal breakdowns. Participants follow along in real time.

Zumba is one option among many. Jazzercise, founded by Judi Sheppard Missett in 1969, blends jazz dance with aerobic exercise. Studios and streaming platforms offer hip-hop cardio, Bollywood-style sessions and other music-led routines. Ubisoft's Just Dance video game series scores players on how closely they match the choreography on screen.

Tempo is the first lever on calorie burn. A faster song demands quicker footwork and more steps per minute. Range of motion is the second. Deep knee bends, high knees, full arm sweeps and small jumps move the body through more distance than a shuffle in place. The third lever is rest. A dancer who stops to drink water or wait between every track lets the heart rate settle. Moving straight from one song into the next keeps it elevated.

The format also trains coordination. Routines pair footwork with arm patterns, turns and changes of direction. That challenges balance and rhythm alongside the cardiovascular system. Beginners can learn the footwork first. The arm patterns can be layered on once the steps feel familiar.

Group classes add a social structure. A live session supplies a fixed schedule and an instructor who sets the pace. A solo workout at home has neither unless the dancer builds them in.

At home, dance cardio needs very little: a cleared patch of floor, a screen and supportive shoes. Footwear deserves attention. Running shoes with deep tread can grip the floor during pivots and strain the knees. Cross-trainers or dance-fitness sneakers with smoother soles turn more easily. People in apartments can swap jumps for low-impact steps to limit noise for downstairs neighbors.

That flexibility suits winter. A session can start the moment the music does, with no drive to a gym and no warm-up in freezing air. It fits into a dark evening after work.

High-intensity interval training, or HIIT, alternates short bursts of near-maximal effort with brief recovery periods. It is defined by the timed pattern of work and rest, not by any single exercise.

The best-known format is the Tabata protocol. It comes from research led by Izumi Tabata at Japan's National Institute of Fitness and Sports, published in 1996. The protocol calls for 20 seconds of maximal-intensity work followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated for eight rounds. The full set lasts four minutes. The original study used a stationary cycle ergometer. The effort was meant to be close to exhausting by the final rounds.

Most gym and home HIIT sessions are less extreme than the original Tabata format. A common structure pairs 30 seconds of hard work with 30 seconds of easy movement. Another uses 40 seconds on and 20 seconds off. Beginners often flip that pattern, working for 20 seconds and resting for 40.

The work-to-rest ratio is the main dial on intensity. Shorter rest leaves less recovery before the next burst. Heart rate then stays higher across the session, and that sustained effort drives calorie burn in an interval workout. Very short rests at a truly maximal effort usually lead to a drop in output in the later rounds. Slightly longer work periods at a hard but repeatable pace can keep the total workload high.

Interval timing works with almost any movement. Sprints on a spin bike, hard pulls on a rowing machine and fast treadmill efforts all fit the format. So do floor moves such as mountain climbers or high knees.

The efforts are demanding, so HIIT is usually spaced through the week rather than done daily. Training plans commonly place an easier day or a strength session between interval days to allow recovery.

Beginners can scale the format in three ways. They can lengthen the rest periods or cut the number of rounds. They can also swap jumping moves for low-impact ones, such as step-backs in place of burpees. Several minutes of easy movement before the first interval prepares the muscles and joints for the hard efforts.

For winter training, the appeal is time. A complete interval session, including a warm-up and cool-down, can fit into 20 to 30 minutes. That suits short days and dark evenings, when a long outdoor run is harder to schedule.

Indoor cycling is low-impact cardio that works mainly the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes and calves. Its two main controls, resistance and cadence, let a rider set the effort precisely without leaving the house.

Cadence $CDNS is pedal speed, measured in revolutions per minute, or RPM. Resistance is how hard the pedals push back. On most spin bikes, a knob or lever sets it. Raising either one, while holding the other steady, increases calorie burn. A rider spinning fast against almost no resistance does less work than the speed suggests. Pushing heavy resistance at low cadence builds leg strength, but it can be hard to sustain. Structured sessions often move between the two, pairing faster seated spins with slower, heavier climbs.

Equipment shapes the experience. A spin bike has a heavy flywheel at the front and a riding position close to that of a road bike. An upright stationary bike seats the rider more vertically. A recumbent bike adds a backrest and places the pedals forward. That layout supports the lower back. Outdoor cyclists can also mount their own bike on a smart trainer and ride virtual courses in apps such as Zwift.

Bike setup affects both comfort and efficiency. A common starting point is to set the saddle level with the hip bone while standing beside the bike. At the bottom of the pedal stroke, the knee should stay slightly bent rather than locked straight. A saddle set too low pushes stress onto the front of the knee. A saddle set too high makes the hips rock from side to side.

Studio classes and home riding suit different needs. Instructor-led classes add music, coaching cues and a group pace that can push effort higher. SoulCycle built its studio business on that format. Peloton streams live and on-demand classes to its connected bikes at home. Riding solo offers more control over timing and session length.

The low impact sets indoor cycling apart from running. The feet never leave the pedals. That spares the knees, hips and ankles the landing forces of each running stride. It also makes cycling a common option for people easing back from injury. For road cyclists, an indoor bike is a way to hold on to fitness through months of ice, snow and early darkness.

Jumping rope is a compact, low-cost cardio workout that builds footwork, coordination and calf endurance. It needs little more than a rope, a patch of sturdy floor and enough headroom for the rope to pass overhead.

Rope length shapes the whole session. A common check is to stand on the middle of the rope with one foot and pull the handles up along the body. For beginners, handle tips that reach about armpit height are a typical starting point. Experienced jumpers often shorten the rope toward chest height to speed up each turn. A rope that is too long slaps the floor ahead and slows the rhythm. One that is too short catches the toes.

Space matters in three directions: above, in front and behind. The rope sweeps a full arc over the head on every turn. Ceiling height, hanging lights and ceiling fans count as much as floor area. A garage, basement or wide hallway often works better than a furnished living room.

The type of rope changes how the workout feels. Beaded and PVC ropes turn more slowly and are easier to time. That makes them a common pick for beginners. Speed ropes made of thin coated steel cable spin faster and are the usual choice for advanced footwork. Weighted ropes put more load on the shoulders and forearms, adding upper-body effort to the session.

Good form keeps each jump low, just high enough to clear the rope. Landings come on the balls of the feet with the knees slightly soft. The elbows stay close to the ribs, and the wrists do the turning rather than the whole arm. Common progressions run from the basic two-foot bounce to the alternate-foot step, high knees and side-to-side skier.

Calorie burn depends mostly on skip speed and how long a person keeps the rope moving without a miss. Frequent trips break the rhythm and lower the effort. Double-unders, where the rope passes under the feet twice in a single jump, demand a higher jump and quicker wrists. That raises the work involved in each repetition.

Every session involves a long run of small landings, which load the ankles, calves and Achilles tendons. A wooden floor or rubber gym mat absorbs more of that impact than bare concrete or tile. Cushioned cross-training shoes help too. In an apartment, a mat also cuts the noise that reaches neighbors below.

Boxers have long used the rope for footwork and conditioning, often skipping in timed rounds that mirror a fight. Beginners can borrow that structure with short rounds of skipping separated by rest. Each round can grow longer as misses become rarer. For winter, the rope folds into a bag and needs no power, machine or gym membership.

The kettlebell swing is a hip-hinge movement that trains the glutes, hamstrings and core while driving the heart rate up. Paired with a few other kettlebell lifts in a circuit, a single bell can serve as both a strength session and a cardio workout.

The swing starts with the bell on the floor between the feet. The lifter pushes the hips back, keeps the spine neutral and hikes the bell back between the legs. A sharp drive of the hips forward then sends it out in front of the body. The arms act as connectors. The power comes from the hips, not the shoulders.

Two versions are common in gyms. The Russian swing stops the bell at about chest height, with the arms roughly parallel to the floor. The American swing carries it all the way overhead. That overhead finish lengthens the path of the bell. It also demands more shoulder mobility and makes it harder to keep the lower back neutral at the top of each rep.

A circuit adds movements the swing leaves out. The goblet squat, with the bell held by its horns at chest height, trains the quads and an upright torso. The clean brings the bell from the floor to the rack position, resting against the forearm and the front of the shoulder. The Turkish get-up takes a lifter from lying on the floor to standing with the bell locked out overhead, then back down again. It is slow and deliberate, and it tests shoulder stability and coordination more than conditioning.

Bell weight and pace set the calorie burn. A heavier bell moved for the same number of reps asks more of the working muscles. A faster pace with shorter breaks keeps the heart rate elevated across the whole session. Long pauses between rounds pull the workload down.

Lower-back safety comes down to technique. The swing should be a hinge rather than a squat, with the shins staying close to vertical. Each rep should finish with the lifter standing tall and the glutes contracted, not leaning backward. Rounding the spine to chase the bell on the backswing is a common error, and it shifts strain onto the lower back.

For winter training at home, a single kettlebell fits in a closet corner. Bells were traditionally sized in a Russian unit called the pood, equal to about 16 kilograms. Modern bells come in a range of lighter and heavier sizes, sold in kilograms or pounds.

A rowing machine works the legs, core and upper body in one linked stroke. Calorie burn on an indoor erg follows the power a rower puts into each drive. That power appears directly on the machine's monitor.

Erg is short for ergometer, a device that measures work done. Competitive crews have long used ergs to keep training through winter, when rivers and lakes are too cold or frozen to row on. Home and gym models come in air, magnetic, water and hydraulic designs. Concept2's air-resistance rowers are a common sight in gyms and at indoor rowing competitions. The rower stays seated throughout. That keeps impact on the knees and ankles low.

Each stroke follows a fixed order. The drive starts at the catch, with shins close to vertical and arms straight. The legs push first. The torso then swings back from the hips, and the arms finish by drawing the handle toward the lower ribs. The recovery reverses that sequence: arms extend, the body tips forward and the knees bend to slide the seat back to the catch. Pulling with the arms before the legs have finished is a common error. It shifts work away from the large leg muscles and onto the smaller muscles of the arms and shoulders.

The damper lever on an air rower is often mistaken for a resistance dial. On a Concept2 machine, it runs from one to 10 and controls how much air flows into the flywheel housing. A higher setting makes each stroke feel heavier and slower to accelerate, much like rowing a larger, slower boat. It does not by itself make the workout harder. Resistance on an air rower comes from how hard the rower pulls. A faster-spinning flywheel pushes back with more force.

Stroke rate and power are separate measures. Stroke rate counts strokes per minute. Power reflects how hard and how fast each drive moves the handle. A high rate with weak strokes can produce less work than a slower rate with strong leg drive.

The monitor reports that work as watts, as a pace per 500 meters or as a running calorie estimate. Raising the wattage, holding a faster split or extending the session all increase the energy a workout demands.

Stair climbing lifts your full body weight upward with every step. That puts sustained work on the glutes, quadriceps and calves. It can be done on a gym stepmill or in an ordinary building stairwell. Both options keep training going when sidewalks are icy.

Each step works like a small single-leg press. One leg drives the body up while the other swings through to the next stair. The hamstrings help extend the hip, and the core holds the torso upright. The body works against gravity the whole time. Heart rate climbs quickly as a result, even at a modest pace.

Gym machines come in two main styles. A stepmill, such as the StairMaster StepMill, has a revolving set of stairs that rolls downward like a short escalator. The user keeps climbing to stay in place. A stepper uses two pedals that move up and down without a full step cycle. The stepmill more closely copies the motion of a real staircase. Both let the user set a step speed and hold it for an entire session.

A building stairwell costs nothing and is common in apartment blocks and office towers. It offers real stairs with landings, which break up the climb with brief turns. It has no speed setting, so the climber controls pace alone. Check building rules first. Some stairwell doors lock from the stairwell side, and some are fitted with alarms.

Posture has a direct effect on calorie burn. Leaning on the side rails of a machine shifts part of body weight onto the arms. The legs then lift less, and the workout gets easier. Standing tall with only a light touch on the rails for balance keeps the full load on the legs.

Pace and step pattern are the other levers. A faster step rate raises effort. Taking two stairs at a time lengthens each stride and works the glutes and hips through a deeper range of motion. Alternating single and double steps adds variety within one session.

The way down needs attention in a real stairwell. Descending puts braking force through the knees and the front of the thigh, which can strain sensitive joints. Riding the elevator down and then repeating the climb spares the knees that load. A stepmill avoids the descent entirely.

Lap swimming in an indoor pool is a full-body, low-impact workout. Water supports most of a swimmer's body weight. The arms, legs, back and core can work hard without the pounding of running or jumping.

That buoyancy makes swimming an option for people with sore knees, hips or ankles. Each stroke pulls against the resistance of the water rather than against gravity. The shoulders, lats and chest drive the pull. The hips, glutes and legs supply the kick. The core holds the body in a long, flat line, which reduces drag as the swimmer moves through the water.

Lap swimmers usually rotate among four strokes. Freestyle, also called front crawl, is the fastest and the one most people use for continuous laps. Backstroke uses a similar alternating arm pattern on the back. It keeps the face out of the water and makes breathing simple. Breaststroke combines a simultaneous arm sweep with a frog-style kick, and it is the slowest of the four in competition. Butterfly moves both arms together over the water with an undulating dolphin kick. It is the most technically and physically demanding of the four. Most recreational swimmers use it only in short bursts.

Stroke choice is one of three main levers on calorie burn. The other two are pace and the time spent resting at the wall. A swimmer who glides through easy breaststroke and pauses after every length uses far less energy than one holding a steady freestyle pace. Shortening rest between lengths keeps effort high across the session. Swimming sets on a fixed send-off time, where each repeat starts at a set point on the clock, does the same. Technique also matters. A swimmer with inefficient form can tire quickly while covering little distance.

Two common pieces of pool equipment let swimmers target one part of the body. A kickboard is held out in front of the swimmer. The arms stay still and the legs do the work. A pull buoy is a foam float squeezed between the thighs. It keeps the legs afloat without kicking and shifts the load to the arms, shoulders and back. Fins and hand paddles add speed or resistance. They also change stroke mechanics, and swimmers tend to use them in limited doses.

Pool length shapes how a workout is counted. Many U.S. pools are 25 yards long, while long-course competition pools measure 50 meters. Swimmers often plan sets by distance rather than minutes. A pace clock on the wall helps them track intervals and rest.

The winter case for swimming rests on heated indoor pools at gyms, YMCAs, community recreation centers and universities. The water temperature stays steady regardless of snow or ice outside. The main seasonal adjustment comes after the swim. Wet hair and damp skin lose heat quickly in cold air. Drying off fully and covering the head before leaving the building limits that heat loss on the way home.

A treadmill lets runners and walkers set an exact speed and incline. Those two settings are the main ways to change how many calories a session burns.

The machine moves a motorized belt beneath the user at a chosen pace. In the U.S., consoles usually show speed in miles per hour, while most other markets use kilometers per hour. Incline is shown as a percentage grade, and raising it tilts the front of the deck upward. With no wind, ice, traffic lights or uneven pavement, a runner can hold a target pace for an entire session. That precision suits training plans built around specific paces.

Speed is the first lever. A faster pace covers more ground each minute, and heart rate and breathing climb to match. The jump from walking to running also changes the movement itself. Running includes a moment when both feet leave the belt. That raises both the effort and the impact on each landing.

Incline is the second lever. Each step on a raised deck lifts the body upward as well as forward. That shifts more of the work onto the glutes, hamstrings and calves than flat walking does. Heart rate can climb to a demanding level even at a walking pace. For people who want to avoid the pounding of running, incline walking offers a lower-impact way to raise the intensity.

How a person holds on matters too. Gripping the handrails, especially on a steep incline, lets the arms carry part of the body's weight and often shortens the stride. The legs do less work, and the calorie burn drops. The console calculates its calorie readout from settings such as speed, incline and any body weight entered. It has no way to detect someone leaning on the rails. A light touch for balance keeps most of the effort on the legs.

Safety starts before the belt moves. Most treadmills have a safety key that clips to clothing. If the user drifts too far back or falls, the key pulls free and the belt stops. A safe start means standing on the side rails, starting the belt at a slow speed and then stepping on. Clear space behind the machine reduces the risk if someone slips off the back.

In winter, a treadmill at home or in a gym supports steady runs, interval sessions and long incline walks after dark or during a snowstorm.

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:38 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 1:47 pm

Seattle startup Ganaz, which provides payroll and HR tech for agricultural workers and employers, has been acquired by Beacon Holdings.

Ganaz co-founder and CEO Hannah Freeman announced the deal Wednesday on LinkedIn, saying the public benefit corporation “is in great hands” at Beacon, which “is building momentum for our next exciting season.”

Freeman indicated she is stepping away from the company to “catch my breath, spend more time with my daughter, and dream about what’s next,” she wrote. “I’ll miss our team & customers, but will be cheering you on from the sidelines.”

Ganaz launched in 2017 and has raised more than $10 million, with its last disclosed funding round in June 2021. That financing valued the company at $26 million, according to PitchBook. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Beacon, based in Toronto, buys software businesses serving traditional industries and provides shared technology and operational resources. The company said in September that its portfolio included 45 software businesses.

Ganaz’s platform provides employee onboarding, training, communication and analytics tools. It also offers a Mastercard payroll card that gives unbanked workers access to digital banking. Employers save time and money by skipping paper checks, while workers keep more of their pay by avoiding check-cashing and high remittance fees.

Ganaz received GeekWire’s 2023 Geeks Give Back Award. “We founded Ganaz to make life better for farm workers, and we do that by building technology that agricultural employers love and can’t live without,” Freeman told GeekWire in 2023. “We build our tools to help both workers and employers prosper, and that kicks off a virtuous cycle that helps agricultural communities prosper as well.”

At that time, the startup was serving more than 250,000 agricultural workers in the U.S. and Mexico and 100 employers in the sector.

The company has about 17 employees, according to LinkedIn. Freeman did not say in her post whether Ganaz will continue as a subsidiary or whether its employees will receive job offers from Beacon. GeekWire has reached out to Freeman for comment and will update the story with any reply.

#5496. What Solana’s Alpenglow Switch Actually Changes at Slot 459,653,000

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

For about 400 milliseconds this afternoon, Solana will stop landing user transactions. That isn't a failure.

It's the scheduled handoff between two consensus systems, and it's probably the only "400 ms" figure that matters today.

Many people heading into the Alpenglow launch still treat 400 ms block times and 12.8-second finality as the bar to beat. Those are the old chain's numbers. They describe TowerBFT, the system Alpenglow is replacing, so Alpenglow shouldn't be checked against them. If you go through Solana's own documentation, you'll find the right benchmarks before the first post-launch numbers arrive.

According to Solana's official Alpenglow page, the upgrade's feature gate activates at the start of epoch 1064 on Wednesday, October 21, at about 13:20 UTC. The Solana Foundation says to treat that time as an estimate and to watch the epoch instead.

The new consensus doesn't take over the moment the epoch begins. TowerBFT keeps running for the first 5,000 slots, and Alpenglow takes control at slot 459,653,000. Anza, the team behind the main Agave client, put that switch at around 14:00 UTC.

That time isn't fixed. Solana Compass calculated that with about 375,000 slots left before the switch, each millisecond of drift in average slot time moves the boundary by roughly six minutes. Using epoch 1062's pace, it estimated the switch at about 14:02 UTC.

The transition itself has a cost. Solana Compass reports a gap of roughly two slots, about 400 ms, during which blocks carry only votes and user transactions don't land. So the 400 ms everyone is watching for will turn up, just as a pause rather than a block time.

This is where much of today's coverage gets it wrong.

Block time first. Solana's page says slots moved from 400 ms to 200 ms in a separate "reduced slot times" upgrade, which finished this month. That change isn't part of Alpenglow. It was already running before today. Solana Compass measured epoch 1062 averaging 217.7 ms per slot over 26.1 hours. Checking Alpenglow against 400 ms would mean grading it against a number the network had already beaten before the switch.

Then finality. The 12.8 seconds is TowerBFT's figure. Under that system, a block became final only after enough votes built up over 32 slots. Alpenglow's stated target is about 150 ms, which Solana describes as 99% faster than TowerBFT.

Solana is careful about that 150 ms figure, and I think readers should be too. The Foundation calls it an expectation, not a constant, and says one-round finality comes in lower. Galaxy's engineers, quoted by Solana Compass, call it a design target rather than a measured result. As I noted when looking at how CertiK verifies a TPS claim, a target is a claim until someone measures it on the live network.

Alpenglow is Solana's first replacement of its core consensus since TowerBFT, and today's launch only covers part of it.

The first phase, Votor, ships in Agave 4.3. Validators now send votes directly to each other and combine them into certificates, instead of submitting votes as on-chain transactions. Per Solana's page, votes are no longer transactions and no longer appear in blocks. A block can finalize in one round if at least 80% of stake notarizes it. Otherwise, a second round uses 60% thresholds.

Proof of History no longer paces block production. Execution stays the same: the SVM, programs, transactions and fees don't change.

The second phase, Rotor, will replace Turbine, Solana's block propagation layer. Solana lists it as "not yet scheduled." If someone credits today's numbers to "Alpenglow" as a whole, half of the design hasn't shipped yet.

The security trade-off is also worth knowing. TowerBFT needed more than two-thirds of stake for confirmation. Alpenglow tolerates 20% malicious stake plus 20% offline stake. Solana Compass notes that slashing for double voting is defined but not enabled in this first version.

Validators also pay differently. TowerBFT voting cost about 1 SOL per epoch in vote transaction fees. Alpenglow replaces that with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch Validator Admission Ticket (SIMD-0357), which is burned. A validator that can't pay doesn't vote or produce blocks in the next epoch.

In my view, this is the detail most likely to affect today's real numbers.

Alpenglow's fastest finality depends on the one-round fast path, which needs at least 80% of stake to notarize a block. On the morning of October 20, a tracker run by Pumpkin's Pool, cited by SolanaFloor and reported by Solana Compass, flagged 151 validators holding 20.3% of stake as unprepared. The day before, that figure was 45%.

The math is uncomfortable. If 20.3% of stake really couldn't vote, only 79.7% would be left, which is just short of the fast-path threshold. In that case, blocks would need the slower second round, and finality would land above the headline figure.

I expect that number to drop before the switch, since operators have been upgrading quickly. But it's the main reason I wouldn't trust any finality figure from the first hour without also checking how much stake is actually voting. Validators without a registered BLS key, or that miss the required client version, stop voting entirely. Their delegators also stop earning inflation rewards.

There's already one public reference point. Solana's page links to a community cluster explorer run by Valid Blocks, where Alpenglow has been running on Agave 4.3.2.

When I checked this morning, it showed an average finalization time of 131 ms over the past hour, ranging from 111 ms to 156 ms. Average slot time was 215 ms. That's inside Solana's target range.

That cluster had 62 active validators and about 10.2 million SOL staked. Mainnet is far larger, more spread out geographically, and runs under real load. Test-cluster results are a strong sign, but they aren't proof of how mainnet will perform.

You don't need to wait for a press release to know whether the switch happened. Solana's getAgGenesisCert RPC method returns null while the cluster is still on TowerBFT and returns a genesis certificate once Alpenglow is live. Nodes older than Agave 4.3 return a "Method not found" error, which shouldn't be confused with null.

Once the certificate shows up, here's what I'll be watching over the first few epochs:

One caveat for developers: according to Anza's operator notes, the Clock sysvar's unix_timestamp now estimates when the parent block ended, not when the current block began, and should be treated as approximate. Any timing tool that reads block timestamps may need adjusting.

If Alpenglow delivers, Solana goes from finality you wait for to finality you'd barely notice. I'll believe the 150 ms figure once mainnet consistently shows it.

#5495. Research prediction: Shift from digital banking to AI-driven finance will transform financial services in 2027

The coming year will signal an abrupt transition from digital banking to intelligent finance, as AI agents and operating models reshape the ways that financial firms acquire customers and provide advice.

This is the central thesis of a new Forrester Research report, “Predictions 2027: Banking and Investing.” The findings were summarized from data involving 915 respondents in the U.S., U.K., and Canada.

Forrester identified several key points of transition. These included fundamental changes through automation in financial discovery and guidance journeys, as well as a belief that although one-third of banks will announce an AI transformation program, only 5% will succeed.

“In 2027, financial services will enter a new phase in which intelligence becomes the primary source of value creation,” said Forrester researchers in the report. “AI assistants are reshaping how customers discover, evaluate and act on financial products; investment participation is expanding despite persistent economic anxiety; and banks are racing to determine whether AI will merely enhance existing operations or fundamentally transform them.”

Forrester’s prediction of a 5% success rate is based on a belief that many banks will rebrand existing AI initiatives as AI-native without significant changes in operational infrastructure. Retention of legacy processes and operating models will prevent an ability to scale AI deployment, a fundamental requirement that AI technology providers such as Dell Technologies Inc. are emphasizing to their clients in the financial services world.

“Ultimately, I think we’ve enough proof points now that AI works and it works really well and it gives you speed and efficiency in your company,” according to David Kennedy, chief financial officer of Dell, during a recent interview with theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. “The question is, can you do that at scale?”

One way that financial institutions will pursue scale is through mergers and acquisitions. Forrester predicts that AI banking technology M&A will increase by 50% in 2027. Acquisition of proprietary data assets, governance capabilities, and AI-native orchestration will require an ability to navigate hybrid computing environments, a need that compute providers such as Advanced Micro Devices Inc. has seen among its own customers.

“As a provider of AI compute, we want to make sure that we are enabling those enterprises to not only run their AI tasks through the frontier APIs in the cloud, but we are providing them infrastructure that they can host open-weight models very efficiently on-prem,” said Suresh Andani, corporate vice president of compute and enterprise AI at AMD, in an interview with theCUBE. “Every enterprise conversation I’m in, that’s a key topic of discussion.”

Another key topic involves AI agents and their growing influence in the enterprise. According to Forrester’s findings, 40% of banks will launch AI assistants next year. The challenge for many financial institutions will be leveraging AI assistants to deliver differentiated guidance using proprietary data, decisioning and specialist expertise to guide customers. This is where keeping proprietary knowledge in-house can become a distinct advantage, according to John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.

“It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” Roese told theCUBE. “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these new forms that really captured what you know and do differently than your competitors.”
