#5494. How cold is too cold to exercise outside? 10 things to weigh before a winter workout

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How cold is too cold to exercise outside depends on wind, wetness, clothing and health — these 10 cold-weather factors help you judge whether a winter workout makes sense

The thermometer gives only part of the answer. A calm, dry morning and a windy, wet one can share the same reading. They still pull heat from the body at very different rates. Moving air strips away the thin layer of warmth that sits next to the skin. Water conducts heat away from the body far faster than still air does. That is why the question of how cold is too cold to exercise outside has no single number attached to it.

Exercise complicates the picture in both directions. Working muscles produce heat. A runner can feel comfortable in conditions that would chill someone standing at a bus stop. That same effort produces sweat. Damp clothing, especially cotton, insulates poorly. The heat that kept a person warm mid-workout disappears quickly once the pace drops or the session ends. A cold-weather workout can feel fine for the first stretch and turn risky later, especially on a long outing far from shelter.

The exerciser matters too. Clothing choices, time spent outdoors and the condition of the heart, lungs and circulation all shape how well someone handles the cold. Someone with asthma may react to cold, dry air. Someone with Raynaud's phenomenon may find their fingers turning white and numb while a training partner feels little discomfort. Icy pavement and early darkness add hazards that have nothing to do with body temperature at all.

The U.S. National Weather Service publishes a wind chill index. It estimates how cold the air feels on exposed skin when temperature and wind speed are combined. It is a starting point for reading a forecast. It cannot account for wet gear, a skipped warm-up or an underlying health condition.

The 10 factors below offer a practical way to judge whether a winter run, ride or walk makes sense on a given day. They are a selection, not a complete checklist. They cover two cold-related injuries, frostbite and hypothermia, along with the clothing and gear choices that lower the risk of both. They also address the warm-up, breathing cold air, footing and visibility, and medical conditions that call for extra care. The last one covers what to do once the workout ends. Each can be read on its own.

Wind chill measures how quickly moving air pulls heat away from exposed skin. On a windy day, outdoor exercise can carry much more cold-weather risk than the air temperature alone suggests. The wind forecast deserves as much attention as the thermometer reading.

Wind speed drives the effect. The faster the wind blows, the faster bare skin loses heat. Gusty conditions can also swing between tolerable and harsh within a single workout. A calm start is no guarantee of calm conditions an hour later.

The U.S. National Weather Service wind chill index is the standard reference for this effect in North America. Environment and Climate Change Canada uses the same formula. The index assumes no sunshine, as though skin were exposed under a clear night sky. Bright sun on the face can make conditions feel somewhat milder than the index indicates. Overcast days and workouts before sunrise or after sunset get no such help.

Many weather apps show a "feels like" reading next to the actual temperature. In cold weather, that number usually reflects wind chill, but providers calculate it in different ways. Checking the wind speed itself shows what the reading is based on.

Wind chill describes heat loss from skin. It does not lower the actual temperature of anything. A water bottle left outside on a windy day will not get colder than the surrounding air. Exposed skin, though, cools toward that air temperature much faster when the wind is blowing.

Exercise adds its own wind. A runner moving into a headwind faces the forecast wind plus the air created by their own speed. A cyclist usually faces even more, because riding is typically faster than running. A day that feels manageable on a slow walk can feel very different on a fast bike descent.

Route planning can reduce exposure. On an out-and-back course, heading into the wind first means the return leg comes with the wind at your back. That puts the harshest stretch at the start, while you are fresh, rather than at the end, when fatigue sets in. Sheltered routes through trees, between buildings or in valleys can also cut the wind compared with open fields, waterfronts or ridgelines.

Covered skin is far less affected than bare skin. The cheeks, nose and ears take the brunt of a cold wind. A windy forecast is a reason to cover more skin, shorten the session or move the workout indoors.

Frostbite is the freezing of skin and the tissue beneath it. It usually strikes the fingers, toes, ears and nose first. Its early signs are numbness, tingling or stinging, and skin that turns pale, gray or waxy. Spotting those changes early gives an exerciser time to get inside before lasting damage sets in.

The extremities are vulnerable for a simple reason. When the body gets cold, it narrows blood vessels near the surface to protect the heart, lungs and other vital organs. Less warm blood reaches the hands and feet as a result. The ears and nose sit out in the open with little fat or muscle to hold heat.

The mildest form of cold injury is frostnip. Skin feels very cold and may sting, then goes numb and looks red or pale. Frostnip does not cause permanent harm, and the skin recovers once it is rewarmed. It is still a sign that conditions are cold enough for more serious injury.

Frostbite that goes further changes how skin looks and feels. Skin can turn white, grayish-yellow or bluish and take on a waxy appearance. It may feel hard or unusually firm to the touch. Blisters can form after rewarming. In the deepest cases, tissue can turn black and die, and the muscles or joints underneath may stop working normally.

Numbness makes frostbite easy to miss during a workout. A runner focused on pace may not feel a toe going cold inside a shoe. A training partner can help by checking for pale patches on the cheeks, nose and ears. Anyone exercising alone can stop briefly to wiggle fingers and toes and check whether feeling has returned.

The response to suspected frostbite is to get indoors and out of wet clothing. Rewarm the affected area gently in warm water, not hot water. Avoid rubbing the skin, which can damage frozen tissue. Heating pads, stoves and fires are also risky. Numb skin cannot sense heat. It burns easily.

Rewarming should not begin if the area could freeze again before reaching shelter. Thawing followed by refreezing causes worse damage than staying frozen a little longer. Hard skin, blisters, darkened tissue or numbness that lingers after rewarming call for prompt medical care.

Hypothermia is a dangerous drop in the body's core temperature. It can set in during exercise when cold combines with wind or wet conditions. Early signs include strong shivering, fumbling hands and a loss of coordination. Later signs include confusion and slurred speech.

Frostbite damages specific patches of skin and tissue. Hypothermia affects the whole body. The body normally produces enough heat to keep its vital organs within a narrow temperature range. When it loses heat faster than it can make it, that balance breaks down. The heart, nervous system and other organs then begin to work poorly.

Shivering is usually the first signal. It is the body's attempt to generate heat through rapid muscle contractions. A runner or hiker may also notice that their hands have become clumsy. Zipping a jacket or opening a snack can suddenly feel difficult. Stumbling, slowed movement and unusual fatigue often follow.

As the condition worsens, the brain is affected. Confusion, memory lapses, drowsiness and slurred or mumbled speech are common warning signs. This creates a specific danger. A person with hypothermia often cannot recognize what is happening to them. They may insist they feel fine or decide to press on when they should stop. In severe cases, shivering can stop altogether. That is a sign of deepening hypothermia, not recovery.

Several workout conditions raise the risk. Rain, sleet or wet snow can soak through outer layers and leave clothing wet against the skin. Long efforts drain the energy the body uses to stay warm. An injury, a wrong turn or a broken-down bike can leave someone standing still far from shelter. Their heat output then drops sharply. Hypothermia can also develop at temperatures above freezing, especially when a person is wet and exposed for a long time.

Anyone showing signs of hypothermia needs emergency care. Call emergency services, then move the person somewhere warm and dry if possible. Replace wet clothing with dry layers or blankets. Warm the chest, neck, head and groin first. Warm, nonalcoholic drinks can help if the person is fully alert. Handle them gently, and do not rub their arms and legs.

Exercising with a partner, or telling someone the route and expected return time, means help can arrive sooner if something goes wrong far from home.

Dress for cold-weather exercise in three layers: a moisture-wicking base layer against the skin, an insulating mid layer and a wind- and water-resistant outer shell. Each layer does a separate job. Together they hold in heat while letting sweat move away from the body.

The base layer manages moisture. Exercise produces sweat even on a frigid morning, and this layer's job is to move it off the skin. Fabrics such as polyester, polypropylene and merino wool pull moisture away from the skin and toward the outer surface of the garment. There it can evaporate. A base layer works best when it fits close to the body without restricting movement.

Cotton does not belong in this system. It absorbs water readily and holds it against the skin. It also dries slowly. A cotton T-shirt that soaks through early in a run tends to stay wet for the rest of it. Under a jacket, that shirt can leave a runner damp and chilled partway through a workout.

The mid layer provides insulation. Fleece and wool are common choices because they trap warm air close to the body. How thick this layer should be depends on the conditions and the activity. On a milder day or during a hard interval session, some people skip it entirely. A brisk walk or a slow hike produces less body heat than a tempo run. Lower-intensity outings may call for a heavier mid layer.

The outer shell blocks wind and light precipitation. A wind-resistant jacket keeps gusts from cutting through to the warm layers underneath. A shell that is also breathable lets water vapor from sweat escape instead of trapping it inside. Zippers at the chest and vents under the arms release excess heat without the jacket coming off.

Starting slightly cool is a standard rule of thumb for cold-weather running. The body warms up within the first minutes of steady effort. Someone who feels comfortable standing still at the door is likely to overheat once moving. Overheating leads to heavy sweating, which works against the base layer.

The same principles apply below the waist. Running tights or wind-resistant pants cover the legs. On colder days, some exercisers add a thermal base layer underneath.

Conditions should shape the combination every time. A calm, dry day may need only a base layer and a light shell. Rain, sleet or a strong headwind calls for a more protective outer layer. The value of layering is flexibility — pieces can be added, removed or unzipped as the weather and the workout change.

The hands, feet, head and face need their own coverage on a cold-weather workout. A warm jacket does little for them. Mittens or gloves, wool or synthetic socks, a hat or headband, and a neck gaiter or balaclava close the gaps a good outer layer leaves open.

Mittens hold the fingers together in one compartment. That lets them share warmth and leaves less fabric exposed to the air. Mittens generally run warmer than gloves made of similar material. Gloves give more dexterity for working a zipper, using a phone or gripping ski poles.

Some exercisers wear a thin liner glove under a mitten. The liner stays on when the mitten comes off for a quick task. The pair can also be adjusted as the hands warm up. Convertible styles add a fold-over mitten flap to a fingerless or full glove.

Socks made of merino wool or synthetic fibers such as polyester pull sweat away from the skin. They keep insulating when damp. Cotton socks soak up moisture and stay wet, which chills the feet. Thicker socks add warmth. A sock that makes a shoe tight, though, can squeeze the foot and restrict circulation. Mesh running shoes let wind and slush through. Shoes with a water-resistant upper help on wet or snowy days.

A hat or fleece headband covers the ears, which stick out from the head and have little fatty tissue to insulate them. The head loses heat like any other uncovered skin. A hat matters most when the rest of the body is already dressed for the weather. A thin hat can be tucked into a pocket if it gets too warm partway through a run.

A neck gaiter or balaclava shields the neck, cheeks, chin and nose from wind. A gaiter can be pulled up over the face on an exposed stretch and pushed down once the route is sheltered. Moisture from breathing can leave the fabric damp or icy. A spare gaiter helps on longer outings. Sunglasses or sport goggles protect the eyes from wind and from glare off snow.

A dynamic warm-up done indoors before a cold-weather workout loosens muscles and joints that the cold makes stiffer. It also means stepping outside with blood already flowing to working muscles, rather than asking a chilled body to go from standstill to full effort.

Muscle tissue performs best when it is warm. Cold muscles contract more slowly and stretch less readily. Tendons and the connective tissue around joints also lose some of their give as they cool. A hard effort started in that state asks more of tissue that is not ready for it.

A warm-up raises heart rate gradually and increases blood flow to the legs, hips and core. Breathing deepens. Joints move through a fuller range of motion. These changes take time. Outdoors in winter, the cold air works against them from the first step.

Doing the warm-up inside avoids that problem. A hallway, living room or garage offers enough space. The goal is to leave the door already warm. The first minutes outdoors then go toward holding onto heat rather than trying to generate it.

Dynamic movements suit this job better than long, held stretches. Leg swings, walking lunges, high knees, butt kicks, arm circles and bodyweight squats all move the joints while gradually raising effort. Skipping in place or jumping jacks can bring the heart rate up further. Runners can add hip openers and ankle circles. Cyclists can focus on the hips, knees and lower back. Static stretches held for long periods can wait until after the session, once the body is warm and back indoors.

The warm-up should be thorough but short enough to avoid heavy sweating. Arriving at the door damp sets up heat loss that clothing then has to fight. The target is to feel warm and loose, not soaked. Pulling on outer layers just before stepping out helps keep the heat the warm-up built.

Once outside, the first several minutes should still be easy. An easy jog, a brisk walk or a low-gear spin lets the body adjust to the cold air before pace or power climbs. Picking up speed after that adjustment period avoids an abrupt jump from a warm room straight to full intensity.

The same approach applies to strength or interval work done outdoors in winter. Explosive efforts such as sprints, hill repeats or plyometric jumps place the highest demands on muscles and tendons. Those efforts belong later in the session. By then the body has had time to warm fully in the conditions it is actually working in.

Cold, dry air can make the airways narrow during or shortly after a workout. This condition is called exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. Covering the mouth and nose and getting a treatment plan from a doctor are two practical ways to keep it from cutting a winter session short.

The trigger comes from how the body prepares incoming air. Before air reaches the deeper parts of the lungs, the airways warm it and add moisture to it. At rest, the nose does much of that work. During hard exercise, breathing speeds up and shifts toward the mouth. That bypasses much of the nose's conditioning.

Winter air makes the job harder. Cold air holds little moisture. The lining of the airways loses water and heat as it works to bring each breath up to body temperature. That drying and cooling can prompt the smooth muscle around the airways to tighten.

The symptoms resemble asthma. Coughing, wheezing, chest tightness and shortness of breath are common. Some people notice an unusual drop in stamina or a lingering cough after a cold run rather than obvious wheezing. Symptoms often peak shortly after exercise stops, not at the hardest point of the effort.

The condition is closely linked with asthma. It can also affect people who have never been diagnosed with asthma. Anyone who regularly struggles to breathe during or after cold-weather exercise has a reason to get checked rather than assume a lack of fitness is to blame.

A doctor can confirm the problem with breathing tests, such as spirometry measured before and after exercise. Treatment often includes a short-acting inhaler taken before a workout. The right plan depends on the individual. People who already have a rescue inhaler should carry it on outdoor winter workouts.

A loose scarf, neck gaiter or balaclava over the mouth and nose traps some warmth and moisture from each exhaled breath. The next breath picks some of that back up before it reaches the airways. Breathing through the nose at easier paces does similar work. Keeping intensity lower on the coldest, driest days also reduces how much air the lungs must condition.

Breathing trouble that does not ease with rest or a rescue inhaler is a medical emergency and calls for immediate care.

Slippery footing and poor visibility are winter running hazards that have little to do with the temperature itself. Better traction, a shorter and slower stride and gear that makes a runner visible to drivers address both problems directly.

Black ice is difficult to spot. It forms as a thin, clear glaze that lets dark pavement show through. A frozen road can look merely wet as a result. Bridges and overpasses tend to freeze before other roads. Cold air reaches them from above and below. Shaded stretches, low spots where meltwater pools and patches that thaw by day and refreeze overnight deserve the same caution.

Footwear changes how much grip a runner has. Trail shoes with deep lugs bite into packed snow better than smooth road soles. On icy routes, slip-on traction devices stretch over a shoe and add metal studs, coils or small spikes. Yaktrax and Kahtoola Microspikes are common examples. These devices can feel unstable on bare, dry pavement. They suit routes that stay frozen from start to finish.

Stride mechanics also affect footing. A shorter stride keeps each foot landing closer to the body's center of mass. That lowers the chance of a foot sliding out on contact. Slowing down, keeping the knees slightly bent and taking corners gradually all give more time to react. Icy days suit easy efforts, with faster sessions moved to clear pavement, an indoor track or a treadmill.

Snow also changes the shape of a route. Plowed banks narrow road shoulders and sidewalks, pushing runners closer to traffic. Fresh snow can hide curbs, potholes and storm drains. A route the runner already knows well is easier to judge when its surface is buried.

Darkness makes each of these hazards harder to see. In the Northern Hemisphere, days are shortest around the December solstice. In the Southern Hemisphere, the shortest days fall around the June solstice. The farther a city sits from the equator, the less daylight it gets in winter. Morning and evening workouts often fall in full dark as a result.

Visibility gear works in two directions. A headlamp or handheld light shows the runner the ground ahead, including ice and broken pavement. Reflective material and blinking lights help drivers see the runner. A white light facing forward and a red light facing back match the pattern drivers expect from vehicles. Reflective bands on the ankles and wrists move with each stride. That motion helps drivers recognize a person rather than a fixed object.

Route choice ties these measures together. Well-lit streets make both ice and runners easier to see. Sidewalks keep runners off road shoulders and away from passing cars. Where no sidewalk exists, facing oncoming traffic lets a runner see approaching cars. Drivers in winter may be contending with frosted windshields, low-angle glare and longer stopping distances on slick roads. Telling someone the planned route and expected return time means help can be sent if a fall leaves a runner unable to get home.

Some health conditions make outdoor exercise in cold weather riskier, including heart disease, Raynaud's phenomenon, diabetes and asthma. Anyone with one of these conditions should talk to a doctor before starting or continuing an outdoor winter workout routine.

Heart disease is a central concern. Cold air causes blood vessels near the skin to narrow. That response helps the body hold on to heat, but it also raises blood pressure. The heart then has to work harder to move blood through the body. Physical exertion adds to that demand.

For people with heart conditions, heavy effort in the cold carries added strain. Snow shoveling is a familiar example. It pairs cold exposure with sudden, intense upper-body work, often for people who are not otherwise active. A doctor can advise on safe intensity levels and on which symptoms mean it is time to stop. Chest pain, unusual shortness of breath, dizziness or pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back all call for halting activity and seeking emergency care.

Raynaud's phenomenon affects circulation in a different way. In people with the condition, small blood vessels in the fingers and toes narrow sharply in response to cold or stress. The affected skin can go pale or bluish and lose feeling. As blood flow returns, the area may turn red and throb or tingle. Some people also notice it in the ears, nose or lips. Raynaud's can occur on its own or alongside another condition, such as an autoimmune disease. For outdoor exercisers, keeping the whole body warm — not only the hands and feet — helps limit attacks.

Diabetes can raise cold-weather risk through nerve damage and reduced circulation, particularly in the feet. Reduced sensation means a person may not notice cold injury, blisters or wet socks until harm has already occurred. Checking the feet after a winter workout is a practical habit for anyone with the condition.

Asthma rounds out the list. Breathing cold air can be a particular trigger for people with the condition. Anyone with asthma should raise winter training with their doctor specifically rather than assume a warm-weather routine carries over unchanged.

Get out of damp clothing as soon as a cold-weather workout ends. While you move, working muscles produce enough heat to offset the moisture on your skin. Once you stop, that heat source drops off, and wet fabric keeps pulling warmth away from the body.

A shirt soaked with sweat draws heat from the skin faster than the same shirt does when dry. Sweat also keeps evaporating after the effort ends, and evaporation cools the skin. That cooling is exactly what sweat is for during exercise. After exercise, in cold air, it works against you.

The result is a familiar post-workout chill. Someone can finish the final stretch feeling comfortable, then start shivering a few minutes after stopping. Shivering is the body's attempt to generate heat through rapid muscle contractions. It signals that heat loss has started to outpace heat production.

The riskiest window is the gap between finishing and getting indoors. Standing in a parking lot to stretch, chat or check a fitness watch extends that gap. So does a long walk back to the car after a cooldown. A route that ends at the front door, a parked car or a heated building shortens the exposure.

A dry change of clothes helps when the finish line is not at home. A fresh top, dry socks and a dry hat replace the items that tend to be wettest. A warm jacket thrown over the top blocks the wind while you change. Wet hair keeps cooling the head long after the workout is over. A small towel in the bag helps with that.

Indoors, a warm shower and a hot, nonalcoholic drink help bring body temperature back up. Alcohol widens blood vessels near the skin. That can make a person feel warmer while actually increasing heat loss. A snack also gives the body fuel to keep producing its own heat.

Washing gear and letting it dry completely before the next session prevents starting out in fabric that is still damp. Gloves or a jacket left balled up in a gym bag overnight often stay wet. Putting them back on means beginning the next cold workout already chilled.

#5493. Microsoft Azure revenue surges 48% to $33.2B, beating expectations as cloud and AI demand grows

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:47 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:30 pm

Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations.

The growth suggests that Microsoft is selling cloud and AI computing about as fast as it can install it. Azure revenue rose $10.8 billion from a year earlier, driven by demand for services across the platform, Microsoft said in its quarterly filing. That came even as some new data center capacity arrived late.

For investors worried about Microsoft’s record capital spending, it’s a sign that the company’s massive AI and cloud infrastructure buildout is turning into sales. Microsoft’s shares rose nearly 4% in after-hours trading following the earnings report.

Overall, Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, up 19% and above the $90.75 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance. Earnings were $4.89 per share excluding the impact of its OpenAI investment, compared with expectations of $4.72.

It’s the first time Microsoft has reported Azure’s quarterly revenue figure, not just its growth. The disclosure is part of a new financial structure that took effect this quarter, splitting the company into two segments: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.

Capital spending came in below Microsoft’s forecast. The company spent $45.2 billion, including finance leases, short of the more than $50 billion it expected. Some data center capacity that third parties were supposed to deliver in the quarter was delayed, the company said.

Google Cloud, which includes Google’s Workspace productivity apps, brought in $30.7 billion in revenue in the quarter, up 103% from a year earlier, Alphabet reported Wednesday afternoon.

Amazon reports earnings Thursday afternoon, including AWS results.

Update, 3:05 p.m.:Microsoft expects Azure growth to accelerate again this quarter, to 49% to 50% excluding currency changes, CFO Amy Hood said on the earnings call. “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply,” she said.

Hood said Azure’s growth came from Foundry, Microsoft’s service for building AI apps and agents, and from engineering work that let Microsoft sell unused capacity on its existing servers. That helped make up for delays in new data center capacity that outside providers were supposed to deliver.

Those delays pushed some spending later into the fiscal year. Microsoft now expects to spend about $170 billion on capital expenditures in calendar 2026, down from about $175 billion. It expects to spend more than $50 billion this quarter, and Hood said spending will accelerate in the first half of calendar 2027.

Hood also said Microsoft may tap additional sources of financing to help pay for the buildout, “when we believe it is attractive to do so.” The company still expects to bring in more cash than it spends this fiscal year.

Microsoft’s expense forecast for the December quarter includes an estimate for the buyout offer it announced Monday, Hood said, though she didn’t give the amount.

The company expects total revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion for the December quarter, above the $95.7 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance.

MetaMask is facing fresh questions about its future after Consensys launched a new institutional settlement network targeting banks, asset managers and financial market infrastructure providers.

The announcement puts Consensys’ institutional ambitions in the spotlight just weeks before its planned separation from MetaMask. The move could also leave the popular wallet competing independently while its former parent pursues Wall Street.

Introducing Sovereign Network Interoperability by Consensys.State-of-the-art interoperability that enables institutions to do business freely, settling securities, exchanging currencies and posting collateral across ledgers, without bridges or moving assets onto a shared…

Consensys unveiled Sovereign Network Interoperability at Devcon, introducing infrastructure designed to coordinate transactions across independently operated financial networks. Can MetaMask maintain its position as institutional blockchain adoption accelerates?

The new Sovereign Network Interoperability platform aims to help institutions settle securities, exchange currencies, and move collateral across separate blockchain networks.

Its bridgeless design keeps assets on their original ledgers while coordinating transactions between approved counterparties. Consensys says the system uses cryptographic verification to reduce reliance on additional trusted intermediaries.

The platform targets four major financial workflows, including securities settlement, wholesale payments, collateral mobility, and tokenized fund transactions.

Consensys plans to support Ethereum-compatible networks and protocols such as the Ethereum Economic Zone and Inter-Blockchain Communication. Canton connectivity is also planned.

The launch builds on Consensys’ existing institutional infrastructure, including Linea, Hyperledger Besu and Teku. The company is positioning itself as a technology provider for financial institutions seeking private, always-on blockchain settlement.

MetaMask will focus on consumer finance, expanding beyond its traditional wallet functions into payments, savings, trading and access to financial instruments.

Still, the split creates uncertainty around how resources, intellectual property and shared development capabilities will be allocated.

Consensys has not disclosed separate revenue figures, financing arrangements or detailed asset allocations for the two businesses. This leaves MetaMask facing a strategic challenge. It must continue developing its consumer platform while Consensys builds infrastructure aimed at some of crypto’s largest potential customers.

The institutional settlement push also highlights a potential opportunity for Bitcoin Layer 2 projects seeking to expand beyond payments and decentralized finance.

Bitcoin Hyper is one project positioning itself around this idea, combining a Bitcoin Layer 2 design with a wallet and an execution environment intended to support faster transactions and applications.

#5491. Hottest years on record: 10 topics, from 2016 to 2024 and what 2027 would need

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The hottest years on record, including 2016, 2023 and 2024, explained in 10 topics, plus why 2027 could join them if long-term warming and El Niño line up

For the first time in the Copernicus Climate Change Service record, a full calendar year ran more than 1.5°C warmer than the pre-industrial era. Copernicus put 2024 at 1.55°C above its 1850–1900 baseline. The World Meteorological Organization also reported 2024 as the warmest year in its records.

That milestone came only a year after the previous record. Copernicus put 2023 at about 1.48°C above the same baseline. Before that, 2016 held the title, helped along by a strong El Niño. The record has now changed hands twice since 2016.

The pattern raises a question for anyone tracking climate, energy markets or long-range business risk. Could another year soon join the hottest years on record? The answer depends on two forces working together. The first is long-term warming from greenhouse gases, which sets the base trend. The second is short-term natural variation, such as El Niño. El Niño adds warmth to the global average, and its effect shows up in the year after it peaks.

Both forces mattered in 2023 and 2024. El Niño helped lift those years, but it does not explain the full rise across several years. The longer climb comes from greenhouse gas warming.

The numbers also need context. The Paris Agreement's 1.5°C goal refers to warming averaged over decades, not to a single year. One year above the line, as 2024 was, does not by itself mean the goal has been breached. That distinction matters when reading each new annual figure.

This slideshow is a selection of 10 topics rather than a ranked list. It covers the record years themselves, including 2016, 2023 and 2024, and where 2025 stands while its ranking awaits confirmation. It explains the 1850–1900 baseline behind the figures, and how Copernicus and the WMO report a record year. It also walks through the mechanisms behind each record.

The final slide looks at 2027. It does not offer a forecast. Instead, it sets out what would need to line up for 2027 to join those record years. That means the steady pressure of greenhouse gas warming plus a short-term boost such as El Niño.

2024 is the warmest calendar year on record. The Copernicus Climate Change Service and the World Meteorological Organization both reported it as the warmest year in their records.

Copernicus put 2024 at 1.55°C above the 1850–1900 pre-industrial baseline. It described 2024 as the first calendar year above 1.5°C.

The figure covers a full calendar year, from January through December. That makes it a different kind of measure from a single hot month or a heat wave in one region.

The ranking does not rest on one organization. Copernicus and the WMO each placed 2024 at the top of their own records. The result appears in two separate records, not just one.

The words "so far" in the title matter. 2024 holds the record as of these reports. A later year could still overtake it, just as 2024 overtook the year before it.

2023 was the warmest year on record until 2024 overtook it. The Copernicus Climate Change Service put 2023 at about 1.48°C above the 1850–1900 pre-industrial baseline.

That left 2023 roughly 0.02°C below 1.5°C. The Paris Agreement's 1.5°C goal refers to long-term warming over decades, not to any single year.

Copernicus described 2024 as the first calendar year above 1.5°C. By the Copernicus figures, 2024 ran about 0.07°C warmer than 2023.

Before 2023, the record belonged to 2016. That mark held until 2023, seven years later. The next change came after just one year, when 2024 set a new high.

El Niño helped lift global average temperatures in 2023. Its effect on the global average shows up in the year after it peaks. It also helped lift 2024.

El Niño does not account for the full rise across those years. Long-term warming from greenhouse gases is the base trend underneath it. A short-term boost such as El Niño adds to that trend in a given year rather than replacing it.

2016 held the record for the warmest year until 2023 overtook it. A strong El Niño helped drive the heat that put 2016 at the top.

Among the years that have held the global temperature record in recent succession, 2016 is the earliest. Its mark has since been passed twice, first by 2023 and then by 2024.

The El Niño boost in 2016 came on top of the long-term warming trend from greenhouse gases. It added to that trend rather than replacing it.

The same pairing helped set the later records. El Niño also helped lift 2023 and 2024, while greenhouse gas warming supplied the base beneath them.

The ranking of 2025 among the warmest years is pending confirmation. No verified position or temperature figure for 2025 is available here, so this slideshow does not place the year on the list.

That sets 2025 apart from the record years around it. 2024 is the warmest calendar year in the records of both the Copernicus Climate Change Service and the World Meteorological Organization. 2023 held the record before 2024 overtook it. 2016 held it before 2023.

Any confirmed placement for 2025 would be judged against those years. That comparison works only when every figure is measured against the same reference period. A number built on a different baseline would not line up with the earlier results.

A ranking would also need a named record keeper behind it. Copernicus and the WMO each publish their own annual results. A position for 2025 would be credited to whichever of them reported it, not stated as a general finding.

Until one of those record keepers confirms it, where 2025 sits among the warmest years remains an open question.

A single calendar year above 1.5°C does not mean the world has missed the Paris Agreement target. The 1.5°C goal refers to long-term warming measured over decades, not the temperature of any one year.

That distinction now applies to a real case. The Copernicus Climate Change Service described 2024 as the first calendar year above 1.5°C.

The record year before it sat on the other side of the line. In the Copernicus record, 2023 came in just under 1.5°C. Two record years in a row straddled the threshold, one below and one above. That shows how close individual years now run to that line.

The Paris goal is built around a sustained level of warming. A long-term measure averages many years together. Averaging smooths out the swings that push any one year up or down.

Single years carry short-term noise. El Niño is the clearest example of that noise, and it helped lift both 2023 and 2024. A year boosted that way can sit above the long-term level.

The reverse also holds. A year without that boost can land below the long-term level while the underlying trend keeps rising. Judging the goal on one year would mean judging it partly on natural swings rather than on greenhouse gas warming.

Greenhouse gas warming is the base trend beneath those swings. That base trend is what a decades-long measure is designed to track.

For anyone reading annual climate reports, a record year and the Paris goal measure different things. A record year is a statement about one calendar year. The Paris measure is a statement about sustained warming.

A year above 1.5°C shows that annual temperatures can now reach the threshold. It cannot show, on its own, whether the long-term average has crossed it. That question can only be answered by looking at warming across decades.

El Niño adds warmth to the global average temperature in the year after it peaks, not only while the event is under way. It helped lift both 2023 and 2024, two consecutive years that each set a new high in the Copernicus record.

El Niño is the warm phase of a natural climate pattern in the tropical Pacific Ocean. During an El Niño, surface waters across a wide stretch of that ocean run warmer than usual. The pattern recurs on its own rather than being caused by greenhouse gas emissions.

The timing matters for annual temperature rankings. Records are kept by calendar year, but an El Niño event does not start in January and end in December. Its effect on a given year's average depends on when the event peaked.

That lag explains why a record-setting year can arrive after an El Niño has already passed its peak. A reader looking only at when an El Niño was strongest would miss part of the effect.

For anyone reading a list of record years, this means a year's rank reflects timing as well as the underlying climate. Two years with similar long-term warming can land in different places, depending on where an El Niño peak falls.

El Niño is a short-term boost, not the main driver of rising temperatures. It does not explain the full rise across 2023, 2024 and the years before them. El Niño adds to the long-term warming trend for a period, then fades.

That makes the El Niño share of a record year temporary and tied to a single event. The warming that remains after it fades comes from greenhouse gases.

Long-term warming from greenhouse gases is the base trend beneath the hottest years on record. El Niño can lift a single year above that trend, but it does not explain the full multi-year rise in global temperatures.

One way to picture the relationship is a rising slope with bumps on it. The slope is the greenhouse gas trend. The bumps are short-term natural variation, and El Niño is the best-known source of them. A bump can push one year above the line. Once it passes, the slope is still there.

The record years fit that shape. A strong El Niño helped drive the heat of 2016, the record holder until 2023. El Niño also helped lift 2023 and 2024, the years that took the title after it. Each of those boosts was temporary. A temporary ocean pattern cannot explain a climb that has continued across several years. That part of the rise comes from the base trend.

The distinction shapes how any new record should be read. A record year reflects both forces at once. Separating them shows which part fades when El Niño ends and which part stays in place. Short-term boosts come and go, while the level they push off from keeps rising.

The 1850–1900 baseline is the reference period Copernicus used to measure how warm recent record years were. Each annual warming figure shows how far a year's global average temperature sat above the average for those five decades.

Every warming figure needs a starting point. Without one, a number in degrees Celsius would have nothing to be measured against. The baseline supplies that reference. The period stands in for pre-industrial conditions, which gives the baseline its name.

Because it is an average across five decades, the reference is not tied to any single year. A warm or cool year inside the 1850–1900 window has little pull on the overall average.

The numbers built on it are differences, not raw temperatures. Climate reporting calls such a difference an anomaly. An anomaly shows how much warmer or cooler a year was than the reference period. It does not show what a thermometer read in any one place.

A shared baseline makes years comparable. Copernicus reports different years against the same 1850–1900 average. The gap between their figures therefore reflects a real difference in warmth, not a change in the yardstick.

The baseline stays fixed as the climate warms. Each new record is set against the same pre-industrial average, not against the year it replaced. So a rising series of anomalies tracks warming built up since the late 1800s.

The choice of baseline also shapes the size of the number. Measuring the same year against a later, warmer reference period would produce a smaller anomaly. A reading quoted against one period cannot be set beside a reading quoted against another without adjustment.

The same reference period gives the 1.5°C threshold its meaning. That line is measured from 1850–1900 conditions, not from a recent decade. A year counted as above 1.5°C sits above it relative to the pre-industrial average.

The Copernicus Climate Change Service and the World Meteorological Organization each name a record year by comparing it with their own temperature records. Both reported 2024 as the warmest calendar year in those records.

The unit being ranked is the calendar year. A record covers January through December as a whole. A single hot month or season does not earn the title.

The wording of each finding also sets its limits. The phrase "warmest in its records" refers to the period each organization's data covers. It is a statement about that record, not about every year in Earth's history.

Copernicus and the WMO reached the same conclusion about 2024. The record was reported by two organizations rather than one. When both bodies name the same year, the record does not hinge on a single organization's report.

For 2027 to join the hottest years on record, it would need two things working together. One is the long-term warming trend driven by greenhouse gases. The other is a short-term boost such as El Niño. That pairing explains how a record year forms. It is not a forecast for 2027.

Greenhouse gas warming sets the floor each new year starts from. Because that floor has kept rising, a short-term boost of a given size lands on a warmer starting point than it would have in earlier decades. El Niño on its own cannot account for the climb across several years.

The timing of El Niño is what makes it relevant to any specific year. Its added warmth shows up in the global average in the year after it peaks. Applied to 2027, the question is whether an El Niño peaks during 2026. If one does, 2027 could receive that boost. If none does, 2027 would be leaning on the base trend alone.

The record years show the pairing at work. El Niño helped lift 2023 and 2024. A strong El Niño also helped drive the heat of 2016, the record holder before them. In each case, the short-term push arrived on top of the long-term trend rather than replacing it.

Setting a new record outright and joining the hottest years are different tests. A new record would mean beating 2024, the warmest calendar year in the records of both Copernicus and the World Meteorological Organization. Ranking among the warmest years is a lower bar, and a year can clear it without passing 2024. How high 2027 might land depends partly on the size of any boost it receives.

Specific numbers for 2027 belong to named forecasters and their dated releases. The U.K. Met Office publishes an annual global temperature forecast. NOAA issues outlooks on El Niño and La Niña conditions. Any temperature or probability for 2027 should come from one of those releases, read alongside its publication date.

#5490. OpenAI to acquire developer tooling startup Pierre Computer

OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to acquire Pierre Computer Company Inc., a low-profile developer tooling startup.

The terms of the deal were not disclosed. Observers pegged it as a shot at Microsoft Corp.’s open-source software repository GitHub for the age of artificial intelligence agents.

Pierre operates a cloud service that AI agents can use to store the code they generate. It can also store related files such as software licenses and interface design elements. According to Pierre, the service provides significantly better performance than competing technologies. It helped one customer, AI startup Lovable Inc., cut code retrieval latency by about 70%.

Pierre also develops a collection of popular open-source libraries. Two of those libraries, Trees and Diffs, underpin the interface of OpenAI’s Codex programming tool.

Large software projects contain upwards of hundreds of code files that are organized in dozens of folders. Many programming tools include a sidebar specifically designed to help developers navigate those folders. Trees, the first Pierre-developed library used by Codex, marks it easier to implement such sidebars.

Trees can equip a folder navigation sidebar with a search feature and drag-and-drop controls for moving subfolders. Additionally, it flags code files that have been recently added or updated. Developers review those files first when performing tasks such as troubleshooting an outage.

Diffs, the other Pierre library that OpenAI has integrated into Codex, is also designed to power programming tool interfaces. In particular, it can be used to implement the main interface that shows the code the user is currently editing.

When a code file is updated, Diffs points out the specific lines of code that changed to spare developers the hassle of manually finding them. It can show changes in a separate interface section or in-line.

OpenAI will continue to offer Trees and Diffs under an open-source license after the acquisition closes. Additionally, it plans to integrate the features of Pierre’s paid code hosting service into Codex. In the longer term, the Pierre team will help OpenAI “ship new products and platforms.”

The effort will place an emphasis on building software that can optimize coding agents. In particular, OpenAI hopes to streamline agent workflows that involve Git. That’s an open-source tool developers use to manage code files. Trees, Diffs and Pierre’s paid storage service all provide built-in support for Git.

OpenAI makes extensive use of the tool internally. On Monday, the company revealed that it has built a software engine called Pando to boost the performance of its internal Git environment. The engine reduces the amount of time it takes OpenAI engineers’ coding agents to create and read code files.

#5489. Bigger than Bing or Xbox: Microsoft’s OpenAI haul reaches $10B in quarterly revenue

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 4:28 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:33 pm

OpenAI generated $10 billion in revenue for Microsoft in the quarter ended Sept. 30, about 11% of the Redmond company’s total revenue, according to its quarterly filing Wednesday.

The amount is up sharply. In the fiscal year that ended in June, Microsoft recorded $24.1 billion in revenue from its business with OpenAI, or about $6 billion a quarter on average.

That $10 billion surpasses some of Microsoft’s longest-running businesses. Xbox brought in $5.4 billion in the quarter. Search and advertising, which includes its Bing search engine, generated $6.6 billion. Windows licenses sold through PC makers, along with Surface and other Microsoft devices, brought in $3.6 billion.

The total covers revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI, as well as other business between the companies, such as OpenAI’s use of Azure to train and run its AI models. Microsoft didn’t say how much came from each, or how much of Azure’s growth came from OpenAI.

Azure revenue rose 48% to $33.2 billion in the quarter, beating Wall Street’s expectations and the company’s own forecast of 44% to 45% growth.

Microsoft has begun disclosing its revenue from OpenAI because its stake of about 24% makes OpenAI a “related party” under accounting rules, requiring it to report the business they do with each other.

Microsoft first reported the number in its annual report in July, as a full-year total. This is the first time it has given a quarterly figure.

The original AI alliance: Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, eventually committing $13 billion, and became its exclusive cloud provider. ChatGPT ran on Azure when it launched in late 2022.

The companies have loosened their ties since then. OpenAI restructured as a public benefit corporation in October 2025, and Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal to supply OpenAI’s computing capacity. OpenAI committed to buy an additional $250 billion in Azure services. An April 2026 agreement gave OpenAI broader freedom to use other cloud providers.

OpenAI has also agreed to keep sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030.

In addition, Microsoft sells access to OpenAI’s models to business customers through its Azure OpenAI Service, and the models became the foundation for its Copilot products, putting Microsoft at the front of the generative AI boom. That revenue comes from Microsoft’s own customers, so it isn’t part of the $10 billion.

Microsoft, for its part, now builds its own AI models and offers models from Anthropic and others.

Many customers, not a few: Asked by Bernstein Research analyst Mark Moerdler whether AI growth on Azure was coming from big businesses or AI-native companies, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella didn’t mention OpenAI.

He said he doesn’t want Azure’s AI business to depend on a few big customers, and that broad adoption by businesses is just getting started.

Nadella described it as “a decade-long thing,” and contrasted it with relying on “four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you” to show a few quarters of growth. That, he said, is “not a business as far as I’m concerned.”

He added that Microsoft has large customers who want to buy capacity, “and as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some. If not, we will be patient.”

Later in the call, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges brought up the fact that OpenAI made up 11% of revenue. Nadella didn’t address the number but praised OpenAI’s latest models and said customers are increasingly mixing models from different companies, or training their own.

He cited Microsoft’s tools for routing each task to whichever AI model handles it best. If you use AI coding agents, Nadella said, you want Anthropic and OpenAI “to compete for your workload, not like once a quarter, but for every task.”

New risk language: Microsoft also expanded a warning in its quarterly filing about the risks of depending on outside AI providers. The company builds products such as Copilot on AI models from outside companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. It now says it has “limited visibility into or control over” how those models are designed, trained, secured and tested.

Without naming OpenAI or Anthropic, the same section notes that some of these AI partners are also “significant customers of Azure,” and that the benefits Microsoft expects from those relationships “may not be realized or sustained.” It says those partners could change how much they buy, and that Microsoft itself may change how it allocates scarce data center capacity or prices it.

Microsoft is an investor in both companies. According to its latest filing, it owns about 24% of OpenAI, down from about 25% in June and about 27% after OpenAI’s restructuring a year ago, and has put $12.0 billion of a promised $13.0 billion into the company.

In addition, Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, and its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment. Microsoft hasn’t disclosed the size of its Anthropic stake, and Anthropic’s IPO filing earlier this week didn’t specify it either.

#5488. Reno's freeze-free season grew 69.6%, the largest gain of 16 ranked U.S. locations

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Longer allergy seasons can follow longer freeze-free growing seasons — see 10 of 16 U.S. locations ranked by how much theirs grew since the 1970s

Pollen season starts where frost ends. Every night that stays above freezing gives trees, grasses and weeds more time to grow, flower and release pollen. In the places ranked below, those nights now come in longer unbroken runs than they did in the 1970s.

The measure is the freeze-free growing season: the average yearly count of consecutive days with minimum temperatures above 32°F. Climate Crisis 247 ranked 16 U.S. locations by how much that stretch has changed, using a Climate Central analysis. The readings come from station records in the Applied Climate Information System, a NOAA program. The analysis compares the 1970-79 average with the 2015-24 average. Locations are ordered by percent change, not by the number of days added.

The growing season is a stand-in for allergy season, not a direct count of pollen or symptom days. The link runs through plant biology. A year's pollen intensity rises and falls with the length of that year's growing season. Higher carbon dioxide levels can also push plants to make more pollen. Forecasts cited by Climate Crisis 247 put growing seasons in some regions more than a month longer than they were 50 years ago. Those connections tie longer allergy seasons to a warming climate.

This list covers 10 of the 16 ranked locations, presented in the ranking's countdown order from No. 10 to No. 1. They sit in eight climate regions, from the Northeast to the Southwest. Three are in Montana: Bozeman, Helena and Missoula. Their starting points differ widely. In the 1970s, Bozeman averaged 93 freeze-free days a year, while Las Cruces, New Mexico, averaged 196.

Reno, Nevada, holds the No. 1 spot. Its freeze-free season grew 69.6%, from 112 days to 190. That is the largest gain among all 16 ranked locations by a wide margin. Missoula follows at 39.4%, rising from 104 days to 145. Las Cruces now averages 253 days above freezing, the highest 2015-24 figure in this selection.

Bozeman's freeze-free growing season has grown 25.8%. It went from an average of 93 days a year in 1970-79 to 117 days in 2015-24. Local plants now have a longer window to grow and release pollen.

Bozeman sits at No. 10 in the Climate Crisis 247 ranking, which Yahoo News published.

Bozeman added 24 days to its average yearly run of consecutive days with overnight lows above 32°F. Its 1970s baseline of 93 days is the shortest among the 10 locations in this selection. Its recent average of 117 days is also the lowest of the group.

Bozeman falls in the Northern Rockies and Plains climate region. Helena and Missoula carry the same regional label.

Helena's freeze-free growing season averaged 152 days a year in 2015-24, up from 118 days in the 1970s. The 28.8% increase puts the Montana city at No. 9 among the 16 U.S. locations in the Climate Crisis 247 ranking.

That works out to 34 more days a year in an unbroken run without a freeze. For local trees, grasses and weeds, those days add time to grow, flower and release pollen before cold weather returns.

Helena shares the Northern Rockies and Plains climate region with Bozeman and Missoula. Among those three, it started with the longest 1970s baseline. It also has the longest 2015-24 average.

Its percentage gain is larger than Bozeman's 25.8% and smaller than Missoula's. Measured in days added rather than percent, Helena also lands between the two. Bozeman gained fewer days, and Missoula gained more.

Marquette, Michigan, now averages 132 consecutive days a year with daily lows above freezing, up from 106 days in 1970-79. That 24.5% expansion puts the city at No. 8 of the 16 locations ranked.

The gain works out to 26 more freeze-free days a year on average. Trees, grasses and weeds around the city have that added time to grow and shed pollen.

Marquette started from a short base. Among the 10 locations in this selection, only two averaged fewer freeze-free days in the 1970s. Both are in Montana: Bozeman and Missoula.

Marquette's season is still short by this selection's standards. Only Bozeman, Montana, posts a lower 2015-24 average among the 10. Marquette's recent figure of 132 days also falls below the 147-day average that Toledo, Ohio, recorded in 1970-79.

Marquette's 24.5% rise is the smallest percent increase among the 10 locations here. Tupelo, Mississippi, comes closest to it.

Marquette is the only Upper Midwest location in this selection.

Toledo's freeze-free growing season averaged 186 days a year in 2015-24, up from 147 days in 1970-79. That 26.5% increase places the city at No. 7 among the 16 U.S. locations Climate Crisis 247 ranked.

The gap works out to 39 more days a year. That is more than five weeks of additional time with overnight lows above freezing. The recent average now covers roughly half the calendar year.

Toledo is the only city in this selection from the Ohio Valley climate region. Its 1970s baseline of 147 days was already longer than that of any of the three Montana cities on this list.

The figures do not show whether the extra days arrived in spring, in fall or at both ends of the season. They count consecutive days above freezing, not days with pollen in the air.

That timing is relevant to ragweed. Ragweed pollen is the leading cause of allergy symptoms in late summer and early fall. The plant is most common in the Midwest, the region that includes Ohio.

The effects of warming on pollen extend beyond the calendar. Climate change can shift when pollen season starts and ends. It can also change how long the season lasts and how much pollen plants produce. Those changes increase people's exposure to pollen. They also raise the risk of allergy and asthma symptoms.

Tupelo, Mississippi, averaged 237 consecutive days a year with minimum temperatures above freezing in 2015-24, up from 190 days in 1970-79. That 24.7% increase places the city at No. 6 in the source's countdown of 16 ranked U.S. locations.

In raw terms, the change adds up to 47 more frost-free days in an average year. Each of those days pushes back the point at which a freeze cuts off the season for local trees, grasses and weeds.

Tupelo is the only location from the South climate region among the 10 covered here. It also entered the comparison with a long season already in place. Among these 10, only Las Cruces, New Mexico, started the 1970s with a longer average freeze-free stretch. The same order holds in the recent decade. Tupelo's 2015-24 average is the second-longest in this selection, again behind Las Cruces.

That high starting point shapes how the percentage reads. A moderate percent gain on a 190-day base translates into a large number of added days. Only Marquette, Michigan, posted a smaller percent increase among these 10.

Concord, New Hampshire, posted a 36.3% increase, yet it gained 41 days. That is six fewer than Tupelo added. Because the ranking runs on percent change, Concord sits two places above Tupelo despite adding fewer days.

Tupelo's 1970s average is the same figure Reno, Nevada, the No. 1 location in the ranking, reached in 2015-24.

At 237 days, Tupelo's average freeze-free period now spans roughly 65% of the calendar year.

Las Cruces, New Mexico, now averages 253 consecutive days a year with minimum temperatures above 32°F, up from 196 days in the 1970s. That 29.1% increase places the city at No. 5 among the 16 U.S. locations in the ranking.

Measured in days rather than percent, the city's typical freeze-free run grew by 57 days between 1970-79 and 2015-24.

No other city in this selection started from a higher baseline. Its 1970s average already exceeded the 2015-24 average in seven of the other nine cities covered here. Only Tupelo, Mississippi, and Medford, Oregon, now average more than 196 days.

That high starting point shapes the percentage. When a season is already long, each added day makes up a smaller share of the total. The same number of added days would produce a larger percent change in a city with a short 1970s season.

The city sits in the Southwest climate region. It is the only Southwest location among the 10 cities in this selection.

A freeze-free stretch of 253 days leaves most of the calendar open for trees, grasses and weeds to grow and release pollen.

Concord, New Hampshire's freeze-free growing season has expanded 36.3%. It averaged 113 days a year in 1970-79 and 154 days a year in 2015-24.

That change places Concord at No. 4 in Climate Crisis 247's countdown of 16 U.S. locations. It is the only location from the Northeast climate region among the 10 covered here.

Measured in days, Concord now averages 41 more consecutive days a year with minimum temperatures above 32°F than it did in the 1970s. That is nearly six more weeks a year in which local plants can grow and release pollen.

Missoula, Montana, added the same 41 days. Its percent gain was larger, at 39.4%. The difference comes from the starting point. Missoula began with a shorter season, so the same number of added days made up a bigger share of it.

Medford, Oregon, shows the reverse pattern. Its percent change of 36.5% is close to Concord's. Medford started at 156 days and added 57, which is 16 more days than Concord gained. Its longer baseline means those extra days amount to a similar share of the season. The two sit side by side in the countdown, at No. 4 and No. 3.

Reno, Nevada, offers a third comparison. It began the 1970s with almost the same freeze-free season as Concord. Its percent gain, however, was nearly twice as large. Two locations with nearly matching baselines ended up far apart. In this selection, a similar starting length did not produce a similar gain.

Concord's 113-day baseline falls in the lower half of the 10 locations in this selection. Its current average of 154 days sits just above that of Helena, Montana, which now averages 152 days.

Medford, Oregon's freeze-free growing season averaged 213 days a year in 2015-24, up from 156 days in 1970-79. That 36.5% increase puts Medford at No. 3 in the countdown of 16 ranked U.S. locations.

Counted in days, the change comes to 57 more consecutive days a year with overnight lows above freezing. The measure tracks the longest unbroken run of nights that stay above 32°F. In Medford, that run now lasts nearly two months longer than it did in the 1970s.

Medford is the only location in this selection from the Northwest climate region. Its percent gain edges past Concord, New Hampshire's 36.3% by 0.2 percentage points. Only Missoula, Montana, and Reno, Nevada, rank higher in the source's list.

Medford also started from a longer baseline than Concord. Its 1970s average of 156 days was 43 days longer than Concord's 113. Even from that higher starting point, Medford's season grew by more than a third.

The gap between the two cities has widened in absolute terms. In 2015-24, Medford's 213-day average ran 59 days longer than Concord's 154. A similar percentage gain adds more days to a season that was already longer at the start.

Missoula's freeze-free growing season grew from an average of 104 days a year in 1970-79 to 145 days in 2015-24, an increase of 39.4%. That is the second-largest percentage gain among the 16 U.S. locations in the ranking.

That works out to 41 more consecutive days a year with overnight lows above 32°F than in the 1970s. Only Reno, Nevada, posted a larger percentage increase. Missoula trails it by 30.2 percentage points. Medford, Oregon, follows Missoula at No. 3 with 36.5%, starting from a longer 1970s baseline of 156 days. That leaves 2.9 percentage points between the No. 2 and No. 3 spots.

The ranking places Missoula in the Northern Rockies and Plains climate region. It gives the same label to Helena and Bozeman, the other Montana cities in this selection. Missoula's gain is larger than either of theirs. Helena's season rose 28.8%, and Bozeman's rose 25.8%. Missoula's 1970s baseline of 104 days was shorter than Helena's 118 days but longer than Bozeman's. By 2015-24, Missoula's 145-day average still trailed Helena's 152 days but exceeded Bozeman's 117.

Missoula lies in western Montana, in the area that separates the Sapphire range from the Bitterroot range. No other U.S. municipality fully ringed by the Rocky Mountains is larger.

The city's predominant pollen types span trees, grasses and weeds. Tree pollen comes from alder, maple, elm, juniper, poplar, pine, birch, willow, larch and ash. Grasses, sedge and cattail also contribute. Weed sources include ragweed, pigweed, goose-foot and wormwood/mugwort.

Plant growth in Missoula's ecosystem depends on winter snow. Snowmelt waters vegetation in spring. Runoff from that melt then supplies most of the moisture for plants along rivers and on upland ground through summer and early autumn.

The 145-day average measures frost-free time, not pollen. It does not show when Missoula's allergy season begins, how long symptoms last or how high pollen counts climb.

Reno, Nevada's freeze-free growing season expanded 69.6% between 1970-79 and 2015-24, rising from an average of 112 days a year to 190. No other location among the 16 in the ranking posted a larger percent gain.

That works out to 78 more days a year in Reno's average run of consecutive days with lows above 32°F. Those added days give trees, grasses and weeds in the West climate region a longer stretch to grow and release pollen. Reno is the only location from that region in this selection.

Reno started from a modest base. In the 1970s, its 112-day average sat close to those of colder northern locations in the ranking. Concord, New Hampshire, averaged 113 days in that decade, and Helena, Montana, averaged 118.

Those two places have gained less since then. Concord now averages 154 days and Helena 152. Reno's 190-day average runs 36 days longer than Concord's and 38 days longer than Helena's.

Reno has also overtaken Toledo, Ohio. In the 1970s, Toledo's season averaged 147 days, well ahead of Reno's. By 2015-24, Toledo averaged 186 days, a few days short of Reno's 190.

Reno has narrowed the gap with Medford, Oregon, too. In the 1970s, Medford's freeze-free season averaged 156 days, 44 days longer than Reno's. By 2015-24, Medford's 213-day average led Reno's by 23 days.

The largest percent gain is not the same as the longest season. Tupelo, Mississippi, averaged 190 days in the 1970s, the same length as Reno's current average. Tupelo has since climbed to 237 days. A location that starts with a long season needs far more added days to post a large percentage increase.

Summer heat in Reno is uneven. Neighborhoods near the airport run much hotter than the tree-shaded homes close to the Truckee River. Downtown, heavily paved sidewalks around casinos and shopping centers offer little relief.

#5487. Zillow agrees to pay $212.5M to settle investor lawsuit over failed home-flipping business

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 6:40 pmOctober 29, 2026 at 7:46 am

Zillow Group will pay $212.5 million to settle a shareholder class action lawsuit over its handling of Zillow Offers, the home-flipping business it shut down in 2021.

The lawsuit alleged that Zillow executives painted an overly positive picture of Zillow Offers in the months before the shutdown, without disclosing how poorly the company was able to predict home prices. That kept the stock artificially high until Zillow revealed the problems and announced the shutdown in November 2021, according to the complaint.

The Seattle-based company disclosed the settlement Wednesday in an SEC filing. About $48 million of the payment is expected to come from insurance. The deal requires court approval and includes no admission of wrongdoing.

In a statement, a Zillow spokesperson said, “We are pleased that the parties have reached a resolution on the matter.”

The settlement comes about three weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear Zillow’s challenge to the case’s class status. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups backed Zillow’s petition.

Steve Berman, managing partner of Seattle law firm Hagens Berman, the court-appointed class counsel, told Real Estate News he believes it’s the largest single securities settlement in the history of the Western District of Washington, the federal court district that includes Seattle.

Separate shareholder lawsuits filed on the company’s behalf against its leaders, known as derivative suits, remain pending, according to the filing.

Zillow bet its future on buying and selling homes in 2019, when co-founder Rich Barton returned as CEO and projected the business would reach $20 billion in annual revenue within three to five years. The company used its pricing algorithms to buy houses, fix them up and resell them.

The effort unraveled in the fall of 2021. An analyst report found that two-thirds of 650 homes it sampled from Zillow’s inventory were listed for less than the company paid.

Days later, Zillow shut down the business, cut about 2,000 jobs and took a $304 million inventory writedown, with Barton citing the unpredictability of its home-price forecasts. Zillow’s stock fell 32% over two days, according to Reuters.

The original lawsuit, filed that month in federal court in Seattle, cited upbeat statements executives made in the months before the shutdown.

They included a September 2021 remark by Jeremy Wacksman, then Zillow’s chief operating officer and now its CEO, that “the strength and the appeal for Zillow Offers just continues to grow.” Investor Jeremy Jaeger later became the lead plaintiff.

The class covers investors who bought Zillow Class A or Class C shares between Aug. 5 and Nov. 2, 2021. If the judge grants preliminary approval, Zillow will pay the money into a settlement fund within 20 business days.
