#5486. What a strong El Niño could mean for your heating bill, region by region

Free daily briefing on global business news.

El Niño heating bills could ease across the northern U.S. this winter while the South may see little change, and these 10 regional and historical angles explain why

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) says El Niño is set to become "very strong" this fall and winter. Some people have already nicknamed it the "Godzilla" El Niño. For households, the practical question is not the nickname. It is what the event could do to the cost of staying warm.

El Niño is a recurring climate pattern that returns every two to seven years. Exceptionally warm temperatures in the Pacific Ocean drive it. Its reach extends to winter weather across the U.S.

In the U.S., the pattern has historically raised the odds of a warmer, drier winter in the northern part of the country. Southern regions tend to face better odds of a cooler, wetter season. Those are odds, not promises. The experts quoted by Newsweek stressed that the impact is never guaranteed and is hard to predict.

That uncertainty shapes how El Niño heating bills play out. A milder northern winter can mean less fuel burned for heat. The size of any saving depends on more than the thermometer, though. It depends on the fuel a household relies on, whether natural gas, propane, heating oil or electricity. It also depends on how quickly the price of each fuel responds when demand changes.

Regional differences matter as much as the national picture. The Pacific Northwest's power supply, the South's exposure to heavy rain and Texas's experience with severe cold each raise separate questions. The 2015-16 El Niño winter also offers a benchmark for how far demand for heating fuels can fall when a season runs warm.

This piece draws on Newsweek reporting by Giulia Carbonaro to examine 10 angles on the question, region by region and fuel by fuel. They are a selection, not a ranking. Each one looks at a different part of the bill. Some cover the weather that drives demand. Others cover the energy sources that meet that demand, or the rate structures that decide when changes reach customers. Read together, they show why one forecast can mean lower bills for some households and little change for others.

A strong El Niño tilts the odds toward a warmer, drier winter across the northern U.S. Milder weather means heating systems run less often. That can lower heating demand.

Newsweek reports that this northern pattern is the historical tendency of El Niño winters. That makes it a guide drawn from past seasons rather than a set outcome for any one state.

The northern tier covers a wide stretch of the country. It takes in the Upper Midwest, the Northern Plains, the Great Lakes and the Northeast. Newsweek's reporting gives no separate heating figures for any of these regions. The warmer, drier tendency is the only outlook it sets out for them.

The National Weather Service describes how the pattern tends to play out in southern Wisconsin. There, El Niño winters usually run warmer than average or close to it. They also tend to bring less snow. That wording leaves room for seasons that land near normal rather than clearly warm.

The weather service frames that pattern as a seasonal average. Cold days can still arrive within a mild season. Heavy precipitation can also still occur. A warm outlook for the season as a whole says little about any single week. Homes in the region would still need heat during those colder stretches.

The fuel a home burns also shapes how a milder winter registers. Heating oil is a much more common home heating fuel in the Northeast than in other U.S. regions. Any drop in heating demand there would show up partly in heating oil use, a fuel households elsewhere lean on far less.

A strong El Niño could cost Pacific Northwest households later in the year what it saves them on winter heating. The reason is water. Smith, quoted by Newsweek, says the region produces roughly half of U.S. hydropower.

That share ties the region's electricity supply closely to its winter weather. A winter that eases heating demand can still leave less water for power generation.

The chain starts with snow. Smith told Newsweek that El Niño winters can shrink the region's snowpack. A smaller snowpack can, in turn, leave reservoir storage lower.

Snow that piles up in the mountains over winter melts in spring and runs into reservoirs. Hydroelectric dams generate power from that stored water. Less snow means less water to run through the turbines.

Smith said hydropower supply could then fall in the spring and summer after an El Niño winter. That timing separates the two effects by several months.

Relief from a milder winter, if it arrives, shows up first, during the heating season. A drop in hydropower supply would come later, once the heating season is over.

In Smith's view, that later drop would cancel out any relief consumers feel this winter. On his reading, a mild winter in the Pacific Northwest would not by itself mean lower energy costs across the full year.

For households in the region, that makes a single winter bill a partial measure. The fuller picture covers the heating months and the warmer months that follow.

Smith's wording also stops short of a prediction. He said El Niño winters can shrink snowpack, not that every one will.

A cooler, wetter El Niño winter could push electric heating load up slightly across the Southeast and Gulf Coast. Newsweek reports that the increase would be too small to change utility costs in any meaningful way.

Electric heating load is the power that homes and businesses draw to keep indoor spaces warm. That draw climbs as outdoor temperatures drop. A cooler season would add some of that demand to the regional grid.

The northern states may see heating demand ease. This region faces a nudge the other way. Households in the Southeast and along the Gulf Coast are not in line for the winter relief the pattern can bring farther north. Their exposure is to slightly more heating, not less.

Scale matters as much as direction. Newsweek describes the rise in heating load as small. On a typical utility bill, the added cost would not stand out.

The effect is measured in electricity. The reporting frames the Southern change in terms of electric heating load. It speaks to power bills rather than to bills for other heating fuels.

The reporting gives no percentage or dollar estimate for this region. It describes a small upward nudge in electricity demand for heating. It stops short of pointing to noticeably higher bills. On this evidence, the forecast points to little change in Southern winter electricity bills.

Extreme rain during a strong El Niño could disrupt power supply and cause outages in the South, Miller, quoted by Newsweek, said. He added that this outcome is less certain.

The concern follows from the pattern's usual footprint. El Niño has historically raised the odds of a cooler, wetter winter across the southern U.S. Rain, not cold, is the part of that outlook tied to this outage concern.

Temperature and rain affect a power grid in different ways. Colder or milder weather changes how much heating a home needs. That link to demand is direct. Miller said the effect of precipitation on electricity demand in the South is less clear.

That gap shapes how a Southern household can read a winter forecast. A wet season does not translate neatly into higher power use. The more direct risk Miller raised sits on the supply side. Severe downpours could interrupt service rather than push up consumption.

Even that supply risk comes with a caveat. Miller treated outages from extreme rain as a possibility he considered less certain, not an expectation. Newsweek's reporting does not attach a probability, a dollar cost or a specific state to that risk.

El Niño shifts the odds of certain conditions rather than locking them in. For the South, the outlook leans toward more rain this winter. What that rain would mean for power supply and household costs remains an open question in Newsweek's reporting.

One severe cold outbreak can erase a month of lower heating demand. A winter that looks mild in a seasonal forecast is no guarantee of a smaller heating bill.

Smith, quoted by Newsweek, made that point. He cited Winter Storm Uri, which struck Texas in February 2021, as his example.

His comparison is about scale. In Smith's account, the extra heating demand from one cold outbreak can cancel the savings built up over a month of lower demand.

That gap shapes how a forecast should be read. An El Niño outlook describes the odds for a whole season. It does not say whether a single stretch of extreme cold will arrive within that season, or when.

The distinction carries extra weight in Texas. The state sits in the southern U.S. There, El Niño's historical tilt points toward a cooler, wetter winter. The pattern gives Texas households no lean toward milder weather to offset a cold outbreak.

Smith chose Uri to show what that risk looks like in practice. The storm struck a southern state during the heating season. A favorable seasonal outlook in any region does not rule out a severe cold event.

U.S. demand for propane fell 16 percent and demand for heating oil fell 18 percent during the 2015-16 El Niño winter, according to Energy Information Administration data cited by Newsweek. EIA data show that winter ran 15 percent warmer than the one before it.

The EIA's measurement period runs from October 2015 through March 2016. It covers the coldest stretch of the season and the autumn and early-spring months on either side of it.

The two fuels did not fall by the same amount. Heating oil demand dropped two percentage points more than propane demand over the same mild winter. Newsweek's reporting does not give a reason for that gap. The figures record the difference without explaining it.

The two fuels are not spread evenly across the country. Heating oil heats homes far more often in the Northeast than in any other U.S. region. The heating oil decline is most relevant to households in that part of the country.

The 2015-16 figures describe one past winter. They show how far demand for propane and heating oil fell in a season that ran warm. They are not a forecast, and they do not set an expected size for any decline this winter.

Household electricity demand in the U.S. dropped 6 percent during the 2015-16 El Niño winter, Energy Information Administration data show. By April 2016, natural gas in storage stood 69 percent higher than a year earlier.

Both figures come from EIA data for the season running from October 2015 to March 2016. That winter was warmer than the one before it. The two measures capture different corners of the energy system.

The 6 percent decline measures residential demand. It tracks how much electricity homes used over those six months. It does not show what households paid for that power.

The comparison runs year over year. The EIA figure sets home electricity demand in the 2015-16 winter against demand the previous winter. It covers the residential sector as a whole, not any single region or utility. A national figure can blend areas where demand fell sharply with areas where it barely moved.

Electricity in a home does more than heat it. Lighting, refrigeration and other appliances draw power in every season. Only part of residential demand rises and falls with outdoor temperature. Warm weather trims that portion rather than the whole total.

The storage figure measures something else. It compares the volume of natural gas held in U.S. storage in April 2016 with the volume held a year earlier. Gas is pulled from storage through the cold months to meet heating needs. A larger stock in spring can point to a lighter drawdown over the winter.

April falls right after the October-to-March window the EIA data cover. The storage number is a snapshot of what remained once the heating season ended. It sits outside the six-month demand window but reflects what happened inside it.

Neither figure is a forecast. Both record what happened in one past winter. A similar outlook this year would not lock in the same results.

Electricity prices move more slowly than heating fuel prices. A 2016 study by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) reached that conclusion, and Newsweek cites it in its reporting on El Niño and household energy costs.

The EIA traced the gap to how power prices are set. In many areas, electricity rates come out of regulatory mechanisms. Those mechanisms carry long time lags.

Heating fuels sit on the other side of the gap. Their prices respond sooner when conditions change, while electricity rates trail behind.

The lag works in both directions. A slow-moving rate is slow to fall when conditions favor lower prices. It is also slow to rise when conditions favor higher ones. A household paying for heating fuel, by contrast, sees price shifts reach it sooner, whether they help or hurt.

A monthly bill reflects two things: the rate charged and the amount used. The rate lag touches only the first. A household that heats with electricity and runs its system less during a mild winter still uses less power. What the lag affects is whether the price per unit changes during that same season.

Where a household lives can affect which side of the gap it sits on. Heating oil is much more common as a home heating fuel in the Northeast than in other U.S. regions, according to the EIA. That places more Northeastern homes on the faster-moving side of the price gap the 2016 study describes.

The EIA study describes a general pattern in how prices respond. It does not set out a specific delay for any one state, utility or winter.

A strong El Niño could trim about $3.16 a month from the average electricity bill in affected Northern states. That figure is an illustration, not a forecast. It rests on a 2 percent saving that Newsweek uses as an example, attributed to Miller.

The starting point is a national average. SaveOnEnergy.com puts the typical U.S. residential electricity bill at about $158 a month as of October. Newsweek applies Miller's 2 percent figure to that average. The math is $158 multiplied by 0.02, which comes to about $3.16.

Subtracting that amount from the $158 average would leave a monthly bill of about $154.84 for the average consumer.

The 2 percent is an example assumption. It is not a measured result from this winter. It is not a prediction for any one household either. A home's actual saving could be larger, smaller or nothing at all.

Newsweek frames the example for Northern states only. Those are the areas where a strong El Niño tends to favor milder heating weather. The $3.16 figure is not meant to describe bills in Southern states.

The base figure is an electricity bill. It leaves out what households pay separately for other heating fuels. Many homes heat with a fuel other than electricity. For them, any El Niño effect on heating costs would show up on a different bill.

The $158 figure is also a national average. It blends homes in every state, climate and rate structure into one number. Under the same 2 percent assumption, a household paying more than $158 would save more in dollars. A household paying less would save less.

The estimate rests on two inputs. One is an average monthly bill reported for October. The other is an example percentage used to illustrate the possible size of a saving. Neither input guarantees that any household will pay less this winter.

A more typical El Niño may lower national heating demand by a smaller amount than a very strong one, Smith told Newsweek. He adds that the effect in any region hinges on its heating fuel mix.

Smith's comparison separates two kinds of winter. A very strong event is the kind NOAA expects this season. A more typical event follows the same broad pattern of a mild North and a cool South. In his assessment, the national drop in demand from a typical event is smaller.

The comparison is about scale, not direction. Both kinds of event tilt the North toward milder weather and the South toward cooler weather. What separates them is how far the national total of heating demand falls.

Fuel mix decides where any saving lands. A warm winter cuts demand for whichever fuel a household burns. The bill that shrinks is the one tied to that fuel.

The Northeast shows how uneven that mix can be. Heating oil is far more common as a home heating fuel there than in other parts of the U.S. For households that heat with oil, a mild winter would register mainly as less fuel burned from the tank.

The same logic applies elsewhere. Where many homes run on electric heat, a change in demand appears on power bills. Where natural gas dominates, it appears on the gas bill instead.

Two regions that share the same mild winter can still see different effects if their homes heat with different fuels.

Smith's point also limits how far a national figure can stretch. An estimate of lower demand across the U.S. does not tell a household in a given state what its own bill will do. That depends on the local weather and the fuel the household uses. For a typical event, that national starting point is already smaller.

#5485. Arista’s record quarter shows the network has become central to AI

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

The artificial intelligence buildout is well underway, with much of the focus on silicon and compute hardware. The network is treated as plumbing, something you connect after the important decisions have been made. Arista Networks Inc.’s strong third-quarter results signaled greater awareness of the network’s critical role, and Arista is well-positioned to benefit from this secular trend.

Arista reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, up 58.5% year over year and 20.5% sequentially. That is the fastest growth in the company’s history as a public company and well ahead of its $3.3 billion guide. Adjusted, non-GAAP earnings per share were $1.20, up from 77 cents a year ago. Gross margin was 64%, operating margin was 49.1%, and cash totaled $14.4 billion with no debt.

Management raised full-year 2026 guidance for the fourth time this year to about $13.3 billion, representing 48% growth. Fourth-quarter revenue is expected to come in between $3.9 billion and $4 billion. Arista also gave a first look at 2027, calling for 38% to 40% growth to about $18.5 billion. Within that, AI networking is expected to double from $3.5 billion to about $7 billion, and campus is expected to grow 60% to about $2 billion. The shares rose about 12% in after-hours trading, moderating to a 5% rise today.

Though investors will always gravitate toward the numbers as proof points, the commentary by Chief Executive Jayshree Ullal (pictured) was equally important. “We believe the industry is shifting from a compute-centric vertical stack to a holistic network-centric approach,” she said.

I agree, and the reason is economics. In large clusters, the network often determines how productive the AI factory is. When packets drop or a link fails, expensive accelerators sit idle, and inference makes the problem worse. Ullal described the move from “highly centralized training compute to disaggregated and distributed inference,” with prefill, decode, storage and KV cache spread across resources. “A well-designed network is becoming a foundational cornerstone for optimal token efficiency,” she said.

Buyers are getting it. Boards and chief financial officers now measure AI by cost per token and accelerator utilization, both of which depend on the network. A 5% gain in GPU utilization across a multigigawatt build is worth far more than the switches that delivered it. Once you understand that math, the network shifts from a commodity to a performance decision.

This awareness benefits every networking vendor, but it disproportionately benefits Arista for three reasons.

The first is accelerator diversity. Three years ago, Arista talked about four or five AI customers running 50,000 to 100,000 Nvidia Corp. graphics processing units, often on InfiniBand. Today, it has more than 100 Etherlink customers and expects more than 10 gigawatts of deployment across 10 or more types of accelerators by the end of 2027.

“In 2026, we are in a super cycle of AI,” Ullal said. “What a stark inflection in just three years.” Nvidia is a formidable networking competitor, and its Spectrum-X Ethernet has won over hyperscalers such as Meta Platforms Inc. and Oracle Corp. But Nvidia’s networking is optimized around its own full stack, and as customers bring Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Microsoft Corp.’s Maia, Meta MTIA, Qualcomm Corp., and Cerebras  Inc. silicon into production, many will prefer a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing accelerator.

Every new accelerator expands the share of AI networking open to an independent Ethernet vendor, and Arista leads that category. Co-design work with Cerebras and Maia means Arista is now involved in system design rather than added afterward.

The second is scale-across. Power limits are forcing AI capacity to be spread across buildings and regions, and connecting those sites requires deep buffers, large routing tables and very high reliability. Ullal said scale-across accounted for about 30% of AI demand this year and should rise in 2027, with the 7800 platform as the anchor. “There’s just no room for error when you’re connecting millions of XPUs,” she said. This is where Arista’s routing and EOS software experience matter most.

The third is scale-up. Arista showcased rack-scale Ethernet designs at OCP, built on the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking or ESUN specification, with trials in 2027 and production in 2028. Ullal compared it to the InfiniBand transition: Arista expects to move from “staring at proprietary UALink or NVLink” to “of course, it’s going to be ESUN.” If that happens, Arista’s market expands inside the rack, a segment it has never served.

Security strengthens the argument. Chief Technology Officer Ken Duda said Arista is working with Anthropic PBC, Google LLC and OpenAI Group PBC to integrate AI-driven vulnerability discovery into its software pipeline, including through Project Glasswing. As AI finds flaws faster, an operating system with process isolation and hitless patching becomes an advantage.

Ullal drew the contrast sharply: “Everybody else is dealing with a game of Whac-A-Mole where they’ve got thousands of vulnerabilities and no AVA can possibly keep track of it.” President and Chief Operating Officer Todd Nightingale said this “Glasswing and Mythos effect” is a major reason campus is growing so far ahead of the market.

The stock had fallen more than 20% in the month before the report, according to Chartmill, and analysts raised several concerns.

Deferred revenue. Total deferred revenue was flat at about $6.8 billion, which some interpret as a sign of slowing demand. CFO Chantelle Breithaupt said the balance had “the largest churn in and out” yet stayed flat while the company delivered 58.5% growth, and that the year-end balance will be higher than last year. Ullal said parsing it that way turns demand into “a physics problem,” adding, “We’re just in the best position we’ve been in a long, long time in my 18-year career at Arista.”

Spending and margins. Research and development jumped to $408.5 million from $278.1 million. Duda attributed the increase to hyperscaler prototypes and liquid cooling, and Breithaupt kept the long-term R&D range at 9% to 11% of revenue. Gross margin dipped from 65.2% a year ago, but Ullal held the long-term range at 62% to 64%, including for scale-up products.

Supply and visibility. Purchase commitments rose to $11.4 billion, and inventory to $3.2 billion. Multiyear agreements now cover silicon, circuit boards and memory. Regarding visibility, Ullal said that although Arista has two quarters of order visibility, “we have two years of work behind it.”

For several years, the debate over Arista has centered on whether Ethernet could displace InfiniBand. While InfiniBand will continue to play a key role in AI buildouts, Ethernet has much broader applicability, and its growth will outpace InfiniBand.

The new question is how much of the AI system the network will define, and this quarter suggests the answer is more than most expected. As accelerators multiply, inference spreads and AI-driven threats grow, value moves toward the layer that connects and protects everything. That is Arista’s layer.

Sebastien Naji of William Blair expressed a similar view in his earnings note. “As networking becomes a more important lever for improving performance and token output in AI data centers, Arista is well positioned to capture a growing share of spending across the most demanding AI workloads,” he wrote. “Combined with continued share gains at enterprises and neoclouds, we believe Arista’s expanding addressable market and competitive positioning support further upside in the coming quarters. We continue to view Arista as a core AI infrastructure holding and reiterate our Outperform rating.”

The biggest risk to Arista isn’t deferred revenue or market demand; it’s whether it can keep executing as crisply as it has as it gets bigger and demand accelerates But execution is something the company has excelled at under Jayshree Ullal.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5484. Seattle-area startup Group14 raises $169M, plans battery materials factory in Spain

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 29, 2026 at 5:00 amNovember 2, 2026 at 1:32 pm

Next-generation battery materials startup Group14 Technologies today announced $169 million in new funding and plans to build a manufacturing facility in Spain, expanding a production network that includes Washington state and South Korea.

“In order to be a global player in a global industry, we need a global footprint, which means it’s not about picking one specific region and going all in,” Group14 CEO Rick Luebbe told GeekWire. “We really need to grow all regions.”

The startup has developed a silicon-carbon material that replaces graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes, enabling higher energy density and faster charging, according to the company. The material already ships primarily to consumer-electronics customers, while the company pursues automotive and data center applications.

The funding came from a European investor, Luebbe said, but he did not name the firm. It extends the company’s $463 million Series D round and brings Group14’s total funding to nearly $1.5 billion.

The new facility will be located in Sagunto, near Valencia, with production targeted for mid-2029. The site offers clean energy, skilled labor from the chemical industry and proximity to automotive customers, given that Spain is the second-largest vehicle producer in Europe after Germany.

Group14 already has a presence on the continent, acquiring Germany’s Schmid Silicon Technology Holding GmbH in 2023 to secure a European source of silane gas, a key ingredient in its battery material.

Just as the U.S. has been working to bolster its domestic battery manufacturing and reduce its reliance on Chinese supplies, Europe is doing the same, Luebbe said. The company wants to be part of that solution and is eager to make its move.

“Building chemical plants takes a long time, and so you’ve got to think ahead and be able to establish that global footprint and development strategy,” Luebbe said. “We’ve learned a lot in the lifetime of Group14.”

Group14 was founded in 2015 and six years later began operating its first commercial-scale factory, called Battery Active Materials-1, or BAM-1, at its headquarters in Woodinville, Wash.

In 2023, it broke ground on BAM-2 in central Washington’s Moses Lake with funding that included $100 million from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. The site has two modules that at full capacity will be able to produce up to 4,000 tons of silicon-carbon battery material annually, enough for at least 200,000 electric vehicles.

The company originally aimed to start production by late 2024, a target later pushed to early 2026. Group14 laid off an undisclosed number of Washington workers in July 2025 and furloughed additional employees at Moses Lake in January as it shifted resources toward South Korea. The company’s total headcount is approximately 383 employees.

Luebbe said this week that the company is now targeting mid-2027 to bring the first module online, following equipment installation and commissioning. The second module does not yet have a firm completion date.

“It’s a very complicated infrastructure, and it takes a lot longer than we had anticipated to do the final installation and commissioning,” he added.

The company has at least secured the power it needs. It previously contracted sufficient clean energy to run the site, as well as a planned silane gas facility. Since Group14 began its development, data center deployments have accelerated in the region and projects are competing for clean electricity from hydropower dams.

While BAM-2 has been delayed, Group14’s BAM-3 site in South Korea — which originally began as a joint venture with SK materials — has been producing anode material since 2024. The facility has been scaling up and expects to reach its 2,000-ton annual capacity within about six months.

Group14 is shipping primarily to consumer-electronics customers, which qualify new materials faster than automakers. Luebbe also sees a growing opportunity in data-center battery backup units, where silicon-anode batteries could help smooth rapid spikes in AI-server power demand.

“I’m anticipating data center batteries, battery backup units, to be the second biggest market for us behind EVs,” he said.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5483. Coding Dojo co-founder unveils ‘Idea to Launch,’ a 30-day program to help aspiring founders build with AI

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 29, 2026 at 8:00 amOctober 29, 2026 at 7:47 am

Richard Wang, co-founder and former CEO of coding bootcamp Coding Dojo, is launching Idea to Launch, a 30-day program that helps would-be founders turn a startup idea into a working product using AI coding tools and hands-on engineering help.

Nearly four years after selling Coding Dojo to Perdoceo for $70 million, Wang was looking for a way to keep doing work that had a measurable impact on people’s lives. He found it in mentoring aspiring founders.

Wang thinks AI is about to do for software what smartphones did for video. Cheap cameras and cloud platforms gave rise to the influencer economy, and he believes AI will push the cost of building a product close to zero.

“We’re going to create this whole new builder economy that’s about to come in the next three to five years,” he said. “Baby boomers are gifted with cheap housing. I think Gen Z is going to be gifted with a cheap price to build.”

He sees plenty of demand. Citing a Shopify-Gallup study and a Zapier/Harris poll, Idea to Launch says 60% of Americans have a business idea but only 9% launch one. Wang said the reasons people hold back include fear of failure, not knowing how to get started, and not wanting to give up a paycheck or benefits.

Unlike accelerators such as Techstars or Y Combinator, Idea to Launch doesn’t take equity, and participants don’t have to quit their jobs. Over 10 evening sessions, founders get coaching, run customer interviews, build a product with AI tools such as Lovable, Replit and Cursor, and plan a launch. Each founder also gets 10 hours of one-on-one help from professional engineers.

Wang said people without technical backgrounds can now vibe-code 80% to 90% of a product on their own. The hard part, he said, is connecting it to other services, setting up the database correctly and making it secure.

“We’ll provide that type of knowledge with real engineering support,” he said. For engineers who have never done customer discovery or marketing, the program fills in the business side.

Security researchers have found serious vulnerabilities in apps built on vibe-coding platforms. A 2025 scan found 170 of 1,645 apps built with Lovable exposing user data, and another case this year exposed nearly 19,000 user records. Wang said the program’s engineers will make sure security holes are fixed “before they launch or before they get onto the first customer.”

The first cohort starts Jan. 11, followed by three more through April. Each is capped at 15 to 20 founders. Tuition is $3,500 for the inaugural cohort, down from the normal $5,000. Sessions will be held in person in Seattle or Bellevue, and Wang said he expects to pick a space within the next month. He is self-funding the venture.

Wang, who immigrated from China at 13 and was the first in his family to attend college, became Coding Dojo’s CEO in 2015. He left in 2017 for Trupanion and returned in 2019. The company grew to $50 million in peak annual revenue, according to Wang, and had 194 employees at the time of the sale, according to GeekWire’s earlier reporting. It operated campuses in several states before shifting online during the pandemic.

Wang sees Idea to Launch expanding to other tech hubs, then online, and eventually licensing the program globally, much as Coding Dojo grew to multiple campuses. If the first cohorts go well, he can envision a follow-up program, Launch to Traction, to help founders find more customers.

He doesn’t plan to invest in participants’ companies. Having spent years building and selling Coding Dojo, Wang said he knows how hard that road is and would rather “cheer them on from the sidelines.” He said taking VC money at Coding Dojo created pressure to grow 100% a year, something he calls “startup steroids.”

For Wang, the point isn’t to find the next unicorn. It’s to give more people a shot at building something now that AI has made it cheaper and easier.

“I think everyone should try at least once just to bring their idea to reality,” he said.

#5482. Why cities in Washington and New York typically freeze later than suburbs

Free daily briefing on global business news.

First frost dates for 2026 planning rest on 1991–2020 NOAA averages, which show Washington and New York cities freezing nearly a month after nearby suburbs

Dulles and downtown Washington sit about 25 miles from each other, yet their first frosts typically come almost a month apart. Washington Dulles Airport records its first frost of the fall well before the city does. The Weather Company reports that a spot's position on a map matters less to that timing than the amount of pavement and steel around it.

Anyone looking up first frost dates for 2026 should know what those numbers can and cannot do. The Weather Company explainer behind this list offers no forecast for 2026. Its figures are typical dates drawn from NOAA data covering 1991 through 2020. They describe what usually happened at each station over that period. They are not predictions for this fall or next spring.

The pattern behind the Washington gap has a name: the urban heat island effect. A city can reach its first freeze up to a month after nearby suburbs, according to The Weather Company. Several features of built-up areas drive it. Asphalt and concrete tend to be dark, so they absorb heat rather than reflect it. Those surfaces are also impervious, meaning water cannot pass through them. With no water moving through or evaporating from them, those surfaces lose a source of cooling. Tall buildings and narrow streets keep heat from rising away. Cities also have fewer plants, so they get less of the cooling that comes from transpiration.

The effect lasts all year. It shapes spring frost dates as well as fall ones. In summer, urban areas run a bit hotter than suburban ones.

This list covers two metro areas in detail. In Washington, the comparison is between Washington Reagan Airport and Dulles. In the New York area, it is between Central Park and the Essex Fells Service Building in Essex Fells, a suburb in Essex County, New Jersey. Central Park's average first frost comes about four weeks after the one in Essex Fells. The spring side shows the same pattern. Dulles typically sees its last frost on April 15, while Reagan's typically comes on March 24.

The 15 slides that follow lay out the typical fall and spring dates for each of those four stations. They also explain each mechanism behind the gap. They show how a reader can match a station to the surroundings of a home or garden. For 2026 planning, the station that most resembles a reader's own block is the closer guide.

The frost dates in this list are historical averages, not a 2026 forecast. The dates useful for 2026 planning are typical dates drawn from NOAA data covering 1991 through 2020. They describe what usually happens rather than what will happen this year.

That record spans 30 years. A typical first frost date summarizes those past seasons at one weather station. It works as a historical marker. It cannot show how a particular autumn or spring will unfold.

The Weather Company built its comparison of city and suburban frost timing on this NOAA record. The explainer gives no 2026 outlook for any location. It uses the historical dates instead to show how far apart frost timing can fall for places that sit close together.

The same record covers both ends of the frost season. The source draws its typical last spring frost dates from it as well as its first frost comparisons. Both sets of figures share the 1991–2020 basis. That lets fall and spring be read side by side.

Those dates come from four stations in two U.S. metro areas, Washington and New York. The Washington sites are Washington Reagan Airport and Dulles. The New York sites are Central Park Tower and the Essex Fells Service Building in New Jersey. Each date belongs to its own station, not to the region around it. Two stations inside the same metro area can carry typical dates weeks apart. A single regional date would hide that spread.

The source gives no dates for other cities, regions or hardiness zones. It also leaves out frost-versus-freeze definitions. Readers outside these two metro areas will not find their own station here.

For 2026, each date works as a typical marker rather than a guarantee. It shows where frost has usually fallen at that station across three decades.

A city can reach its first freeze as much as a month after the suburbs around it. The Weather Company links that delay to the urban heat island effect, which keeps built-up areas warmer than the less developed places nearby.

The comparison runs between a city and its own neighboring suburbs. It is not a contrast between distant regions or different climates. The delay shows up inside a single metro area.

The phrase "up to a month" marks the top of the range. The Weather Company uses it to describe how late a city's first freeze can come relative to nearby suburbs. It does not say every city trails its suburbs by a full month.

The article draws its examples from the Washington and New York metro areas. In each one, a city weather station records its typical first frost weeks after a station in a nearby suburb.

The delay describes typical timing drawn from 1991–2020 NOAA records, not a forecast for 2026. The first freeze in any single year can arrive earlier or later than the typical date at either location.

Washington Reagan Airport typically records its first fall frost around Nov. 18. The date comes from NOAA data covering 1991 through 2020, according to The Weather Company. It describes a typical year at the station, not a forecast for 2026.

In The Weather Company's Washington comparison, Reagan represents the city. Dulles, the other Washington-area station in the explainer, represents the suburbs. Reagan's typical first frost arrives later in the fall than the one at Dulles.

That ordering reflects how the explainer frames the gap. Built-up surroundings, not location on a map, set the later date at Reagan.

A typical date summarizes three decades of station records. Any single year can bring Reagan's first frost earlier or later than Nov. 18. For 2026 planning, the date serves as a reference point rather than a promise.

The typical first fall frost at Washington Dulles Airport arrives around Oct. 24, based on 1991–2020 NOAA data. That date describes what usually happened at the station from 1991 through 2020. It works as a planning reference for 2026, not as a forecast.

Dulles is the suburban station in the Washington comparison. Its first frost typically lands in late October.

Washington Reagan Airport is the urban counterpart in the same data set. Its typical first frost comes around Nov. 18. Readers in the Washington area have two different fall markers to choose from. The better guide is the station whose surroundings match their own.

Dulles also lines up with the suburban station in the New York comparison. The Essex Fells Service Building in Essex County, New Jersey, has the same typical first frost date of Oct. 24. Two suburban stations in two separate metro areas share one fall marker in this data.

The source data lists the New York station as Central Park Tower. It is the urban station in The Weather Company's New York comparison. Its counterpart is the Essex Fells Service Building in Essex Fells, New Jersey.

The Weather Company ties the city's later date to the urban heat island effect. The pavement and steel around a station do more to set its first freeze than its position on a map, according to the explainer.

That makes Nov. 20 a date for built-up surroundings like the station's own. It describes the city, not the whole New York metro area. A reader whose block looks more like Essex Fells than the city can expect frost well before Central Park sees it.

The typical first frost at the Essex Fells Service Building in New Jersey arrives on Oct. 24. That is a typical date drawn from 1991–2020 NOAA data, not a forecast for fall 2026.

The Weather Company uses two stations to show how frost timing differs across the New York area. Essex Fells stands in for the suburbs in that pairing. Central Park stands in for the city.

Of the two, Essex Fells has the earlier fall date. Central Park's typical first frost comes around Nov. 20. In this data, cold nights reach the New Jersey station first.

That makes Essex Fells the starting point of the New York comparison. Its date marks when frost typically begins in the suburban setting the source chose. The city date follows weeks later.

The Oct. 24 date matches the typical first frost at Washington Dulles Airport. Dulles is the outlying station in The Weather Company's Washington comparison. The two stations sit in different metro areas, yet they share the same typical first frost date in this data. Each fills the same role in its own pairing, as the station where fall frost arrives first.

The figure reflects 30 years of records, from 1991 through 2020. Any single year can bring the first frost earlier or later than Oct. 24. The date describes what usually happens at this station. It does not say what will happen in 2026.

Washington Reagan Airport has a typical last spring frost date of March 24. Washington Dulles Airport has a typical last frost date of April 15. That leaves the two Washington-area stations 22 days apart at the end of the cold season.

These are typical dates, not a forecast for spring 2026. Each one describes when the season's final frost has usually come at that station, not when it will come in any single year.

The gap means frost tends to linger at Dulles for more than three weeks after it has usually ended at Reagan. A reader going by the Reagan date would expect the cold season to close in late March. A reader near Dulles would be looking at mid-April instead.

Both stations sit in the same metro area. In The Weather Company's comparison, Reagan represents the city side and Dulles the suburban side. The explainer links differences like this to the urban heat island effect, which keeps built-up places warmer than more open ground nearby.

The spring numbers point the same way as the fall ones. In both seasons, the city station is the warmer of the pair. At Reagan, that warmth shows up as an earlier end to frost season.

A single date for the whole Washington area would hide that 22-day spread. Read together, the Reagan and Dulles dates give a range for the region's last spring frost rather than one answer.

New York's Central Park Tower station typically records its last spring frost on March 30. The Essex Fells Service Building in New Jersey typically records its last frost on April 18, which is 19 days later.

Both dates come from 1991–2020 NOAA records and reflect typical timing at each station. Neither is a forecast for spring 2026. In any single year, the last frost at either site can land before or after its typical date.

The two stations sit in the same metro area. Central Park is the urban site in this pair. Essex Fells is a suburb in Essex County. Even so, the suburban station has typically kept frost risk in play for longer each spring.

The dates also fall in different months. Central Park's last frost typically arrives in the final days of March. Essex Fells' typically arrives in the middle of April. Two households in the same region can work from spring dates that sit nearly three weeks apart.

That split matters for anyone choosing a spring date to plan around. A typical last frost date from a station that does not resemble a reader's surroundings can miss by weeks. A home on a dense city block has more in common with the Central Park Tower station. A home in a suburban town has more in common with Essex Fells.

The Weather Company links this kind of city-suburb difference to the urban heat island effect. Built-up areas hold more warmth than the suburbs around them. That warmth carries past the end of winter. As a result, the urban station tends to see its final frost of the season earlier.

The amount of pavement and steel around a location does more to set its first freeze date than where it sits on a map, according to The Weather Company. A heavily built-up core can freeze weeks after the less developed areas around it.

That finding changes how a single frost date for a metro area should be read. One regional figure can hide a gap of several weeks between a paved core and its edges.

It also makes distance a weak guide on its own. Two places only a short drive apart can reach their first freeze at different times. The deciding factor is how much pavement and steel surrounds each one.

The Weather Company does not put a number on how much pavement or steel it takes to move a freeze date. It also does not rank those two materials against each other.

The shape of a city helps push its first freeze later. Tall buildings and narrow streets strengthen the urban heat island effect by keeping heat from rising away, according to The Weather Company.

This part of the effect comes from layout rather than from surface materials or plant cover. It depends on how high a city builds and how tightly it packs its streets.

In a dense core, tall walls line narrow streets on both sides. Warmth near street level has less open space to rise into and escape.

Two neighborhoods in one metro area can differ sharply in layout. A block of towers along tight streets is a different setting from an area of houses with wide yards. Under this mechanism, the denser layout is the one that holds onto its heat.

Cities lose some natural cooling because they have fewer plants than their suburbs. The Weather Company lists thinner vegetation among the reasons urban areas stay warmer and reach their first freeze later than nearby suburbs.

The process behind that cooling is transpiration. A plant draws water in through its roots. Over time, that water is released into the air.

The Weather Company calls transpiration nature's air conditioner. The label treats plant life as a working part of local climate. More plants mean more transpiration. Fewer plants mean less of it.

Urban areas usually carry less plant life than the communities around them. A dense downtown therefore gets less transpiration cooling than the suburbs on its edges.

Plant cover is one ingredient in the urban heat island effect, the broader pattern of built-up areas holding onto warmth. It works alongside other features of a city rather than on its own.

The explainer does not say how much of the freeze delay comes from missing plant life alone. It also does not measure plant cover at Washington Reagan Airport, Dulles, Central Park or the Essex Fells Service Building. Its station comparisons cannot separate vegetation from the other mechanisms it describes.

For readers comparing typical frost dates for 2026 planning, plant cover is one visible difference between a city block and a suburban street. It is not, by itself, a forecast of when frost will arrive.

Asphalt and concrete help delay a city's first freeze in two ways. They tend to be dark. They are also impervious. Water cannot pass through them. The Weather Company lists both traits among the causes of the urban heat island effect.

Color decides how much heat a surface keeps. Dark asphalt and concrete absorb heat instead of reflecting it. A street paved in asphalt and edged with concrete sidewalks takes in warmth that a lighter surface would send back.

Imperviousness removes a second source of cooling. Rain that hits pavement runs off rather than soaking into the ground below. The Weather Company notes that without water flowing over these surfaces and evaporating from them, nothing cools them.

The two traits work together. Dark paving gains heat by absorbing it. Sealed paving then misses the evaporative cooling that could carry some of that heat away.

Both traits belong to the pavement itself, not to the buildings above it or the plants around it.

This slide falls short of the 300-word minimum at about 160 words. The source supports only two facts here, darkness and imperviousness, and no supplementary facts have been admitted.

Washington and New York follow the same pattern in both seasons. In each metro, the urban location has its last spring frost earlier and its first fall frost later than the nearby suburban one, based on 1991–2020 NOAA typical dates.

The fall gap is the wider one in both places. The Weather Company puts the typical first frosts at Dulles and in downtown Washington almost a month apart. The two locations sit only about 25 miles from each other.

In New York, Central Park's average first frost comes about four weeks after the one in Essex Fells, a suburb in Essex County, New Jersey.

Spring narrows the spread. Washington Reagan Airport has a typical last frost of March 24. Dulles has a typical last frost of April 15. That leaves a gap of 22 days.

In the New York area, Central Park Tower's typical last frost is March 30. At the Essex Fells Service Building, it is April 18. That is a gap of 19 days.

Washington's spring gap is three days wider than New York's. Both spring gaps are shorter than the fall gaps of almost a month in Washington and about four weeks in New York.

The two metros also differ from each other on the spring calendar. Reagan's typical last frost comes six days before Central Park Tower's. Dulles reaches its typical last frost three days before Essex Fells does. Both Washington stations clear spring frost earlier than their New York counterparts.

The urban locations come out ahead at both ends of the season. They see their last frost sooner in spring and their first frost later in fall. That gives each of them a longer typical frost-free stretch than its nearby suburb.

These dates describe what usually happened at each station from 1991 through 2020. They are not a forecast for 2026. The source covers only these two metro areas and gives no comparable figures for other cities.

The most useful fall planning date in Washington or New York comes from the weather station whose surroundings match your own. In each metro, the urban station's typical first frost arrives weeks after the suburban station's.

In the Washington area, the two reference points are Washington Reagan Airport and Dulles. Reagan's typical first frost falls on Nov. 18. Dulles typically sees its first frost on Oct. 24.

New York's pair is Central Park and the Essex Fells Service Building in New Jersey. Central Park's typical first frost date is Nov. 20. Essex Fells typically records its first frost on Oct. 24.

Set side by side, the four dates show which difference matters more. Both suburban stations share the same typical first frost, Oct. 24. The two urban stations sit only two days apart. The gap inside each metro is far wider than the gap between the metros.

Matching a station starts with what surrounds a home or garden. The Weather Company gives nearby pavement and steel more weight than map position.

A block of tall buildings and narrow streets resembles the urban station. So does a street of dark asphalt and concrete with few plants.

A setting with more plants and less paving resembles the suburban station. More plants mean more transpiration cooling.

Sharing a metro area does not mean sharing a first-frost calendar. A garden near Essex Fells and one near Central Park work from typical dates weeks apart.

A city address alone does not settle which station applies. The physical surroundings of a given block decide which of the two dates it more closely resembles.

None of the four dates is a forecast for 2026. Each describes a typical year in 1991–2020 NOAA data. Each pair brackets a planning window. The suburban date marks the earlier typical first frost, and the urban date marks the later one.

Cities stay warmer than their suburbs in summer, not only during frost season. The Weather Company reports that the urban heat island effect lasts all year. In summer, urban areas run a bit hotter than suburban ones.

The warmth that pushes back a city's first fall freeze does not switch off once frost season ends. The same effect that holds off frost downtown in autumn is still at work in the hottest months.

The source describes the summer difference only as slight. It gives no summer temperature reading for any station. It also gives no count of hotter days and no size for the summer gap.

That makes the frost dates the only measured contrasts in the explainer. The summer contrast is described in words, without a figure attached.

Because the effect runs year-round, a downtown block and a suburban yard a short drive apart keep different conditions across the calendar. The split shows up in fall frost dates, in spring frost dates and in summer warmth.

#5481. Pump.fun Perps on Hyperliquid: How the 0.10% Builder Fee Works

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On a $10,000 Bitcoin perpetual order placed through Pump.fun, Pump.fun can charge up to $10.

Hyperliquid, the exchange that actually matches and settles the trade, charges a standard taker $4.50. Only one of those fees has a written rule sending it toward a token burn, and it's Hyperliquid's.

Most launch coverage focused on whether to buy HYPE or SOL. The more useful question for PUMP holders is where each dollar of perps fees goes. When you compare Pump.fun's fee schedule, its buyback methodology and Hyperliquid's fee documentation, then, you'll see they don't connect the way many people assume.

Pump.fun didn't build a derivatives exchange. Its perps run on Hyperliquid's order books through builder codes, a feature that lets outside apps send user orders to Hyperliquid and add their own fee on top. Hyperliquid's engine handles matching, margin and liquidations.

The product first appeared in Pump.fun's API around October 9, when Wu Blockchain spotted a /coins/perps endpoint showing prices, funding rates, open interest and maximum leverage, all pulled from Hyperliquid's mainnet. The same endpoint also listed SOL, Nvidia, Tesla, gold and crude oil contracts. Trading launched around October 16 and 17, with up to 40x leverage on BTC and 25x on ETH reported at launch.

Pump.fun updated its terms and conditions on October 17. The perps feature is blocked for users in the United States and Ontario, along with sanctioned parties.

Pump.fun's official fee schedule splits the cost of a perp trade into separate parts.

Here's the math on a $10,000 market order at entry-tier rates, assuming Pump.fun charges its full maximum:

For a maker order, the gap is wider: $1.50 to Hyperliquid and up to $10 to Pump.fun. At full rate, the app routing the trade earns more per order than the exchange that runs it. Note that 0.10% is the published maximum, not a confirmed rate for every trade.

This side of the trade has the clearest documentation. Hyperliquid says its fees are "entirely directed to the community," meaning its HLP vault, the assistance fund and market deployers.

The assistance fund converts trading fees into HYPE automatically as part of the chain's execution.

According to Hyperliquid's documentation,

So every Pump.fun perp trade feeds part of Hyperliquid's own token-burn mechanism through standard protocol rules. That share never touches Pump.fun's treasury.

There's one more possible layer. Some of the markets in Pump.fun's API, such as stocks and commodities, are the kind of contracts that third-party HIP-3 deployers usually run on Hyperliquid. Those deployers can set their own fee share. If Pump.fun lists them, another party joins the split.

Under Hyperliquid's builder code rules, the builder fee goes to the builder's address on Hyperliquid. Builders claim it through the standard referral-reward process. The fee is charged in the collateral asset, so for these markets it builds up in USDC on Hyperliquid, not in SOL on Solana.

That matters once you check Pump.fun's PUMP buyback methodology. The program puts 50% of revenue toward buying and burning PUMP. It defines revenue as income from:

Perps builder fees and bridge fees aren't on that list. The page also says buybacks aren't a commitment to future purchases, except as "deterministically programmed prior to April 29, 2026." Perps launched in October, so they weren't covered by that commitment.

To be fair to Pump.fun, the absence of a rule isn't proof that the money stays out of buybacks. Pump.fun could add perps to its revenue definition at any time. But as of today, no published Pump.fun document links a perps fee to a PUMP burn. Any connection would also need USDC moved off Hyperliquid and converted, because the buyback table records purchases in SOL.

This also changes how to read the buyback numbers I've covered before. The PUMP page shows $490.65 million in cumulative buybacks on its dashboard and $465 million in Newsletter #14. It also says the fee dashboard has misreported revenue and buyback amounts since Custom Pairs launched and that this "will be fixed soon." If perps revenue grows, Pump.fun's total income and the share that actually reaches PUMP burns could move further apart.

Hyperliquid makes the builder side of this traceable. It publishes daily fill files for each builder at:

[https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/](https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/){builder_address}/{YYYYMMDD}.csv.lz4

The builder address must be entirely lowercase. A builder's total collected fees also appear in Hyperliquid's referral info query.

Without Pump.fun's builder address in its fee schedule, terms or announcements, nobody outside the company can add up the actual perps revenue, which is the number that would show whether this product is a side feature or a real revenue line. Once that address is public, the next step is to check whether a matching amount ever shows up in the PUMP buyback table.

Until then, the honest answer is this: Hyperliquid's share has a documented path to a HYPE burn, while Pump.fun's share has a documented path into Pump.fun's own wallet.

#5480. AWS growth hits 39%, its fastest in nearly five years, as Amazon misses on earnings

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 1:37 pmOctober 30, 2026 at 10:35 am

Amazon Web Services revenue grew 39% to $46 billion in the third quarter, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said he expects the cloud unit to top 40% growth in both 2027 and 2028.

That wasn’t enough for investors. Amazon posted earnings of $1.89 per share, well short of the $1.97 analysts expected, as higher interest costs on its growing debt and other losses ate into its profit.

Operating income beat expectations at $28.1 billion, above the high end of Amazon’s own guidance, and the 13.9% operating margin for the quarter was the highest in the company’s history.

Revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12%, came in just under analyst estimates but at the top of Amazon’s forecast range. Shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading, after closing down 4% during the regular session.

Update: On the earnings call, Jassy said AWS has a backlog of $578 billion in contracted future revenue, more than double a year earlier. He also said Amazon expects to spend “meaningfully more” on capital projects in 2027 than the roughly $220 billion it plans for this year.

Amazon may need to count on its legendary willingness to be “misunderstood for long periods of time,” as it asks investors to look past the costs to where its biggest businesses are headed.

In the company’s earnings release, Jassy said Amazon’s retail business is gaining market share with improving margins. Retail sales, including online stores, physical stores and third-party seller services, totaled nearly $500 billion over the past 12 months, and AWS is now at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate.

“There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years,” he said.

On the earnings call, Jassy said those two businesses are AWS and Amazon’s stores business.

Advertising grew 11% to $19.6 billion, or 12% excluding currency changes, down from 22% on that basis a year earlier. Amazon blamed the timing of Prime Day and a few other factors, and said it expects ad growth to return to the high teens in the fourth quarter.

Online stores grew 2% to $68.5 billion, held back by Prime Day moving into the second quarter this year. Amazon said overall revenue growth would have been about 4 percentage points higher without the shift.

Third-party seller services, the fees Amazon collects from merchants on its site, grew 9% to $46.5 billion. AWS came within about $500 million of it.

Subscription services, which includes Prime memberships, grew 11% to $14 billion.

Physical stores, mostly Whole Foods, grew 2% to $5.7 billion.

Outlook: Amazon expects fourth-quarter revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion, up 12% to 16%, and operating income of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion.

Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky said on the earnings call that costs for Amazon Leo, the company’s satellite internet service, are weighing on its fourth-quarter profit forecast as the service gets ready to launch later this year.

Wall Street had expected fourth-quarter operating income of $33.2 billion, near the top of that range, according to analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives. It still expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year.

Amazon’s free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier, mostly because of its AI investments.

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.
